---

**Fair Market Rent to Be Deemed at 4% of Property Value**  
The Finance Bill 2025 introduces a presumptive rent calculation for commercial properties, proposing that the fair market rent shall be deemed to be at least 4% of the FBR-notified value of the property. This initiative is designed to counter the under-reporting of rental income. However, where actual rent is lower, taxpayers may present credible documentary evidence to the Commissioner to substantiate the declared amount. This ensures a balance between enforcement and fairness in rental income disclosure.

**10% Disallowance for Purchases from Non-NTN Holders**  
To promote documentation and expand the tax base, the Bill proposes disallowing 10% of expenditures incurred on purchases from persons not registered with an NTN. However, exceptions have been carved out, such as purchases of agricultural produce directly from growers and others notified by the FBR. The measure aims to shift commercial transactions toward registered and documented suppliers.

**50% Disallowance on Cash Sales Above Rs. 200,000**  
A strong disincentive is proposed for undocumented sales by disallowing 50% of expenses related to sales where payment per invoice exceeds Rs. 200,000 and is made in cash or through non-banking modes. The provision is intended to reduce cash-based transactions and promote the use of traceable banking channels.

**Depreciation Disallowed on Non-Withheld Purchases**  
To reinforce withholding tax compliance, the Bill proposes that depreciation shall not be allowed on assets acquired without deducting and depositing the applicable withholding tax under Sections 152 or 153. Such assets will be excluded from the depreciation base, discouraging non-compliant asset acquisitions.

**Group Relief Limited to Companies under Normal Tax Regime**  
Group relief will no longer be available to companies taxed under minimum or special regimes. The relief will now be limited strictly to companies taxed under the standard corporate tax structure, aligning the benefit with entities bearing the full corporate tax burden.

**Tax Credit on Housing Loans Reintroduced under Section 63A**  
The Bill revives the tax credit for profit on debt for loans taken to purchase or construct a single residential house (up to 2,500 sq. ft.) or a flat (up to 2,000 sq. ft.). Available once in 15 years per individual, the loan must be secured from scheduled banks or eligible financial institutions, offering targeted relief for first-time homeowners.

**Economic Restrictions for Non-Filers Reinstated**  
To push undocumented individuals into the tax net, the Bill proposes renewed restrictions on non-filers. Ineligible persons will be barred from registering high-value vehicles, purchasing immovable property beyond prescribed limits, operating unrestricted bank accounts, or transacting in securities, reinforcing compliance through transactional limitations.

**Recreational Clubs Excluded from NPO Status**  
Recreational clubs charging membership fees exceeding Rs. 1 million will lose their status as Non-Profit Organizations (NPOs) under Section 2(36). The Bill also proposes taxing income earned from goods or services provided to members, ensuring that profit-making entities are appropriately taxed.

**NPOs Under Table I Made Subject to Section 100C**  
Institutions previously enjoying unconditional exemption under Table I of Clause 66, Part I, Second Schedule, will now be subject to the compliance regime of Section 100C. The merger of Tables I and II ensures a uniform governance and reporting framework for all tax-exempt NPOs.

**Amortization Period for Intangibles Shortened to 15 Years**  
The maximum period of amortization for intangible assets with indefinite useful life is proposed to be reduced from 25 to 15 years. This change aligns with global accounting norms and allows quicker recognition of such expenses, improving tax planning flexibility.

**Inter-Head Adjustment of Business Losses Reversed**  
The 2021 relaxation allowing set-off of business losses against income from property is being withdrawn. The Bill restores the pre-2021 position, maintaining the integrity of income heads and preventing unintended revenue loss through cross-head adjustments.

**Expanded Credit Scope for Sindh Coal Mining Projects**  
Coal mining ventures in Sindh will no longer be required to exclusively supply power generation companies to claim 100% tax credit. The proposed amendment permits sales to multiple sectors, encouraging broader commercial viability without compromising tax benefits.

**Minimum Tax Carryforward Period Reduced to Two Years**  
The carryforward period for minimum tax paid in excess of normal tax liability is proposed to be reduced from three years to two years. This change incentivizes timely adjustment of tax credits and reinforces disciplined tax planning.

**Digital Payments Recognized for High-Value Asset Acquisitions**  
To promote transparency and reduce the use of cash in large transactions, digital payments are now explicitly accepted for purchases of immovable properties exceeding Rs. 5 million and other assets over Rs. 1 million, alongside crossed cheques and other banking instruments.

**Time Limit for Amended Assessments under Section 122 Removed**  
The 120-day statutory time limit (extendable by 90 days) for issuing amended orders under Section 122 is proposed to be abolished. While this provides the FBR more administrative flexibility, it may also introduce prolonged uncertainty for taxpayers.

**No Appeal Effect Order Required if Assessment Upheld**  
Where an appellate authority fully upholds the original tax order, no separate appeal effect order will be issued. However, if any modification is made, a revised appeal effect order will be necessary. This procedural clarification streamlines post-appeal implementation.

**Appeals Before CIR(A) Allowed Without Minimum Tax Threshold**  
The Bill removes the restriction requiring a minimum tax amount to file appeals before the Commissioner (Appeals). Taxpayers may now appeal any assessment and can choose to bypass CIR(A) and approach the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR) directly.

**Time for High Court Reference Extended to 60 Days**  
The timeline for filing a reference before the High Court has been extended from 30 to 60 days. The scope, however, is now limited to pure questions of law, ensuring greater legal clarity and adequate time for preparation.

**ADR Committees May Be Reconstituted for SOEs**  
In cases involving State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), if an ADR Committee fails to decide within 60 days, the FBR may reappoint a new committee with a fresh 60-day deadline. This mechanism aims to avoid indefinite delays and ensure resolution certainty.

**FBR-Bank Data Exchange Enabled for Tax Analytics**  
The Bill authorizes FBR to share taxpayer profiling data with banks to verify alignment between declared income and actual banking activity. Banks will be required to report discrepancies. This override of banking secrecy laws strengthens data-driven tax enforcement.

**Condonation of Delay Capped at Two Years**  
FBR’s discretionary authority to condone delays in filing or compliance will now be limited to a maximum of two years. Beyond this, only a specially constituted committee may grant condonation, and only in cases involving material revenue implications.

**Higher Tax on Cash Withdrawals by Non-Filers**  
The advance tax rate on cash withdrawals exceeding Rs. 50,000 in a day by non-filers is proposed to increase from 0.6% to 0.8%. This amendment further disincentivizes non-filing and promotes migration to the documented economy.

**25% Tax Rebate for Educators Restored Retroactively**  
The long-demanded tax relief for teachers and researchers is proposed to be reinstated with retrospective effect from July 1, 2022. Full-time educators at recognized institutions will again enjoy a 25% reduction in tax on salary income until Tax Year 2025.

This measure aims to curb under-reporting of rental income by property owners. Changes Relating to Disallowance of Purchases from Non-NTN Holders

This provision excludes purchases of agricultural produce directly from growers and others as notified by the FBR. The move emphasizes the importance of dealing with registered suppliers to maintain tax compliance.
Changes Relating to Disallowance on Cash-Based Sales Above Rs. 200,000
A significant compliance measure in the Bill disallows 50% of expenses related to sales where payments exceeding Rs. 200,000 per invoice are received in cash or through non-banking channels. This proposed change intends to reduce untraceable cash transactions and promote the use of banking and digital payment systems, ensuring improved transparency and audit trails.
Changes Relating to Depreciation Blocked if Tax Not Withheld
To enforce withholding compliance, the Bill proposes that depreciation will not be allowed on assets acquired from sellers if the required withholding tax under Section 152 (non-resident) or Section 153 (resident) is not deducted and deposited. Such non-compliant assets will be excluded from the depreciation base, thereby discouraging tax evasion through non-withholding.
Changes Relating to Group Relief Eligibility Tightened
Under the proposed changes, companies taxed under minimum tax or special tax regimes will no longer be eligible for group relief. Only companies whose income is taxed under the normal corporate tax regime may claim group loss adjustments. This amendment ensures that the benefit of group relief remains limited to entities operating under the standard tax framework.
Changes Relating to Tax Credit on Housing Loans Reintroduced
The Bill reintroduces a tax credit under a new Section 63A for profit on debt related to loans obtained for purchasing or constructing a residential house (up to 2,500 sq. ft.) or a flat (up to 2,000 sq. ft.). The loan must be from scheduled banks or other qualifying institutions. This credit is available once in 15 years for a single house or flat, encouraging homeownership while capping repeat claims.
Changes Relating to Economic Restrictions for Ineligible Persons
To strengthen the documentation regime, the Bill reintroduces economic restrictions for "ineligible persons" who have not filed tax returns or do not have sufficient declared resources. Such individuals will be barred from registering vehicles, purchasing immovable properties beyond specified values, transacting in securities, or operating unrestricted bank accounts. These measures aim to push more individuals into the tax net through transactional enforcement.
Changes Relating to Recreational Clubs Lose NPO Status
Recreational clubs collecting more than Rs. 1 million as membership fees will be excluded from the definition of a Non-Profit Organization (NPO) under Section 2(36). The Bill also proposes bringing such clubs under the scope of taxation on income from the sale of goods or services to members. This change ensures that commercial activities masquerading as non-profits are brought within the tax fold.
Changes Relating to Table 1 NPOs Now Subject to Conditions
The exemption structure for NPOs under Clause 66 of Part I, Second Schedule, is being rationalized. Institutions earlier listed under Table 1 who enjoyed unconditional exemptions will now be subjected to the compliance requirements of Section 100C. This merger of Tables 1 and 2 creates a uniform standard, requiring all listed entities to meet governance and compliance conditions to avail tax exemption.
Changes Relating to Faster Amortization for Intangibles
The period of amortization for intangibles with no definite useful life is being reduced from 25 years to 15 years. This adjustment allows for quicker recognition of intangible asset write-offs and aligns more closely with global accounting practices. It provides businesses with improved flexibility in tax planning involving intellectual property and similar intangible assets.
Changes Relating to Set-Off of Business Loss Against Property Reversed
The 2021 relaxation that allowed taxpayers to set off business losses against income from property is being rolled back. The proposed amendment reverts to the pre-2021 rule, disallowing such inter-head adjustments. This reinstatement aims to maintain the integrity of income classification and avoid potential revenue losses due to cross-head adjustments.
Changes Relating to Broader Credit for Sindh Coal Projects
The Bill removes the restriction that tax credit for coal mining projects in Sindh is available only when coal is exclusively supplied to power generation companies. Now, such projects may supply coal to multiple sectors while continuing to enjoy the 100% tax credit, promoting diversification without tax penalties.
Changes Relating to Minimum Tax Carryforward Period Cut
Currently, minimum tax paid in excess of normal tax liability can be carried forward for three years. The Bill proposes to reduce this period to two years. This amendment limits the time within which businesses can utilize such minimum tax, encouraging efficient tax planning and timely utilization of available credits.
Changes Relating to Digital Payments Now Allowed for Large Assets
To promote digitization and transparency in high-value transactions, digital payments have been formally accepted as a valid mode of payment for acquiring immovable properties over Rs. 5 million or other assets over Rs. 1 million. This addition complements existing modes like crossed cheques and demand drafts and strengthens auditability.

Changes Relating to Time Limits on Amendments Removed
The statutory time limit of 120 days to pass amended orders under Section 122 is proposed to be withdrawn. Previously, this period could only be extended by 90 days. The removal of this cap provides more flexibility to tax authorities but may raise concerns about prolonged uncertainty for taxpayers.
Changes Relating to Appeal Effects Streamlined
The Bill proposes that no separate appeal effect order is required where an appellate authority fully upholds the original tax order. However, if the appellate body modifies or partially sets aside the order, a revised appeal effect order will be necessary to determine revised tax liability. This update aims to streamline enforcement while maintaining due process.
Changes Relating to Appeals Allowed Regardless of Tax Amount
The restriction that appeals before CIR(A) could only be filed if the tax amount met a certain threshold is being abolished. Taxpayers may now file appeals before CIR(A) irrespective of the tax amount involved, and they may opt to bypass CIR(A) and file directly with ATIR. This restores the taxpayer's right to appeal and expedites access to justice.
Changes Relating to ⬆️ High Court Reference Period Extended to 60 Days
The time allowed for filing a reference before the High Court has been extended from 30 to 60 days. However, the scope of such references is now limited strictly to pure questions of law, excluding mixed questions of law and fact. This change ensures better preparation time for taxpayers and aligns with appellate hierarchy logic.

Changes Relating to ADR Reappointment for SOEs
If an Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) Committee fails to resolve a case involving a State-Owned Enterprise (SOE) within 60 days, the FBR will be empowered to reconstitute a new committee. The reappointed committee will be bound to deliver its decision within another 60 days. This mechanism seeks to ensure timely closure of ADR proceedings.
Changes Relating to FBR-Bank Data Exchange for Tax Detection
FBR will be allowed to share algorithmic profiles of taxpayers with commercial banks to verify declared income and banking activity. Banks will be required to report discrepancies in declared vs. actual data. This provision overrides all banking secrecy laws and is aimed solely at improving tax compliance using digital analytics.
Changes Relating to Condonation of Delay Capped at Two Years
To align with judicial precedents, the FBR’s discretionary power to condone delays will now be capped at a total period of two years. Further condonation will only be possible through a specially notified committee, and only in cases where substantial revenue losses to the exchequer are involved.
Changes Relating to Cash Withdrawal Tax Raised for Non-Filers
The advance tax rate on daily cash withdrawals exceeding Rs. 50,000 by non-filers is proposed to be increased from 0.6% to 0.8%. This amendment further incentivizes taxpayers to get themselves listed on the Active Taxpayers List and move toward documented banking practices.
Changes Relating to 25% Tax Rebate Restored for Educators
The Finance Bill proposes to restore the 25% tax rebate for full-time teachers and researchers working in approved institutions, effective retroactively from July 1, 2022, and up to Tax Year 2025. This move reverses the earlier repeal of the rebate in 2022 and provides long-demanded relief to the academic sector.

---

**To:**  
The Honorable Federal Minister for Finance  
Ministry of Finance  
Government of Pakistan  
Islamabad

**Subject: Concerns on Proposed Amendment to Clause (66), Part I of Second Schedule – Request for Transitional Relief for Table I Institutions**

**Dear Sir,**

We write on behalf of institutions, foundations, societies, boards, trusts, and funds listed in *Table I of Clause (66), Part I of the Second Schedule* to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. These institutions have historically been granted unconditional income tax exemption due to their public utility, statutory nature, or established national repute. We respectfully submit our concerns regarding the proposed amendment in the Finance Bill 2025 that seeks to merge Table I and Table II and bring all such institutions within the scope of section 100C, thereby subjecting previously exempt entities to additional compliance conditions.

**Legislative Intent of Separate Classification**

The original bifurcation between Table I and Table II was deliberate and rooted in the legislative intent to distinguish between institutions based on their credibility and oversight. Table I comprised government-funded or highly reputable institutions—such as Abdul Sattar Edhi Foundation, Indus Hospital, The Citizens Foundation, the Privatization Commission, SECP, and the Supreme Court’s Water Conservation Account—deemed sufficiently vetted for unconditional exemption. Table II, by contrast, required compliance with section 100C to ensure legitimacy and proper use of tax-exempt status.

The current proposal to merge these tables undermines that distinction. Institutions with longstanding public service contributions and statutory mandates will now be treated on par with newly formed entities, disregarding the prior confidence Parliament placed in their governance and operations.

**Administrative and Compliance Implications**

The proposed amendment will result in significant administrative and compliance burdens for Table I institutions. Previously exempt by law, they will now be required to:

- **Obtain PCP Certification**, requiring a comprehensive review of governance, finances, and impact;
- **Seek NPO approval** under section 2(36) from the Commissioner of Inland Revenue, with detailed documentation;
- **Comply with section 100C conditions**, including annual return filing, withholding compliance, and capping administrative expenses at prescribed limits.

While we support transparency and good governance, these measures, when applied retroactively to established institutions, may disrupt operations and divert essential resources from public service delivery. Many of these organizations already function under government oversight or statutory accountability, rendering some of these compliance requirements duplicative. Furthermore, procedural delays in securing approvals may risk the lapse of their exemption status, with adverse financial and operational consequences.

**Request for Reasonable Transition Period**

If the proposed merger of Tables is enacted, we earnestly request a **phased transition period** to allow orderly compliance. A deferment until at least the close of **Tax Year 2026** would enable affected institutions to prepare and secure the necessary certifications and approvals without jeopardizing ongoing activities. This approach would be consistent with past practice—such as the phased application of NPO approval requirements for Table II institutions from July 2022 onward.

**Conclusion**

Table I institutions have long served as reliable partners to the State in critical areas such as healthcare, education, and social welfare. The previous legislative framework recognized this role through unconditional exemptions, fostering trust and enabling uninterrupted service delivery. While we respect the government’s efforts to harmonize and modernize tax laws, we urge that such reforms account for the unique status of these institutions and avoid imposing abrupt administrative challenges.

We therefore request your kind consideration to either maintain the exemption regime for vetted institutions or, alternatively, grant a sufficient transition period for compliance with the revised framework. We remain available for further engagement on this matter and reaffirm our commitment to public accountability and national development.

**Yours faithfully,**  
*On behalf of institutions listed under Table I of Clause (66), Part I of the Second Schedule*

We write on behalf of the various institutions, foundations, societies, boards, trusts, and funds listed in Table I of Clause (66), Part I of the Second Schedule of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. These “Table I” institutions have long enjoyed unconditional income tax exemptions by virtue of their listing in the law. We wish to respectfully convey our concerns about the proposed amendment in the Finance Bill 2025 that seeks to merge Table I and Table II of Clause 66 and subject previously exempt institutions to the conditions of section 100C of the Ordinance. We further seek your kind consideration for a reasonable transition period, should this amendment be enacted, to allow compliance without disrupting our vital public service activities.
Legislative Intent Behind Table I vs. Table II Classification: When the distinction between Table I and Table II was introduced in Clause 66, it reflected a clear legislative intent to differentiate institutions by their nature and credibility. Table I was reserved for institutions that are either government-funded or of established national repute, deemed worthy of full tax exemption without additional conditions. In contrast, Table II comprised other charitable or non-profit entities that, while eligible for tax relief, were required to fulfill certain conditions under section 100C to ensure their bona fides. The types of institutions in Table I underscore this intent: the list historically included eminent charities and public organizations – for example, the Abdul Sattar Edhi Foundation, Indus Hospital & Health Network, The Citizens Foundation, as well as important government or statutory bodies like the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan, the Privatization Commission, the Supreme Court’s Water Conservation Account, and others. Such institutions were explicitly granted complete tax exemption on any income by law, reflecting Parliament’s confidence in their governance and the public good they serve. This framework acknowledged that Table I institutions, given their oversight (often by the government itself) or their sterling track record, should not be encumbered by the compliance conditions necessary for less-established entities.
Concerns over the Proposed Amendment (Finance Bill 2025): We understand that the Finance Bill 2025 proposes to merge Table I and Table II of Clause (66). This change would abolish the special status of Table I institutions and bring all charitable institutions under a single category subject to section 100C of the Income Tax Ordinance. In effect, even those organizations that previously enjoyed unconditional tax exemptions (by virtue of being in Table I) would now be required to meet the same conditions as any other non-profit organization in order to retain tax-exempt status. We are gravely concerned that this approach overlooks the original rationale for distinguishing Table I institutions. The move effectively treats long-standing, government-endorsed or highly reputable institutions “as ordinary entities needing vetting, which is inconsistent with the trust that earlier legislatures placed in these institutions. While we appreciate the government’s desire to streamline tax policy and prevent abuse of exemptions, we respectfully submit that sweeping Table I into section 100C’s regime may not fully account for the unique character and contributions of these institutions.
Administrative Burdens and Constraints: Should the tables be merged, Table I institutions will face significant new administrative and compliance burdens. Under section 100C and related provisions, a charitable entity must qualify as a “Non-Profit Organization (NPO)” in the eyes of the law – a status that comes with multiple procedural requirements. In practical terms, institutions that have for decades been tax-exempt ipso facto will now have to undergo certification and approval processes to re-earn an exempt or tax-privileged status each year. Specifically, previously unconditionally exempt entities would now need to:
•	Obtain PCP Certification: Apply for and secure certification from the Pakistan Centre for Philanthropy (PCP), the designated evaluation agency of the Federal Board of Revenue. This process involves a rigorous review of the organization’s governance, financial management, and program delivery standards to ensure they meet the official criteria for charitable performance.
•	Seek Commissioner’s Approval as NPO: Formally seek approval from the Commissioner of Inland Revenue under section 2(36) of the Income Tax Ordinance. This approval is mandatory for an organization to be recognized as a tax-exempt NPO. It requires submission of detailed documentation – including constitutional documents, audited financial statements, and evidence of charitable activities – for the tax authorities’ scrutiny and satisfaction that the entity operates not-for-profit.
•	Comply with Section 100C Conditions Continually: Ensure ongoing compliance with the various conditions stipulated in section 100C of the Ordinance to avail the tax benefit. These conditions include timely filing of annual income tax returns, deposit of any required withholding taxes, submission of withholding statements for each tax year, and maintaining administrative expenses below the prescribed threshold (e.g. administrative expenditure not exceeding 15% of total receipts, among other criteria). Additionally, no part of the organization’s income or assets can directly or indirectly benefit any private individual – a condition already inherent to genuine charities, but now subject to formal attestation.
While we do not object to reasonable oversight, the imposition of these requirements en masse on Table I institutions will create considerable challenges. Many of our organizations are large, longstanding public service institutions handling substantial programs (in education, health, social welfare, etc.). Redirecting staff and resources to meet new paperwork, certification audits, and procedural checks will strain our administrative capacities. Moreover, some Table I institutions are public-sector or statutory bodies (for example, government-created funds or boards) which are already subject to government oversight and audit. Forcing such bodies into the same approval process designed for private NGOs may be administratively redundant. There is also an implied risk of disruption – if any institution cannot secure the required PCP certification or NPO approval by the expected date (for reasons of procedural delay or timing), its tax-exempt status could lapse, adversely affecting its finances and operations. We are confident this is not the intent of the reform, which appears aimed at tightening oversight over benami or spurious charities; however, in practice the amendment will bind bona fide institutions in red tape, at least in the short term.
Request for Transitional Period: If the government deems it necessary to proceed with the unification of Table I and II and the application of section 100C to all, then we earnestly request a reasonable transition period for compliance. We note that in prior reforms, the legislature wisely allowed phased implementation for organizations to adjust. For instance, when the requirement of obtaining Commissioner’s approval for NPO status was introduced for Table II institutions, it was not made effective immediately – the condition was deferred and only applied from July 1, 2022 onwards for those entities, with earlier years being exempt from it. This grace period acknowledged the practical reality that organizations needed time to prepare documentation and obtain the necessary approvals. In the same spirit, we appeal for a similar (if not more generous) transition period for the now-affected Table I institutions. A phase-in until (for example) the end of Tax Year 2026 or later would provide a reasonable window for our institutions to: (a) understand the new legal requirements; (b) compile and submit applications for PCP certification; (c) obtain NPO recognition from the Commissioner; and (d) put in place internal compliance mechanisms to meet ongoing section 100C obligations. Such a transition would prevent any sudden loss of tax-exempt status due to sheer administrative timing and would demonstrate the government’s support for the valuable public services these institutions deliver. Ultimately, a staggered implementation would ensure that compliance is achieved without interrupting the charitable and welfare activities that directly benefit citizens.
Conclusion and Appeal: We wish to emphasize that the institutions listed in Table I have been partners of the government in public service, some for many decades. Our work – in fields such as healthcare, education, poverty alleviation, disaster relief, and cultural preservation – aligns with the state’s own development and welfare goals. The original policy of granting us unconditional exemptions was a testament to the high level of trust and importance accorded to our organizations. We fully appreciate the government’s mandate to modernize tax administration and improve transparency. Our plea is that this be done in a manner that recognizes the unique standing of Table I institutions and does not inadvertently hinder their functioning. We are confident that the Ministry of Finance, under your leadership, understands both the institutional significance of these organizations and the administrative realities involved in compliance. We therefore urge you to kindly consider either preserving the spirit of the original law (by continuing unconditional exemptions for the most vetted institutions) or, at the very least, introducing an adequate transition period and support mechanisms to help us comply with the new requirements in due course.
Thank you for your time and thoughtful consideration of this matter. We remain available to engage in dialogue or provide any additional information that may assist in crafting a solution. Our commitment to transparency and the public good is unwavering, and we look forward to working with the Ministry to ensure a smooth alignment of our operations with the national tax framework.
Yours faithfully,

Redirecting staff and resources to meet **new paperwork, certification audits, and procedural checks** will strain our administrative capacities. Moreover, some Table I institutions are **public-sector or statutory bodies** (for example, government-created funds or boards) which are already subject to government oversight and audit. Forcing such bodies into the same approval process designed for private NGOs may be administratively redundant. There is also an implied **risk of disruption** – if any institution cannot secure the required PCP certification or NPO approval by the expected date (for reasons of procedural delay or timing), its tax-exempt status could lapse, adversely affecting its finances and operations. We are confident this is not the intent of the reform, which appears aimed at tightening oversight over *benami* or spurious charities; however, **in practice the amendment will bind bona fide institutions in red tape**, at least in the short term.  

**Request for Transitional Period:** If the government deems it necessary to proceed with the unification of Table I and II and the application of section 100C to all, then we earnestly **request a reasonable transition period for compliance**. We note that in prior reforms, the legislature wisely allowed phased implementation for organizations to adjust. For instance, when the requirement of obtaining Commissioner’s approval for NPO status was introduced for Table II institutions, it was **not made effective immediately** – the condition was **deferred and only applied from July 1, 2022 onwards for those entities**, with earlier years being exempt from it【25†L721-L729】. This grace period acknowledged the practical reality that organizations needed time to prepare documentation and obtain the necessary approvals. In the same spirit, we appeal for a **similar (if not more generous) transition period** for the now-affected Table I institutions. A phase-in until (for example) the end of Tax Year 2026 or later would provide a reasonable window for our institutions to: (a) understand the new legal requirements; (b) compile and submit applications for PCP certification; (c) obtain NPO recognition from the Commissioner; and (d) put in place internal compliance mechanisms to meet ongoing section 100C obligations. Such a transition would prevent any sudden loss of tax-exempt status due to sheer administrative timing and would demonstrate the government’s support for the valuable public services these institutions deliver. Ultimately, a **staggered implementation** would ensure that compliance is achieved *without interrupting the charitable and welfare activities* that directly benefit citizens.  

**Conclusion and Appeal:** We wish to emphasize that the institutions listed in Table I have been **partners of the government in public service**, some for many decades. Our work – in fields such as healthcare, education, poverty alleviation, disaster relief, and cultural preservation – aligns with the state’s own development and welfare goals. The original policy of granting us unconditional exemptions was a testament to the **high level of trust and importance** accorded to our organizations. We fully appreciate the government’s mandate to modernize tax administration and improve transparency. Our plea is that this be done in a manner that **recognizes the unique standing of Table I institutions** and does not inadvertently hinder their functioning. We are confident that the Ministry of Finance, under your leadership, understands both the **institutional significance** of these organizations and the **administrative realities** involved in compliance. We therefore urge you to kindly consider **either preserving the spirit of the original law** (by continuing unconditional exemptions for the most vetted institutions) or, at the very least, **introducing an adequate transition period and support mechanisms** to help us comply with the new requirements in due course. 

Thank you for your time and thoughtful consideration of this matter. We remain available to engage in dialogue or provide any additional information that may assist in crafting a solution. Our commitment to transparency and the public good is unwavering, and we look forward to working with the Ministry to ensure a smooth alignment of our operations with the national tax framework.  

Yours faithfully,  

**[Signature]**  
_On behalf of all institutions, foundations, societies, boards, trusts, and funds listed in Table I of Clause (66), Part I, Second Schedule, Income Tax Ordinance 2001_【3†L1001-L1006】【24†L1737-L1745】.

**To:**  
The Honorable Federal Minister for Finance  
Ministry of Finance, Government of Pakistan  
Islamabad  

**Subject: Concerns on Proposed Amendment to Clause (66), Part I of Second Schedule – Request for Transitional Relief for Table I Institutions**

**Dear Sir,**

We write on behalf of various institutions, foundations, societies, boards, trusts, and funds listed in Table I of Clause (66), Part I of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. These institutions have long benefited from unconditional income tax exemption granted under the law, recognizing their vital role in public service delivery. We wish to respectfully raise concerns regarding the proposed amendment in the Finance Bill 2025, which seeks to merge Table I and Table II and apply the conditions of section 100C across the board, thereby revoking the longstanding exemption framework for Table I institutions. We also request that, should this amendment be enacted, a reasonable transitional period be granted to enable orderly compliance without compromising institutional operations.

The original legislative distinction between Table I and Table II was not arbitrary but grounded in the practical need to differentiate between categories of institutions based on the nature of their establishment, oversight structure, and institutional maturity. Table I historically comprised entities either created or substantially funded by the government, or those with an established national reputation for transparency, scale, and societal impact. Many of these institutions, such as the Abdul Sattar Edhi Foundation, Indus Hospital, The Citizens Foundation, the Privatization Commission, SECP, and the Supreme Court’s Water Conservation Account, either operate under statutory frameworks or are subject to regulatory or public audit mechanisms. By contrast, Table II was designed to accommodate a broader set of non-profit and charitable entities whose activities, though genuine, required further regulatory screening and conditional oversight to ensure appropriate use of tax-exempt status. The classification thereby enabled tax authorities to focus monitoring efforts where the risk of misuse was higher, while allowing institutions already subject to robust controls to function without unnecessary administrative hurdles.

The proposed merger of these tables and the blanket application of section 100C to all institutions overlook the fundamental rationale for differentiated treatment. It places longstanding and well-governed institutions on the same footing as newly formed or less-regulated entities, effectively disregarding the original policy consideration that certain institutions had, by their very structure, already met the objectives now sought to be enforced through section 100C. This shift not only dilutes the principle of risk-based oversight but also sends an unintended signal that even the most reputable or government-affiliated institutions are to be re-evaluated for legitimacy, which may be perceived as counterproductive.

Moreover, the imposition of new compliance requirements—including Pakistan Centre for Philanthropy (PCP) certification, approval as a Non-Profit Organization under section 2(36), and annual compliance with section 100C—will significantly increase administrative burdens for Table I institutions. These requirements involve extensive documentation, procedural scrutiny, and ongoing thresholds such as capping administrative expenditures and filing various returns and statements. While we fully support the objectives of transparency and accountability, the sudden introduction of these obligations on previously exempt institutions may disrupt operations, particularly where resources must be diverted from core programmatic activities to regulatory compliance. In some cases, these institutions already operate under formal audit and performance review systems, rendering additional approval processes duplicative. More critically, any delay in securing these approvals could result in the lapse of tax-exempt status and serious operational and financial uncertainty.

In view of the above, we humbly urge that, if the proposed amendment is enacted, a reasonable transitional window—preferably until the end of Tax Year 2026—be granted to allow affected institutions to realign their governance, compile required documentation, and complete the necessary approval processes without interrupting their ongoing services to the public. This would be consistent with the approach taken in earlier reforms, where compliance conditions were phased in over time to accommodate practical implementation challenges.

The institutions listed in Table I have, for decades, partnered with the State in delivering critical public services across sectors such as health, education, welfare, and disaster relief. The exemption granted to them was not merely a tax concession but a recognition of their institutional significance and proven public value. While we appreciate the government’s commitment to reform and accountability, we respectfully submit that this effort should be pursued in a manner that preserves the integrity and continuity of well-functioning institutions. We therefore request your kind consideration to either retain differentiated treatment for Table I institutions or provide adequate time and facilitation to enable compliance with the new regime.

We remain available for constructive engagement on this matter and appreciate your attention to the concerns of institutions that have long contributed to the national interest.

**Yours faithfully,**  
*On behalf of institutions listed under Table I of Clause (66), Part I of the Second Schedule*

Thank you for your query regarding the taxation of withdrawals from a Voluntary Pension Scheme (VPS) under the Finance Bill 2025–2026. I have reviewed the relevant provisions of the Finance Bill and provide below a clarification on the points you raised:

**1. Applicability of the 50% Taxable Withdrawal Rule:**  
The Finance Bill 2025–26 proposes to **withdraw the current tax exemption on 50% of VPS withdrawals**. In other words, previously a retiree could withdraw up to half of the accumulated VPS balance tax-free, but **this exemption is being removed effective July 1, 2025**【36†L1490-L1495】. The Bill does **not limit this change to new contributions only**; it applies to any withdrawals made after the effective date, regardless of when the contributions were made. **The entire amount withdrawn from a VPS at retirement will become taxable** under the new rules【26†L187-L194】. There is no indication in the Finance Bill of a “grandfathering” for balances accumulated before July 1, 2025 – the change affects the **full VPS balance withdrawn** after that date. This is explicitly noted in budget analyses, which confirm that the previously tax-exempt 50% portion of a VPS withdrawal will now be subject to tax in full【26†L187-L194】. 

**2. Tax Rate on Post-Retirement VPS Withdrawals:**  
Under the proposed amendments, the taxable portion of any VPS withdrawal (which, as noted, would be the entire withdrawal amount going forward) will be **taxed according to the normal income tax provisions and rates** applicable to the individual【36†L1492-L1495】. The Finance Bill does not prescribe a special flat tax rate for these withdrawals. Instead, the withdrawn amount will be treated as part of your taxable income in the year of withdrawal and taxed at your **personal income tax slab rate** for that year【36†L1492-L1495】. In practical terms, this means the lump-sum withdrawal will be added to your other income for the year and taxed **at the progressive rates** in force (up to the highest marginal rate applicable for individuals). For instance, high-income individuals could see the VPS withdrawal taxed at up to **35%**, which is the top marginal rate for salaried individuals under the current Finance Bill proposals【39†L7-L11】. There is no separate concessional rate for these withdrawals – they are simply subject to regular income tax as any other taxable income. 

In summary, **any VPS withdrawals made on or after July 1, 2025 will no longer enjoy the 50% tax-free benefit; the full withdrawn amount will be taxable**. The tax on such withdrawals will be determined by the standard income tax rates applicable to you at that time (i.e. your marginal tax rate based on your total taxable income)【36†L1492-L1495】. These changes are aimed at removing the previously available tax break on retirement withdrawals from VPS, as confirmed by the Finance Bill 2025–26 provisions and expert analyses【26†L187-L194】【36†L1490-L1495】.

Please let me know if you need any further information or clarification. I hope this addresses your questions clearly. 

Sincerely,  
Zuhair

This treatment was based on the principle that although the tariff adjustment income is exempt from tax under the said clause, expenses relating to both taxable and exempt operations must be fairly allocated to determine the correct taxable income.

It is further submitted that our client, being aggrieved by the partial disallowance of allocated expenditures, preferred an appeal before the learned Commissioner (Appeals). The appellate authority, after detailed examination of the facts and legal provisions, accepted our contention in its entirety and decided the matter in our client’s favour, inter alia, confirming the exemption under Clause (102A) and allowing full deductibility of expenses. This appellate order remains valid and operative as of the date of this submission.

In this context, the issuance of the present show-cause notice under section 122(9), whereby the same receipts are now sought to be treated as taxable income, represents a clear departure from the department’s earlier accepted position and amounts to a reversal of its own findings—without any change in facts, circumstances, or applicable law. Such a departure not only violates the principles of legal consistency and certainty but also undermines the finality of departmental proceedings unless lawfully set aside through due appellate process. No plausible reason or legal basis has been provided in the notice for this sudden change in treatment, rendering the proposed action arbitrary and untenable in law.

Furthermore, the so-called “approval” obtained by circulation of a memo fails to satisfy the statutory requirement of a validly constituted Board meeting as envisaged under section 3(7) of the FBR Act. Additionally, any attempt to rely on Rules 3(3) and 3(4) of the FBR Rules to validate actions of the Member (IR-Ops) was declared to be in conflict with the parent statute and, therefore, invalid.

It was, and continues to be, our respectful position that the legal infirmities outlined above fatally undermine the validity of the audit selection and all consequential proceedings initiated thereafter. 2.	At the outset, we respectfully submit that the entire audit selection and approval process leading to this notice is vitiated by fundamental legal defects. As established in the recent Honorable Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Islamabad [ATIR] decision in case of M/s Sprint Oil & Gas Services bearing ITA Nos. 1993/IB/2024 & 95/IB/2025, a copy is enclosed as Annexure ‘A’ for your perusal, none of the steps taken by the Board or its officers complied with the law. Each defect, discussed below, renders the purported approval and consequent proceedings void ab initio.


3.	ILLEGALITY OF APPROVAL UNDER CLAUSE 105A

3.1	Clause 105A of Part IV, Second Schedule to the Ordinance sets out a special audit-selection procedure requiring formal sanction of the Board. In the present case, the Member (IR-Ops), FBR has purported to approve our client’s audit selection, which is outside the mandated process. The ATIR in Sprint Oil case expressly held that an approval by the Member under Clause 105A “is not in compliance with the law”. The ATIR further noted that Clause 105A “stipulates that the Commissioner must directly seek approval from the Board”, meaning no alternative procedure (such as Member-signoff) is permissible. Here the Member (IR-Ops) never obtained the Board’s direct sanction as required. By Sprint Oil’s reasoning, any Clause 105A approval obtained in this manner is legally null and void.


4.	INVALID BOARD “MEETING” UNDER SECTION 3(7) OF THE FBR ACT, 2007

4.1	The FBR Act, 2007 prescribes the procedure for Board meetings. Although, the Board purported to approve the audit by circulation of a memo, the ATIR held that a “meeting held by the Board under section 3(7) of the FBR Act, 2007, exceeded the authority” granted by the statute. In other words, conducting a “meeting” by circulation (without a proper quorum or formal meeting) is not sanctioned by the Act or rules. Consequently, the so-called Board decision in this manner was itself unauthorized. Any action taken at an irregular meeting (including purported approval of our client’s audit) is therefore of no legal effect, having been made outside the scope of section 3(7) of the FBR Act, 2007. In our client’s case, we are not aware of any board meeting with the required quorum that has been held, nor of any circulation of a memo from the Board for the approval of the audit under Clause 105A.


5.	LACK OF FORMAL DELEGATION TO THE MEMBER (IR-OPS)  

5.1	Independently, there was no valid delegation of Board powers to the Member (IR-Ops) for Clause 105A approvals. Section 8 of the FBR Act read with Rule 3(1) of the FBR Rules, 2007 mandates that any delegation of the Board’s functions must be formally notified by the Board. In Sprint Oil, the ATIR emphasized that the Board never issued any such delegation notification. It pointed out that “the power delegated by the Board to the Member had not been formally notified, as required under section 8 of the FBR Act, 2007, in conjunction with rule 3(1) of the FBR Rules, 2007”. Kindly let our client know of any formal notification in this regard, as otherwise, the Member (IR-Ops) has no lawful authority to act as Board. Thus, even setting aside Clause 105A, the Member’s attempt to approve the audit is void for want of any delegated jurisdiction.



6.	ULTRA VIRES EXPANSION BY RULES 3(3) AND 3(4)  

6.1	The Board may not rely on Rule 3(3) or 3(4) of the FBR Rules to cure these defects. Those provisions allow a member (e.g. the Chairman) to act pending formal delegation, but Sprint Oil held that they “conflict with section 9 of the FBR Act” and “improperly broaden its scope”. Section 9 merely preserves the validity of Board actions despite technical defects (such as vacancies) it does not confer any new substantive powers on individual members. Allowing Rules 3(3) or (4) to sidestep the delegation requirement would unlawfully expand the Act. The ATIR therefore ruled that Rules 3(3) and (4) are ultra vires Section 9 and cannot impart authority where none exists. In short, no reliance can be placed on these rules to justify the Member’s actions in our case also. 


7.	INVALIDITY OF SUBSEQUENT PROCEEDINGS 

7.1	Each of the above flaws was found in Sprint Oil to be fatal. The ATIR concluded that because the Board’s initial approval was “flawed”, “all subsequent actions taken, including the issuance of the contested order under section 121… were automatically rendered invalid”. The ATIR ultimately declared the impugned order “illegal, void from the beginning (ab-initio), and without jurisdiction”. By parity of reasoning, the Notice under section 177 issued to our client (and any resulting assessment under section 121) must also be regarded as void ab initio. The entire audit process here also rests on the very same defective foundation that the ATIR in Sprint Oil’s case struck down. As a matter of law, a notice on an invalid selection cannot stand. Accordingly, the impugned Notice and any downstream action are a nullity. For the sake of brevity, the operating paragraphs of aforesaid decision as under: 

“By respectfully following the above judgment, the impugned order dated 13.11.2024 is annulled.

I. The approval granted by the learned Member (IR-Ops), FBR, under clause (105A) of 
Part-IV of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance is not in compliance with the law.

ii. Furthermore, the meeting held by the Board under section 3(7) of the FBR Act, 2007, exceeds the authority granted by the FBR Act, 2007, and the rules formulated under it.

iii. Additionally, the power delegated by the Board to the Member (IROps) has not been formally notified by the Board as required by section 8 of the FBR Act, 2007, in conjunction with rule 3(1) of the FBR Rules, 2007.

iv. Moreover, sub-rules (3) and (4) of rule 3 of the FBR Rules, 2007, conflict with section 9 of the FBR Act, 2007. These rules improperly broaden the scope of section 9, which contradicts the established legal principle that rules cannot extend the scope of statutory provisions.

v. As a result, since the approval granted by the Board under Clause (105A) is flawed, the subsequent actions taken, including the issuance of the impugned ex-parte order under section 121 of the Ordinance, are automatically rendered invalid.”
(emphasis is our)




8.	Conclusion 

8.1	In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the subject notices issued under 
section 177(6) of the Ordinance, is legally unsustainable and void ab initio. The audit selection process, including the purported approval under Clause 105A, suffers from multiple incurable legal defects, each of which independently vitiates the proceedings.

Consequently, the ATIR declared that all subsequent actions, including passage of assessment orders, were automatically rendered invalid.

8.3	Applying the same binding principles to our client’s case, it follows that the notice under 
section 177(6) issued to our client is without lawful authority, and any proceedings emanating therefrom, are null and void. We, therefore, most respectfully request that the notice under section 177(6) for tax year 2019, along with any consequential proceedings, be withdrawn forthwith in the interest of justice and adherence to the rule of law.

**K-Electric Limited**  
KE House, 39-B, Sunset Boulevard, DHA Phase II  
Karachi, Pakistan  

**Date:** June 16, 2025  

**To:**  
The Chairman,  
Federal Board of Revenue (FBR),

**Subject:** Concerns Regarding Proposed Amendment to Section 21(s) of Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Request for Exemption for Utility Service Providers  

**Dear Sir,**  

We write on behalf of K-Electric Limited (“K-Electric”) to respectfully express our concerns about the proposed amendment to Section 21 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – specifically the insertion of clause (s) through the Finance Bill 2025. As understood, this amendment would disallow 50% of the expenditure claimed in respect of any sale where the payment exceeding PKR 200,000 is received *otherwise than through a banking channel or digital means*, against a single invoice【5†L406-L412】. We appreciate that the objective of this proposal is to encourage digital transactions and enhance documentation in the economy. However, we would like to draw your kind attention to the practical challenges this poses for utility service providers like K-Electric, and to request an appropriate exemption or relaxation in this regard.  

K-Electric is the sole electricity utility serving the city of Karachi and its adjoining areas, with a customer base of over **3.7 million** consumers【16†L106-L113】. By the very nature of our operations, we handle an enormous volume of transactions and bill payments on a daily basis. A significant portion of these payments is collected through authorized bank branches and other collection agents that facilitate our consumers. In many cases, customers (including some high-value industrial and commercial clients) make their bill payments in cash at these banks or centers, which then *aggregate and deposit* the funds into K-Electric’s accounts. The initial mode of payment in such instances is cash, due to either customer preference or on-ground operational constraints. Given the diversity and scale of our consumer base, it is **not practically feasible** to ensure that every payment above PKR 200,000 is made via digital channels or crossed banking instruments. This is especially true in situations where customers lack access to digital banking, or during system downtimes when accepting cash is the only way to facilitate timely payment and avoid service disconnection.  

We wish to underscore that **K-Electric fully supports the government’s drive towards a documented, digital economy.** In fact, we have been proactively encouraging our consumers to adopt banking channels and digital payment methods. K-Electric has partnered with financial institutions and fintech platforms (such as Visa and the Savyour cashback app) to incentivize bill payments through digital means【11†L119-L127】. These efforts have led to a substantial increase in digital payments – *over one million* of our customers are now digitally connected users, a significant milestone for us【11†L138-L143】. Despite this progress, a considerable segment of our customer base **still relies on traditional cash payments** for various reasons, including convenience, limited digital literacy, or lack of immediate access to online facilities. We are continuing our efforts to migrate more users to digital platforms, but this transformation is gradual. In the interim, completely eliminating cash-based transactions – especially for high-value bills – is not practically achievable without disrupting customer facilitation.  

In light of the above, the proposed Section 21(s) poses an unintended risk to K-Electric’s operations. Under the new provision, if a payment exceeding PKR 200,000 against a single invoice is received in cash (or by any means other than through a proper banking/digital channel), then **50% of the corresponding expense will be disallowed for tax purposes**【5†L406-L412】. For a utility company like ours, this could translate into a significant disallowance of legitimate business expenditures simply because of the mode of payment chosen by the customer. We emphasize that all such cash receipts are transparently routed through banks and duly documented; nevertheless, the literal application of this clause would still treat them as non-compliant transactions. The financial impact of disallowing half of our valid expenses would be substantial – it would **artificially inflate our taxable income** and, consequently, our tax liability. As a regulated utility, K-Electric operates on relatively thin margins under tariff determinations, and such an additional tax burden would strain our finances. This may in turn **hinder our ability to invest** in critical power infrastructure upgrades and maintenance, which are essential for ensuring reliable electricity supply to the millions of residents and businesses in Karachi. Moreover, if a portion of our legitimate costs is rendered non-deductible, it could eventually necessitate adjustments in our tariff or revenue requirements (subject to regulatory approval) to maintain financial viability. In other words, the burden of this measure might indirectly be passed on to consumers – an outcome we believe is not the intent of the policymaker.  

**We respectfully request that FBR consider granting an exemption or special relaxation for utility service providers like K-Electric with regard to the proposed Section 21(s).** We note that the law already contemplates exceptions in certain cases to account for unique operational realities – for example, direct purchases of agricultural produce from growers have been excluded from analogous disallowance provisions【5†L400-L408】. In a similar vein, we submit that the utility sector merits consideration due to its unique role and constraints. K-Electric’s situation is not one of evading documentation, but rather a reflection of customer payment behaviors and practical limitations in the billing ecosystem. We therefore propose that **collections made through scheduled banks or authorized agents on behalf of utility companies be treated as payments through a banking channel**, even if the original tender from the customer is cash. Alternatively, the FBR may kindly include utility service providers in the category of persons or businesses exempted from the purview of this clause (either by amending the statute or through using the powers to prescribe persons/classes via notification). Such a relaxation would align with the spirit of the law – discouraging **undocumented large cash transactions** – while avoiding inadvertent harm to essential service providers. It would allow K-Electric and other utilities to continue operations without the fear of hefty tax disallowances stemming from modes of payment that are often beyond our immediate control.  

In conclusion, we urge the FBR to **reconsider the blanket application** of Section 21(s) on utility companies and to adopt a facilitative approach in this matter. K-Electric remains fully committed to increasing digital payment adoption and complying with all tax and reporting requirements. We are confident that with a thoughtful exemption or clarification, the FBR can achieve its goal of promoting digital transactions **without disrupting the critical services** that utilities provide. We would be grateful for a favorable consideration of our request, and are ready to provide any additional information or engage in a discussion to find a workable solution.  

Thank you for your time and kind consideration. 

**Yours sincerely,**  

**[Authorized Signatory]**  
Chief Financial Officer  
K-Electric Limited

As per the proposed amendment, fifty percent of the expenditure claimed in respect of a sale would be disallowed where payment exceeding PKR 200,000 is received *otherwise than through a banking channel or digital means*, against a single invoice containing one or more transactions of goods or services.  

We fully appreciate the policy rationale behind this proposed clause – namely, to promote the documentation of the economy and discourage large undocumented cash transactions. However, we wish to highlight that the proposed amendment, if applied without exception, may create serious compliance and operational challenges for utility service providers like K-Electric.

Being the exclusive power supplier to Karachi and adjoining areas, serving over 3.7 million customers, K-Electric collects thousands of bill payments daily through multiple channels. A significant portion of these payments is received via commercial banks or third-party agents authorized to collect payments on our behalf. In several instances, the end consumer tenders cash to the bank counter, which is subsequently credited into K-Electric’s bank account. While the final deposit is routed through a financial institution, the underlying mode of payment initiated by the consumer may technically be classified as a “cash payment,” thereby risking disallowance under the literal reading of proposed section 21(s).

**It is practically impossible**, in a utility billing ecosystem of this scale and diversity, to ensure that every payment above PKR 200,000 is made strictly via crossed banking instruments or digital platforms. Several factors contribute to this limitation: customer preferences, infrastructure gaps, system outages, and the operational design of authorized collection mechanisms. While we continue to promote digital adoption (including incentives for online payments and partnerships with fintech platforms), a complete shift remains an evolving process due to varying consumer capacities and behaviors.

Importantly, the Income Tax Ordinance already acknowledges such practical realities in its existing provisions. In this regard, we respectfully draw your attention to clause (l) of section 21 of the Ordinance, where disallowance is imposed on expenditures incurred in cash exceeding certain thresholds. Recognizing the operational constraints of utility companies, **an explicit exclusion was provided under section 21(l)** for payments made to utility service providers. This legislative precedent reflects the understanding that utilities operate under a distinct model and that strict cash disallowance rules may not be suitable in all contexts.

In light of this, we respectfully submit that **a similar exclusion** ought to be considered under the newly proposed section 21(s) to maintain consistency in treatment and avoid unintended penalization of the utility sector. We recommend that either of the following approaches be adopted:

1. A specific exclusion be inserted in section 21(s) for **utility service providers**, along the lines of the exemption already available in section 21(l); or  
2. A clarification be issued stating that payments collected by authorized banks or agents on behalf of utility companies, even if initially tendered in cash, shall be treated as routed through a banking channel for the purpose of this clause.

The absence of such a safeguard may lead to disproportionate tax disallowances, even in fully documented and bank-reconciled transactions. This could severely distort our tax computations, artificially inflate our taxable income, and adversely impact our cost-recovery framework – ultimately affecting service quality and infrastructure investment.

We remain fully committed to supporting the government’s efforts toward a transparent and documented economy. However, we urge the FBR to consider the unique nature of utility operations and avoid imposing obligations that are operationally impracticable to meet. We would welcome the opportunity to further discuss this matter and provide any additional information that may assist your deliberations.

We sincerely thank you for your time and consideration.

**Yours faithfully,**  
**[Authorized Signatory]**  
Chief Financial Officer  
**K-Electric Limited**

---

### **Chronological History of Events – United Energy Pakistan Limited (Tax Year 2015)**

United Energy Pakistan Limited (UEP), a non-resident company incorporated in Mauritius and engaged in the exploration and extraction of oil and natural gas in Pakistan, e-filed its return for Tax Year 2015 on December 31, 2015. The return declared total income of Rs. 16.66 billion (including royalty) and claimed a refund of Rs. 5.84 billion. This return was treated as a deemed assessment under section 120(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Subsequently, the return was amended under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance on December 27, 2016, revising the income upward to Rs. 16.89 billion and determining tax payable at Rs. 637.42 million. On the taxpayer’s request, the order was rectified under section 221 on January 25, 2017, resulting in a reduced tax liability and a refund of Rs. 4.12 billion.

UEP challenged the amended assessment by filing an appeal before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals-II), who on November 30, 2017, upheld the major additions made in the amended order. The CIR(A) confirmed the application of section 122(5A), the application of the 55% tax rate, the disallowance of the entire exchange loss in the current year, the levy of super tax under section 4B, and the disallowance of tax credit under section 65B. The only relief allowed was the direction to give consequential relief in respect of Workers’ Welfare Fund (WWF). Subsequently, an appeal effect order under section 124(4) was issued on November 5, 2018, confirming the revised income and computing a tax refundable of Rs. 5.10 billion.

Aggrieved by the CIR(A)’s findings, UEP preferred an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR), Karachi. The Tribunal, vide its order dated June 3, 2023, partly accepted the appeal. It confirmed the application of the 55% tax rate, noted that the issue relating to exchange loss was not pressed, deleted the super tax under section 4B, and directed the allowance of consequential relief on WWF and tax credit under section 65B. In pursuance of the ATIR's directives, another appeal effect order dated November 16, 2023, was issued under section 124, reaffirming the total income at Rs. 16.89 billion and computing a revised refundable amount of Rs. 5.10 billion after giving effect to all allowed reliefs, including credit under section 65B and deletion of super tax.

Following this, the taxpayer filed a refund adjustment application under section 170 of the Ordinance, via letter dated January 2, 2024, requesting adjustment of the determined refund against outstanding tax demands. A refund order dated February 28, 2024, was passed under section 170(4), partially accepting the refund claim. The tax authority acknowledged verified tax deducted at source amounting to Rs. 2.72 billion and payments under section 137(2) and for WWF, but rejected a portion of Rs. 1.398 billion on the ground that the corresponding CPRs were marked with "Tax Year 2014." As a result, a net refund of Rs. 3.19 billion was determined and adjusted against outstanding tax demands for Tax Years 2020 (Rs. 197.59 million), 2021 (Rs. 1.25 billion), and 2023 (Rs. 1.74 billion). The balance refund was reduced to NIL.

In response to the partial rejection of refund, particularly the disallowed Rs. 1.398 billion in tax credits and Rs. 515.98 million in refund adjustment from Tax Year 2014, UEP preferred another appeal under section 129 before the CIR(A), Karachi. In the appellate proceedings concluded on May 23, 2024, the CIR(A) highlighted that UEP operates on a special tax year (January–December) and accordingly, the taxes deducted during calendar year 2014 pertain to Tax Year 2015. The CIR(A) referred to section 168(2) of the Ordinance, which allows tax credit in the year in which the tax is deducted, and noted that a previous departmental rectification order dated March 31, 2015, had similarly instructed UEP to claim such tax credit in Tax Year 2015. The CIR(A) concluded that the rejection of Rs. 1.914 billion refund by the DCIR—without prior notice or opportunity of hearing—was procedurally flawed, violated principles of natural justice, and ignored binding legal provisions. Consequently, the appellate authority annulled the refund rejection and remanded the matter for fresh consideration after verification of tax challans and allowing credit in either Tax Year 2014 or 2015.
