# Response to Sindh Revenue Board Notice dated 13 June 2025

**Date:** June 18, 2025  
**To:** The Commissioner, Sindh Revenue Board, Karachi  
**From:** Engro Elengy Terminal (Private) Limited  
**Subject:** Sindh Sales Tax on Royalty – Reply to Notice dated 13 June 2025

Dear Sir,

## Background and Reference to Previous Notice

- Reference is made to the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) notice No. SRB/COM-IV/AC-32/TO/Co/2018 dated 20 April 2018 addressed to Engro Elengy Terminal (Private) Limited (EETPL)【1†L28-L36】, as well as the recent Notice dated 13 June 2025 on the above subject (“Notice”). We write on behalf of EETPL in response to the Notice, to contest the assertions therein and to clarify the factual and legal position for the record.

## Royalty Included in Taxable Value (No Short Payment of SST)

- **SST Already Paid on Royalty:** EETPL has consistently included the royalty paid to Port Qasim Authority (PQA) in the value of its taxable services and has charged and deposited Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on the gross amounts billed to its customers. In practice, the so-called royalty is recovered from EETPL's customers as a reimbursable expense, forming part of the tariff in EETPL’s invoices【19†L255-L263】. Accordingly, SST has been duly paid on these amounts as part of the total services provided by EETPL. The Notice’s contention that sales tax was not paid on the royalty component is therefore **factually incorrect**. 

- **No Shortfall in 2016–2018 Period:** The earlier SRB notice of April 2018 had alleged that neither EETPL nor PQA declared the royalty amounts in their returns and thus “failed to pay” SST on franchise services, purportedly resulting in a shortfall of Rs. 131,351,156【18†L23-L32】. This allegation was misplaced. EETPL’s returns for the relevant periods reflected the full value of services (including any royalty amounts passed through to customers), and the SST on such gross receipts was duly deposited. There was, therefore, no loss of revenue to the Sindh Government in respect of those amounts.

## Royalty is Not a Franchise Fee – No Taxable Service by PQA

- **Nature of Royalty vs Franchise:** The core premise of the Notice – that the royalty paid to PQA constitutes consideration for "franchise services" provided by PQA – is denied. The royalty paid under the Implementation Agreement between EETPL and PQA is essentially a charge for concession/lease of port land and facilities, not a fee for any franchised business operation or service rendered by PQA【19†L247-L255】. In fact, the royalty is calculated based on throughput (e.g. per ton of LNG handled) as part of the concession terms, and it is **not** tied to any specific service or management support from PQA to EETPL.

- **No Franchise Relationship:** It is noteworthy that PQA, being a statutory federal authority established under the PQA Act, does not engage in any "franchise" or business-format licensing arrangement with EETPL. PQA has simply granted EETPL the right to develop and operate the LNG terminal (a function PQA itself could have undertaken) in exchange for the royalty. This arrangement does not meet the definition of a **“franchise”** under Section 2(46) of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, which envisages a franchisor granting a franchisee the right to carry on the franchisor’s business (using its business model, brand, mark, etc.) in return for a fee【9†L478-L487】【9†L498-L506】. There is no use of PQA’s name, trademark, business model or any marketing plan by EETPL – all of which are essential elements of a true franchise relationship【9†L498-L506】. Simply put, **PQA provides no franchisor-type services** to EETPL in respect of the royalty arrangement.

- **Substance of the Transaction:** Our position (which is also the subject of pending litigation) is that the royalty paid to PQA cannot be re-characterized as a taxable service fee when, in substance, it is a charge for permission to use port infrastructure and land. As noted by our tax advisors, unless PQA provides some service **other than the provision of land**, the payment by EETPL cannot be treated as consideration for any taxable service under the Sindh sales tax law【19†L271-L278】. In the present case, the royalty is not linked to any identifiable service from PQA – it is the quid pro quo for the concession rights granted to EETPL. Thus, the contention that EETPL is receiving a franchise service from PQA is without factual or legal merit.

## Legal Opinions and High Court Proceedings

- **Expert Opinions Supporting EETPL’s Stance:** The above position is fortified by independent legal opinions obtained by EETPL from reputable law firms, as well as by arguments raised in court proceedings:  
  - *Osmani & Afzal Associates (Tax Advisors):* In February 2018, Osmani & Afzal rendered an opinion that the “royalty” payable to PQA is essentially consideration for land lease/concession rights and **not** a payment for any franchise or service provided by PQA. They emphasized that SST can only be levied if the payment is genuinely for a listed taxable service – which requires showing that PQA performed a service for EETPL beyond merely granting land access【19†L271-L278】. In their view, since the payment is made “not against any specified services provided by PQA to EETPL” but rather for use of land/facilities【19†L247-L255】, treating it as a franchise fee is incorrect.  
  - *Fazleghani Advocates (Legal Counsel):* A detailed legal opinion from Fazleghani Advocates echoed the same analysis. Fazleghani concluded that the relationship between PQA and the terminal operators (including EETPL) is **not** that of a franchisor and franchisee. PQA, as a regulatory/public authority, simply grants a concession and does not impart any business methodology or ongoing service to the operators. Therefore, the Province of Sindh **cannot impose SST on the royalty** received by the PQA under such concession agreements【17†L1349-L1357】. Even assuming (for the sake of argument) that the arrangement fell under a taxable category, the law places the obligation to pay the tax on the service provider (PQA) and not on the service recipient【17†L1371-L1379】 – a point particularly relevant for the period before the 2019 amendment (discussed below).

- **Pending High Court Litigation:** It is pertinent to mention that EETPL and other aggrieved parties have challenged SRB’s characterization of the PQA royalty as a taxable “franchise” service in the High Court of Sindh. Constitutional Petition No. D-3738/2018 (along with connected petitions) is pending before the High Court, in which it has been argued, inter alia, that: **(i)** the royalty paid to PQA is not a franchise fee or service under the law; **(ii)** PQA provides no franchise or service to the terminal operators – it merely grants a concession/license, which is not a taxable service; and **(iii)** any attempt to levy or recover SST on the royalty (especially from the recipients of the concession) is ultra vires and unlawful. These petitions remain sub judice. In these circumstances, the issuance of the present demand notice – effectively asserting the same contested position – is unwarranted and premature, amounting to a disregard of the ongoing court proceedings on this matter.

## Burden of Proof and Section 18 of SST Act

- **Joint Liability Requires Proof of Unpaid Tax:** The Notice invokes Section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 to impute **joint and several liability** on EETPL for the alleged unpaid tax on royalty【1†L63-L69】. We respectfully submit that this provision cannot be triggered absent clear proof that the tax in question was actually due on a taxable service and remained unpaid by the primary service provider. The burden lies on SRB to first establish, with cogent evidence, that a taxable service was rendered by PQA and that the corresponding SST was not paid by the provider **or** the recipient【19†L218-L226】. Mere assumptions or unsubstantiated information suggesting non-payment (as recited in the Notice) are not sufficient grounds to saddle the recipient with liability. Notably, Osmani & Afzal had observed that **unless it is conclusively established** that a payment falls within a taxable service category (such as franchise), SST cannot be imposed on that payment【19†L218-L226】. In this case, not only is the very nature of the “service” in dispute, but, as explained, EETPL has in fact remitted SST on the relevant amounts through its own output tax returns – thereby negating the premise that any tax has gone unpaid.

- **Improper Invocation of Section 18:** Section 18 does not give the SRB carte blanche to recover an arbitrary amount from a service recipient without due process. It provides a mechanism for holding a recipient secondarily liable **only if** tax on a taxable service was payable and remained unpaid. Here, since **no taxable franchise service exists** in the first place (the royalty not being a taxable service) and, furthermore, no tax has actually been short-paid, invoking Section 18 against EETPL is factually and legally baseless. We urge SRB to appreciate that joint liability under Section 18 is a tool to prevent tax evasion in genuine cases of unpaid tax – not a means to penalize taxpayers by re-characterizing legitimate transactions and bypassing the need to prove tax liability. Any such action without meeting the evidentiary burden would be contrary to the spirit of the law and principles of justice.

## No Retrospective Tax Obligation on Recipient (Section 13(3) & 2021 PTD 484)

- **No Withholding Liability Pre-2019:** The demand raised in the Notice is also **legally untenable** because it effectively seeks to impose a withholding agent obligation on EETPL for periods prior to the law permitting such an arrangement. It is highlighted that the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 was amended (via the Sindh Finance Act 2019) to insert sub-section (3) in Section 13, which for the first time made service recipients liable to pay tax in certain situations (i.e. as withholding agents). This amendment came into effect on 01 July 2019. **Before that date, EETPL had no statutory obligation to withhold or pay SST on services received from PQA.** Any demand treating EETPL as liable for PQA’s tax prior to July 2019 is beyond the mandate of the law as it stood then. In other words, for the period under dispute (2016–2018), the liability to charge, collect, and pay SST on any service provided by PQA would rest with PQA as the service provider (per Section 9 of the Act)【17†L1371-L1379】, and EETPL was not designated by law as a withholding agent.

- **High Court Judgment – 2021 PTD 484:** The above position is confirmed by authoritative jurisprudence. The Hon’ble Sindh High Court has held, in a judgment reported as *2021 PTD 484*, that the insertion of Section 13(3) via the Finance Act 2019 **cannot be applied retrospectively** to impose tax liability on service recipients for periods prior to 01.07.2019【5†L997-L1005】. In that case, the High Court unequivocally ruled that a person receiving a service was not liable to pay SST on that service as a withholding agent before the enactment of the 2019 amendment【5†L999-L1008】. Consequently, any attempt by SRB to recover the purported SST on royalties from EETPL for the pre-July 2019 period is contrary to law. The impugned Notice, to the extent it asserts such retroactive liability on EETPL, is **without jurisdiction** and liable to be set aside on this ground alone.

## Conclusion and Prayer

- For the foregoing reasons, EETPL maintains that the demand raised through the Notice dated 13 June 2025 is entirely unfounded in fact and law. The allegation that SST was not paid on the royalty is disproved by EETPL’s tax payment records. The characterization of the royalty as a “franchise” service has no legal basis, given the nature of the transaction and the applicable law. Moreover, SRB’s attempt to proceed against EETPL under Section 18 (and to invoke a withholding liability retrospectively) is unsustainable. We therefore respectfully request the SRB to **withdraw the Notice** forthwith, in the interest of justice and to avoid unnecessary litigation.

- Please consider this response as a bona fide effort to resolve the matter without recourse to further legal proceedings. EETPL remains hopeful that the clarifications provided above will allow SRB to review its stance. Nevertheless, our client reserves all its rights and remedies under the law (including the right to contest any adverse action in the appropriate legal forums) if the demand is not withdrawn or otherwise resolved favorably.

Sincerely,  
**Engro Elengy Terminal (Private) Limited**  
*(Through Authorized Signatory)*

# **Internal Memo:** Finance Bill 2025 – Changes to Voluntary Pension Scheme (VPS) Withdrawals

**To:** All KE Employees  
**From:** KE Finance & HR Departments  
**Date:** June 18, 2025  
**Subject:** **Proposed Tax Law Changes Affecting VPS Withdrawals and Retirement Funds**

---

**Dear Team,**  

The Government’s Finance Bill, 2025 (Budget proposals) includes **significant changes to the tax treatment of retirement savings**, particularly the Voluntary Pension Scheme (VPS) and Provident Fund (PF). This memo explains the proposed amendments and how they may impact your retirement withdrawals. **It is crucial for all employees to understand these changes and plan accordingly.**

## **Overview of Proposed Changes**  

Under current law, certain withdrawals or transfers of retirement funds are tax-exempt. The Finance Bill 2025 **proposes to remove key tax exemptions effective July 1, 2025**. In summary:  

- **Provident Fund transfers to VPS will no longer be tax-free.** *(Clause 23C exemption to be withdrawn)*【26†L1186-L1189】  
- **The 50% tax-free lump-sum withdrawal from VPS at retirement is being eliminated.** *(Clause 23A exemption to be withdrawn)*【26†L1178-L1185】  
- **Any VPS withdrawals after June 30, 2025 will be treated as taxable income** (no longer exempt), potentially taxed at your marginal rate (up to **35%** for top bracket)【26†L1178-L1185】【23†L883-L888】.  
- **Post-retirement annuity or pension income will now be taxed** (previously often exempt). A new **concessionary tax schedule** is proposed for individuals who **only** have pension/annuity income: **0% tax on annual pension up to PKR 10 million, and 5% tax on the amount exceeding PKR 10 million**【24†L927-L931】. (If you have other income sources, your pension will be taxed at normal rates.)  

These changes are **pending approval of the Finance Bill 2025**, but are expected to take effect from the **2025-26 tax year (starting July 1, 2025)**. Below are details on each change and recommended actions for employees.

## **1. End of Tax-Free Provident Fund (PF) Transfers to VPS**  

**Current Rule:**  Clause (23C) of the tax law currently allows you to transfer your accumulated **Provident Fund** balance into an approved **Voluntary Pension Scheme** **without any tax**. This means employees could move PF money into a VPS account to continue investing for retirement and defer taxes.  

**Proposed Change:** **Clause (23C) is being **omitted**** – the **tax exemption on PF-to-VPS transfers will be removed**【26†L1186-L1189】. If this proposal is enacted, any amount transferred from an approved PF to a VPS will **no longer be tax-free**. In effect, moving your PF money into a VPS would be treated as a **taxable withdrawal** of the PF. 

**Impact:** Going forward, **employees should avoid transferring Provident Fund balances to VPS**, as it would trigger taxation (where previously it did not). If you were considering shifting your PF into a VPS for additional retirement benefits, be aware that this strategy will no longer provide a tax advantage under the new law.

## **2. Removal of 50% Tax-Free VPS Withdrawal at Retirement**  

**Current Rule:** Under Clause (23A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, when an individual retires (or in case of disability or death), they can withdraw **up to 50% of their VPS accumulated balance completely tax-free**【26†L1178-L1185】. This tax-free lump sum has been a major benefit of the VPS – you could take half your pension savings in cash without paying income tax, and use the rest for an annuity or periodic payments.  

**Proposed Change:** **Clause (23A) is being **omitted**** – the **50% tax-free withdrawal benefit at retirement will no longer apply**【26†L1178-L1185】. **All withdrawals from a VPS, regardless of amount, will become **fully taxable income** after June 30, 2025**. In other words, if you take a lump-sum from your VPS upon retirement (or disability/death payout to your heirs), **the entire amount would be subject to income tax** under the new rules.

**Impact:** Any **VPS withdrawal made on or after July 1, 2025 will be added to your taxable income for that year**. Depending on the amount, this could push you into a higher tax bracket. **The maximum individual tax rate is 35%** (for the highest income bracket)【23†L883-L888】【9†L1115-L1120】, so a large pension withdrawal could be taxed at rates up to 35%. For example, currently you could withdraw half your VPS savings tax-free; after the change, **withdrawing that same amount could incur significant tax (potentially one-third of the sum)**. This dramatically reduces the net cash you’d receive from your pension fund if taken as a lump sum.

> **⚠️ Important:** **Any VPS withdrawals after June 30, 2025 will **no longer enjoy the 50% tax-free benefit**.** They will be taxed in full as per your income slab. Employees nearing retirement this year **should strongly consider withdrawing by June 30, 2025** to avail the current tax exemption on 50% of their balance.

## **3. New Taxation of Annuity/Pension Income Post-Retirement**  

**Current Situation:**  Many employees use their remaining VPS balance (the other 50% after the lump sum) to buy an **annuity** or take programmed monthly withdrawals to receive a regular pension. Previously, **pension or annuity payments** (especially from approved pension schemes or commuted pension from employers) were largely **exempt from tax** under various clauses. For instance, pension payments from a former employer or an approved scheme have been tax-free up to certain limits.

**Proposed Change:** The government is **withdrawing existing pension/annuity exemptions** (e.g. clauses for employer pensions and commutations are being removed alongside VPS clauses)【26†L1211-L1217】. Instead, a **concessionary tax rate** is introduced for retirees drawing pension/annuity income. If **pension/annuity is your only source of income** and you are under 70 years of age, your pension will be taxed as follows in a tax year:  

- **Annual pension income up to PKR 10 million: 0% tax** (completely tax-free)【24†L927-L931】  
- **Annual pension income above PKR 10 million: 5% tax on the amount exceeding PKR 10 million**【24†L927-L931】  

In simple terms, retirees relying solely on pensions would pay almost no tax unless the pension is extremely high. **However, if you have other income (salary, business, etc.) alongside the pension, then the pension amount will be taxed at normal income tax rates** rather than the special low rate【12†L1164-L1172】. 

**Impact:** For a typical KE retiree, this means your **monthly pension or annuity payments from VPS will now be taxable**, though at a very low rate in most cases. For example, if your total annual pension is PKR 2 million, it remains fully under the 0% threshold (no tax). If it’s PKR 12 million, the first 10 million is tax-free and the excess 2 million is taxed at 5% (which is PKR 100,000 in tax). These rates are much lower than regular income tax rates and serve to ease the burden on retirees【24†L927-L931】. 

Additionally, pension providers (including VPS fund managers or insurance companies paying annuities) will now be **required to withhold income tax on pension/annuity payments** for individuals under 70【12†L1172-L1179】. This means any taxable portion of your pension will likely be deducted at source. **For retirees aged 70 or above**, the law does not impose this tax (pensions for senior seniors may remain fully exempt, as the new tax is targeted at under-70 individuals).

## **4. Recommended Actions for Employees**  

Given these upcoming changes, **employees are advised to review their retirement plans** and take action **before June 30, 2025** if necessary. Key recommendations are:  

- **Consider Withdrawing VPS Funds **Before June 30, 2025**** – If you are **planning to retire or otherwise withdraw your VPS balance soon**, it may be financially advantageous to do so **on or before June 30, 2025**. By withdrawing before this cutoff, you can still benefit from the **current law’s tax break**: 50% of your accumulated VPS balance would be **tax-free**, and only the remainder would be taxable (or used for annuity). **Any withdrawals after this date will be fully taxable** under the new rules【26†L1178-L1185】. *(Note: Premature withdrawals before retirement age may have other tax implications; please consult if in doubt.)*  

- **Avoid Transferring Provident Fund (PF) to VPS Going Forward** – Under the new law, transferring your Provident Fund savings into a VPS will **no longer shield that money from tax**. You would effectively be taxed on that transfer as if you cashed out your PF. If you were considering moving your PF to a VPS for extra growth or tax benefit, **reconsider this strategy**. It may be wiser to keep your PF as is, or explore other investment options, since the **tax-free transfer benefit is ending**【26†L1186-L1189】.  

- **Plan for Tax on Retirement Income** – Be prepared that **any form of retirement payout – lump sum or monthly pension – could now incur income tax**. When planning your retirement finances, factor in that **monthly VPS pensions will have a small tax (withheld at source)** and large lump-sums will be taxed at your normal rate. If you anticipate a high pension income **and have other sources of income**, consult a tax advisor for optimal planning (for example, staggering withdrawals over years to avoid higher tax brackets).  

- **Stay Informed** – These changes are currently **proposals** in the Finance Bill 2025. We expect them to be enacted in the Finance Act by July 1, 2025, but if there are any alterations (for instance, if any proposal is not passed or is modified by Parliament), we will update you. **Keep an eye on official communications** from HR/Finance as the budget is finalized. In the meantime, plan under the assumption that these rules will apply from July 2025 onwards.  

> **🔔 Important Date:** **June 30, 2025** – Last day to make any VPS withdrawals under the old tax rules. *If you are retiring soon and wish to take advantage of the current 50% tax-free withdrawal, ensure your paperwork and withdrawal request are completed before this date.* After this, **new tax rates will apply to all withdrawals**.

## **Conclusion**  

We understand that changes in tax laws can be confusing or concerning, especially when they affect your hard-earned retirement savings. These proposed amendments aim to bring more retirement payouts into the tax net, so it’s important to be aware and act prudently. **Our HR and Finance teams are available to answer your questions** regarding how the Finance Bill 2025 might affect your individual situation. We strongly encourage employees, particularly those nearing retirement or with substantial VPS investments, to **review their options ahead of the changes**.

In summary, **the Finance Bill 2025 will end the tax-free advantages previously available for VPS withdrawals and certain pension incomes**. To **maximize your benefits and avoid unnecessary tax**, plan any withdrawals or transfers **before the June 30, 2025 deadline**, and be prepared for the new taxation regime on retirement income thereafter. 

Please treat this matter with priority and reach out if you need guidance. We are here to help you navigate these changes.

**Regards,**  
___  
**KE Finance Department** – *Tax Advisory Unit*  
**KE Human Resources** – *Employee Benefits Section*  

**Sources & References:** *Finance Bill 2025 – Draft Tax Amendments (Income Tax Ordinance, 2001)*【26†L1178-L1185】【26†L1186-L1189】; *Crowe Tax Memorandum – Finance Bill 2025*【23†L883-L888】; *KPMG Budget Brief 2025*【24†L927-L931】; *PwC Tax Update – Federal Budget 2025*【12†L1164-L1172】.

Dear Team,
The Government’s Finance Bill, 2025 (Budget proposals) includes significant changes to the tax treatment of retirement savings, particularly the Voluntary Pension Scheme (VPS) and Provident Fund (PF). This memo explains the proposed amendments and how they may impact your retirement withdrawals. It is crucial for all employees to understand these changes and plan accordingly.
Overview of Proposed Changes
Under current law, certain withdrawals or transfers of retirement funds are tax-exempt. The Finance Bill 2025 proposes to remove key tax exemptions effective July 1, 2025. In summary:
•	Provident Fund transfers to VPS will no longer be tax-free. (Clause 23C exemption to be withdrawn)
•	The 50% tax-free lump-sum withdrawal from VPS at retirement is being eliminated. (Clause 23A exemption to be withdrawn)
•	Any VPS withdrawals after June 30, 2025 will be treated as taxable income (no longer exempt), potentially taxed at your marginal rate (up to 35% for top bracket).
•	Post-retirement annuity or pension income will now be taxed (previously often exempt). A new concessionary tax schedule is proposed for individuals who only have pension/annuity income: 0% tax on annual pension up to Rs 10 million, and 5% tax on the amount exceeding Rs 10 million. (If you have other income sources, your pension will be taxed at normal rates.)
These changes are pending approval of the Finance Bill 2025, but are expected to take effect from the 2025-26 tax year (starting July 1, 2025). Below are details on each change and recommended actions for employees.
End of Tax-Free Provident Fund (PF) Transfers to VPS
Current Rule: Clause (23C) of the tax law currently allows you to transfer your accumulated Provident Fund balance into an approved Voluntary Pension Scheme without any tax. This means employees could move PF money into a VPS account to continue investing for retirement and defer taxes.
Proposed Change: Clause (23C) is being omitted – the tax exemption on PF-to-VPS transfers will be removed. If this proposal is enacted, any amount transferred from an approved PF to a VPS will no longer be tax-free. In effect, moving your PF money into a VPS would be treated as a taxable withdrawal of the PF.
Impact: Going forward, employees should avoid transferring Provident Fund balances to VPS, as it would trigger taxation (where previously it did not). If you were considering shifting your PF into a VPS for additional retirement benefits, be aware that this strategy will no longer provide a tax advantage under the new law.
Removal of 50% Tax-Free VPS Withdrawal at Retirement
Current Rule: Under Clause (23A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, when an individual retires (or in case of disability or death), they can withdraw up to 50% of their VPS accumulated balance completely tax-free. This tax-free lump sum has been a major benefit of the VPS – you could take half your pension savings in cash without paying income tax, and use the rest for an annuity or periodic payments.
Proposed Change: Clause (23A) is being omitted – the 50% tax-free withdrawal benefit at retirement will no longer apply. All withdrawals from a VPS, regardless of amount, will become fully taxable income after June 30, 2025. In other words, if you take a lump-sum from your VPS upon retirement (or disability/death payout to your heirs), the entire amount would be subject to income tax under the new rules.
Impact: Any VPS withdrawal made on or after July 1, 2025 will be added to your taxable income for that year. Depending on the amount, this could push you into a higher tax bracket. The maximum individual tax rate is 35% (for the highest income bracket), so a large pension withdrawal could be taxed at rates up to 35%. For example, currently you could withdraw half your VPS savings tax-free; after the change, withdrawing that same amount could incur significant tax (potentially one-third of the sum). This dramatically reduces the net cash you’d receive from your pension fund if taken as a lump sum.
Any VPS withdrawals after June 30, 2025 will no longer enjoy the 50% tax-free benefit. They will be taxed in full as per your income slab. Employees nearing retirement this year should strongly consider withdrawing by June 30, 2025 to avail the current tax exemption on 50% of their balance.
New Taxation of Annuity/Pension Income Post-Retirement
Current Situation: Many employees use their remaining VPS balance (the other 50% after the lump sum) to buy an annuity or take programmed monthly withdrawals to receive a regular pension. Previously, pension or annuity payments (especially from approved pension schemes or commuted pension from employers) were largely exempt from tax under various clauses. For instance, pension payments from a former employer or an approved scheme have been tax-free up to certain limits.
Proposed Change: The government is withdrawing existing pension/annuity exemptions (e.g. clauses for employer pensions and commutations are being removed alongside VPS clauses). Instead, a concessionary tax rate is introduced for retirees drawing pension/annuity income. If pension/annuity is your only source of income and you are under 70 years of age, your pension will be taxed as follows in a tax year:
•	Annual pension income up to Rs 10 million: 0% tax (completely tax-free)
•	Annual pension income above Rs 10 million: 5% tax on the amount exceeding Rs 10 million
In simple terms, retirees relying solely on pensions would pay almost no tax unless the pension is extremely high. However, if you have other income (salary, business, etc.) alongside the pension, then the pension amount will be taxed at normal income tax rates rather than the special low rate.
For a typical KE retiree, this means your monthly pension or annuity payments from VPS will now be taxable, though at a very low rate in most cases. For example, if your total annual pension is Rs 2 million, it remains fully under the 0% threshold (no tax). If it’s PKR 12 million, the first 10 million is tax-free and the excess 2 million is taxed at 5% (which is PKR 100,000 in tax). These rates are much lower than regular income tax rates and serve to ease the burden on retirees.
Additionally, pension providers (including VPS fund managers or insurance companies paying annuities) will now be required to withhold income tax on pension/annuity payments for individuals under 70. This means any taxable portion of your pension will likely be deducted at source. For retirees aged 70 or above, the law does not impose this tax (pensions for senior seniors may remain fully exempt, as the new tax is targeted at under-70 individuals).
Recommended Actions for Employees
Given these upcoming changes, employees are advised to review their retirement plans and take action before June 30, 2025 if necessary. Key recommendations are:
•	Consider Withdrawing VPS Funds Before June 30, 2025 – If you are planning to retire or otherwise withdraw your VPS balance soon, it may be financially advantageous to do so on or before June 30, 2025. By withdrawing before this cutoff, you can still benefit from the current law’s tax break: 50% of your accumulated VPS balance would be tax-free, and only the remainder would be taxable (or used for annuity). Any withdrawals after this date will be fully taxable under the new rules. (Note: Premature withdrawals before retirement age may have other tax implications; please consult if in doubt.)
•	Avoid Transferring Provident Fund (PF) to VPS Going Forward – Under the new law, transferring your Provident Fund savings into a VPS will no longer shield that money from tax. You would effectively be taxed on that transfer as if you cashed out your PF. If you were considering moving your PF to a VPS for extra growth or tax benefit, reconsider this strategy. It may be wiser to keep your PF as is, or explore other investment options, since the tax-free transfer benefit is ending.
•	Plan for Tax on Retirement Income – Be prepared that any form of retirement payout – lump sum or monthly pension – could now incur income tax. When planning your retirement finances, factor in that monthly VPS pensions will have a small tax (withheld at source) and large lump-sums will be taxed at your normal rate. If you anticipate a high pension income and have other sources of income, consult a tax advisor for optimal planning (for example, staggering withdrawals over years to avoid higher tax brackets).
•	Stay Informed – These changes are currently proposals in the Finance Bill 2025. We expect them to be enacted in the Finance Act by July 1, 2025, but if there are any alterations (for instance, if any proposal is not passed or is modified by Parliament), we will update you. Keep an eye on official communications from HR/Finance as the budget is finalized. In the meantime, plan under the assumption that these rules will apply from July 2025 onwards.
Important Date: June 30, 2025 – Last day to make any VPS withdrawals under the old tax rules. If you are retiring soon and wish to take advantage of the current 50% tax-free withdrawal, ensure your paperwork and withdrawal request are completed before this date. After this, new tax rates will apply to all withdrawals.
Conclusion
We understand that changes in tax laws can be confusing or concerning, especially when they affect your hard-earned retirement savings. These proposed amendments aim to bring more retirement payouts into the tax net, so it’s important to be aware and act prudently. Our HR and Finance teams are available to answer your questions regarding how the Finance Bill 2025 might affect your individual situation. We strongly encourage employees, particularly those nearing retirement or with substantial VPS investments, to review their options ahead of the changes.
In summary, the Finance Bill 2025 will end the tax-free advantages previously available for VPS withdrawals and certain pension incomes. To maximize your benefits and avoid unnecessary tax, plan any withdrawals or transfers before the June 30, 2025 deadline, and be prepared for the new taxation regime on retirement income thereafter.
Please treat this matter with priority and reach out if you need guidance. We are here to help you navigate these changes.
Regards,

**To:** Umair Malik, Deputy Commissioner (Audit), Zone VI–Range B, Large Taxpayers Office (LTO) Karachi  
**From:** [Your Name], Tax Consultant (Authorized Representative for K‑Electric Limited)  
**Address:** 39-B, K-E House, Sunset Boulevard, DHA Phase-II, Karachi. _(NTN: [K-Electric’s Tax Number])_  

**Date:** June 20, 2025  

**Subject:** Response to Notice under Section 122(9) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Tax Year 2019 (Bad Debt Write-off Recovery Efforts)  

Dear Sir,  

We write on behalf of **K-Electric Limited (“K-Electric”)** in reference to your notice dated June 3, 2025 issued under Section 122(9) for Tax Year 2019. We understand that the notice seeks justification for the bad debt write-offs claimed by K-Electric in Tax Year 2019, specifically regarding the recovery efforts made prior to writing off these receivables. K-Electric is fully committed to compliance, transparency, and robust governance in all financial matters. In this response, we detail the extensive recovery measures undertaken, the rigorous verification by auditors, and the Board of Directors’ oversight and approval of the write-offs, supported by documentary evidence. We respectfully submit that the bad debts were written off only after **exhausting all possible recovery avenues**, and thus the write-off claim is bona fide and allowable under the law. Below, we provide a structured explanation of our recovery efforts and governance practices in this regard.

## Background of Bad Debt Write-off for TY 2019  
During the relevant period (FY 2018–2019), K-Electric provided electricity to millions of consumers in Karachi. A small fraction of customers defaulted on payments to the extent that their outstanding dues became **unrecoverable despite best efforts**. In line with prudent financial management and regulatory guidelines, K-Electric wrote off certain bad debts in FY 2019, amounting to **Rs. 4,050 million (relating to ~10,353 defaulter accounts)**【7†L17908-L17916】. It is emphasized that this write-off was not undertaken lightly; it followed a **comprehensive, multi-step recovery process** and was executed under a formal Board-approved policy. These debts were also part of a **tariff adjustment claim** allowed by our power sector regulator (NEPRA) under the Multi-Year Tariff 2017–2023 framework, which required strict proof of irrecoverability and Board certification【7†L17910-L17918】【7†L17926-L17934】. The following sections detail the recovery efforts and verification steps that preceded the write-off, demonstrating K-Electric’s full compliance with both tax law and regulatory expectations.

## Recovery Efforts and Disconnection Verification  
**1. Disconnection of Defaulting Consumers:** K-Electric maintains a strict disconnection policy for non-paying consumers as part of its credit risk management【13†L4451-L4458】. All consumers whose debts were considered for write-off had been **permanently disconnected from the power supply prior to June 30, 2019**【7†L17932-L17939】. In the case of inactive accounts, the customer status was updated as “inactive” in the SAP billing system before year-end, ensuring no active service remained【7†L17932-L17939】. By cutting off supply, the Company signaled to defaulters that recovery was pursued to the fullest extent before any debt was written off.  

**2. Physical Site Surveys of Defaulters:** For each disconnected defaulter, K-Electric field teams carried out **on-site surveys** to verify the situation on ground【7†L17961-L17969】. These physical consumer survey forms (sample attached) documented critical evidence, including:  

- Whether the meter was present at site and in a disconnected state, or removed【3†L47-L55】.  
- Whether any **illegal abstraction** of power (“hook” connections or supply from neighboring premises) was observed, indicating ongoing theft despite formal disconnection【3†L49-L57】.  
- The status of the premises (e.g. intact, demolished, inaccessible). Notably, many defaulters’ premises were found **vacant, demolished, or removed** due to government anti-encroachment drives, meaning the customer no longer occupied a traceable location【7†L17975-L17983】. In such cases, physical recovery was impossible as the site itself had ceased to exist.  
- The presence of **Aerial Bundled Cable (ABC)** infrastructure in the area【3†L72-L80】. (K-Electric has deployed ABC cables in high-loss areas to prevent illegal connections; finding ABC in the area supports that any prior illegal hook-up would have been removed【3†L72-L80】.)  
- Photographic evidence: Surveyors captured dated photographs of the premises and meters to visually confirm that **no active electricity connection** remained【2†L99-L104】. Photographs of meter terminals, service poles, and premises entrances were taken as proof of disconnection (or, where applicable, evidence of tampering).  

Each survey form was signed by the surveyor (and, where possible, acknowledged by any local representative) to serve as an auditable record. These **Physical Consumer Survey Forms – Debtor Write-off Verification** clearly show that by the time of write-off, the defaulters’ connections were cut and **no electricity was being consumed** by or billed to those premises【3†L45-L53】【3†L72-L80】. In cases where the customer could be contacted, the surveyor also inquired whether they would opt for any bill adjustment schemes if offered, or the reasons for non-payment, but most defaulters were either untraceable or unwilling to settle outstanding dues【3†L88-L96】【3†L100-L108】. This on-ground verification process fulfilled the dual purpose of enhancing recovery (by giving one final chance for engagement) and documenting irrecoverability for each account.

**3. Consumer Engagement and Incentive Schemes:** K-Electric made **extensive efforts to rehabilitate defaulting customers** before final write-off. Multiple incentive and recovery schemes were introduced to facilitate payments from chronic defaulters【13†L4451-L4458】. Notably:  

- **“Current Bill ka Waada” and “Payment Loyalty Reward (PLR)” Schemes:** Defaulters were invited to join schemes whereby if they consistently paid current bills, or paid a portion of arrears, **the remaining old dues could be deferred or partially waived** as a reward. The surveyed defaulters were explicitly offered these options where feasible【2†L177-L184】. Only those who either refused such offers or failed to comply with installment plans were eventually considered for write-off.  
- **Installment Plans:** Many customers were offered easy installment schedules for arrears【13†L4451-L4458】. Write-off was considered only if the customer defaulted even on such facilitated plans or if the customer could not be located to negotiate terms.  
- **Recovery Agency Efforts:** Before abandoning recovery, **professional recovery agencies** engaged by K-Electric attempted to trace and collect from the defaulters【2†L181-L189】. Each defaulted case was referred to these agencies, who employed legal notices, field visits, and skip-tracing to locate the debtors. For cases where agencies also failed, the agencies issued **“no recovery possible” certificates**, confirming that all reasonable collection efforts had been exhausted with no success【2†L181-L189】. These certificates are on record for the subject debts and are available for inspection.  

Through these measures, K-Electric ensured that **write-off was truly a last resort**. Only those accounts were written off where: (a) the connection had long been severed; (b) the customer was either untraceable or demonstrated persistent non-responsiveness; (c) all incentive schemes and recovery tactics yielded no result; and (d) the passage of time and circumstances (e.g. demolished premises) rendered the chance of future recovery virtually nil. Any defaulter who showed willingness to pay, or who could be feasibly pursued further, was **not** granted a write-off. This careful selection is evidenced by the auditors’ notes that they even **excluded certain cases from write-off where they believed further recovery efforts were warranted**【2†L109-L117】【2†L119-L127】. K-Electric’s management similarly only put forward those cases for write-off that met the irrecoverability criteria as per the Company’s **“Policy and Procedures for Write-off of Bad Debts.”**  

## Internal Assessment and Justification Process  
K-Electric has instituted a robust internal process to justify and approve any bad debt write-off, ensuring multiple layers of review and documentation before an account is written off. The process for the FY 2019 write-offs included:  

- **Case Preparation by Business Units:** Each defaulting consumer’s case was individually prepared by the relevant Integrated Business Centre (IBC) – essentially the field office responsible for the customer. The IBC teams compiled all relevant data (consumer history, amount due, recovery steps taken, survey findings, etc.) and provided a **written justification as to why the debt should be considered irrecoverable**. This included confirming that the above-mentioned recovery efforts (disconnection, notices, offers, agency efforts) had been carried out.  
- **Internal Audit Review:** All proposed write-off cases were then **submitted to K-Electric’s Internal Audit Department for independent review**【2†L145-L148】. Internal Audit verified the evidence for each case – for example, checking that the customer was truly disconnected, that outstanding dues were correctly stated, and that documentation of recovery attempts (surveys, notices, agency certificate) was complete. The Internal Audit function in K-Electric is both rigorous and independent, reporting directly to the Board Audit Committee, which ensures that any write-off recommendation is scrutinized for compliance with policy and factual accuracy. Only after Internal Audit’s clearance were cases moved forward.  
- **Management Approval Committees:** K-Electric’s management set up dedicated committees at the head-office level to review the IBC cases and internal audit feedback. These committees included senior executives from the Finance, Customer Service, and Legal functions. They evaluated if all **“Policy for Write-off”** conditions were met and whether any alternative action (such as legal recourse) remained available. Each case file had to be **approved at the management committee level** before being escalated to the Board.  
- **Documentation and Record-Keeping:** For transparency, every step in the write-off proposal was documented. This includes the **Physical Survey Forms**, disconnection orders, copies of legal notices sent, any replies from customers, recovery agency reports, and internal approval memos. These records were indexed and made available to external auditors and, if required, can be furnished to tax authorities to substantiate the irrecoverability of each debt.

This multi-tiered internal process demonstrates that the Company took a **conscientious approach** to the write-offs. Far from expensing bad debts in a perfunctory manner, K-Electric **justified each account’s write-off on its individual merits**, with thorough cross-functional vetting. Such diligence reflects the Company’s commitment to compliance and prudent financial management.

## Audit Verification and External Oversight  
Perhaps most importantly, the **statutory external auditors** of K-Electric (A.F. Ferguson & Co. for FY 2019, as noted in the Annual Report) performed an extensive **independent verification of the bad debt write-offs**. This audit verification was conducted in conjunction with K-Electric’s tariff petition requirements, but it also squarely addresses the concern of whether sufficient recovery efforts were made. We highlight below the key audit procedures and findings (the Auditor’s Verification Report for bad debt write-offs is attached for reference):  

- **Confirmation of Disconnection and System Status:** The auditors **verified in K-Electric’s SAP system** that each defaulting consumer account had been marked as inactive (for permanently disconnected customers) on or before 30th June 2019【2†L53-L61】. They ensured no active billing was occurring on those accounts post-disconnection, which is a critical first test for a valid write-off.  
- **Physical Site Verification by Auditors:** In addition to reviewing K-Electric’s internal survey reports, the auditors themselves (with the help of **independent third-party surveyors engaged by the audit firm**) **visited numerous consumer locations** to validate the on-ground situation【2†L95-L104】. They physically inspected the premises to confirm that: (a) the electricity meters were removed or non-functional; (b) no illegal hook connections were supplying the location; and (c) in many cases, the premises were either vacant, demolished, or otherwise non-existent【2†L75-L84】【2†L97-L104】. The auditors’ teams took **geotagged photographs** during these visits, evidencing that there was no active connection or practical means to recover the outstanding amounts. (It is noteworthy that in certain areas with law-and-order challenges, special security was arranged so auditors could safely perform these verifications【2†L85-L93】, underscoring the thoroughness of the exercise.)  
- **Review of Survey Evidence and Rejection of Exceptions:** The auditors independently reviewed the results of all field surveys and supporting documents compiled by K-Electric【2†L106-L115】. They exercised an **objective judgment** on each case – in fact, the auditors **reserved the right to reject any case that did not meet the stringent write-off criteria**【2†L109-L117】. Indeed, they did **highlight and exclude certain cases** where they believed additional recovery efforts were still feasible【2†L109-L117】. This impartial filtering by external auditors provides strong assurance that only truly irrecoverable debts were finally written off.  
- **Traceability Checks:** The auditors required K-Electric to **demonstrate the lack of traceability of defaulters** as a condition for write-off. For each case, the Company provided information (where available) such as the customer’s last known contact details, national identity number (CNIC), and any update on their whereabouts. The auditors **verified that these defaulters could not be traced through available information** – effectively confirming that **no further legal or personal follow-up could yield recovery**【2†L123-L131】. If any actionable lead had existed (e.g. a known new address of the defaulter), those cases would not have qualified for write-off.  
- **Assessment of Partial Recoveries:** In some instances, K-Electric negotiated **partial settlements** with defaulters – for example, a customer might have paid a portion of the dues in exchange for restoration or continued service, with the remaining balance proposed for write-off due to inability to pay in full. The auditors **scrutinized such cases to ensure that any amount written off was genuinely the unrecoverable portion** and that the concession was granted to achieve at least some recovery【2†L129-L137】. They verified that such partial write-offs were necessary to **maintain the customer as a paying consumer going forward or to recover some portion of the debt**【2†L129-L137】. This procedure ensured that write-off was used strategically, not to forgive debt arbitrarily but to maximize overall recovery (a fact which in turn supports that K-Electric acted in good faith to recover amounts wherever possible).  
- **Verification of Internal Approvals and Board Authorization:** Crucially, the auditors **confirmed that all internal approval steps had been completed** – i.e., each case file bore evidence of review by the IBC (business team), Internal Audit department, and approval by the competent authority. Most importantly, the auditors **obtained the Board of Directors’ resolution approving the bad debt write-off**. They verified that K-Electric’s Board of Directors had formally approved the total write-off amount, and that the Board’s resolution explicitly certified **“the Company has made all best possible efforts to recover the amount being written-off”**【2†L147-L155】【7†L17940-L17944】. This independent acknowledgment by auditors (evidenced in their report and in the Annual Report disclosures) underscores that the **highest level of corporate governance was applied** to the write-offs, and that an external professional assessment concurred on the irrecoverability of these debts【7†L17953-L17955】.  

The external auditors’ involvement and the described procedures demonstrate a high degree of transparency. An extract from K-Electric’s Annual Report 2019 summarizes that the **statutory auditors verified the bad debt write-off claims and confirmed that the debts were not recoverable despite exhaustive efforts by the Company**【7†L17953-L17961】. It is highly unlikely that such write-offs would have been approved by both the Board and external auditors if any doubt remained regarding potential recovery. 

## Board of Directors’ Oversight and Governance  
**K-Electric’s Board of Directors** has been fully engaged in overseeing the issue of long-outstanding receivables and any decision to write off bad debts. The corporate governance around this matter in FY 2019 included the following elements:

- **Policy Approval:** The Board had approved a formal **“Policy and Procedures for Write-off of Bad Debts”** which set out clear criteria and steps to be followed before a debt can be written off【7†L17946-L17954】. This policy (approved by the Board Audit Committee and then the full Board) aligns with both accounting standards and regulatory guidelines, ensuring that write-offs are handled consistently and prudently.  
- **Board Audit Committee Review:** The Board Audit Committee (comprising non-executive and independent directors) reviewed management’s proposals for bad debt provisions and write-offs as part of its mandate to oversee financial reporting and internal controls. The Committee’s report for 2019 (enclosed in the Annual Report) indicates that the Board and its committees place strong emphasis on **safeguarding assets, ensuring accuracy of records, and compliance with policies**【13†L4525-L4533】. In practice, this meant the Audit Committee vetted the list of defaulters proposed for write-off, asked critical questions about the recovery actions taken, and satisfied itself that all possible efforts had been made. Only then did it recommend the write-off to the full Board for approval.  
- **Board Approval and Certification:** At the Board meeting approving the annual financial statements for FY 2019, the **Board of Directors passed a resolution to write off the specified bad debts**, amounting to Rs. 4.05 billion. The Board’s resolution explicitly **certified that all best possible recovery efforts had been exhausted in respect of these debts**, in accordance with the Board-approved policy【7†L17940-L17947】. This statement is also disclosed in note to the financial statements, underscoring the Board’s assurance of due diligence. The Board’s approval was a mandatory step not only by internal policy but also per NEPRA’s regulatory requirement for claiming these write-offs in the consumer tariff【7†L17940-L17948】. Thus, the Board was keenly aware that by approving the write-off, it was also attesting to regulators and stakeholders that K-Electric had done everything feasible to recover the dues.  
- **Continuous Oversight of Recovery Strategies:** The Board actively oversees management’s strategies to reduce bad debts and improve recoveries. In 2019, under the Board’s guidance, K-Electric intensified various **recovery initiatives** – for example, introducing **new collection schemes for non-paying consumers, disconnection drives, rebates for clearing old arrears, and technological measures like ABC cables to curb power theft**【13†L4451-L4458】. These efforts, reviewed at Board level, demonstrate that the Company’s leadership was focused on minimizing the need for write-offs by improving collections. The **Annual Report 2019** notes these strategies as part of the Company’s risk mitigation for credit risk, indicating a proactive approach authorized and endorsed by the Board【13†L4451-L4458】.  
- **Governance and Transparency:** K-Electric’s governance framework ensures transparency with all stakeholders, including regulators like NEPRA and the FBR. The Annual Report affirms that the **Board reviews and approves the Company’s financial statements, with focus on significant judgments and compliance**【13†L4525-L4533】. Any material write-off of receivables falls into this purview. Furthermore, K-Electric engages in **regular dialogues with NEPRA** and shares timely information to maintain transparency【13†L4465-L4473】, which in 2019 included information on bad debt write-off claims. This culture of transparency is indicative of K-Electric’s approach to also cooperating fully with tax authorities. We have disclosed in our accounts and to our power regulator the nature and extent of bad debt write-offs, and we now provide the same clarity to the LTO through this explanation and the supporting documents.

In summary, **the decision to write off bad debts in Tax Year 2019 was governed by a rigorous framework of approvals and oversight**, culminating in the Board of Directors’ authorization. The Board’s involvement is a strong safeguard against any abuse of bad debt expense claims – it ensures that management cannot simply “brush off” collectible debts. In this case, the Board was satisfied (and declared so in writing) that the debts were indeed uncollectible despite all efforts【7†L17940-L17947】. This high-level oversight should give confidence that the write-off deduction claimed by K-Electric is genuine and backed by solid governance.

## Conclusion and Prayer  
K-Electric assures the LTO Karachi that the **bad debt write-offs claimed in Tax Year 2019 are fully justified** by the facts and were made in accordance with law. The Company **exercised utmost diligence and good faith** in pursuing every reasonable recovery measure before concluding that these debts had become impossible to recover. Only after **field surveys, customer outreach, legal recourse, and third-party recovery attempts** had failed were the debts written off. The process was marked by transparency at each step – verified by independent auditors and approved at the highest levels of the Company’s management and board. We have enclosed supporting documentation, including:  

- **Auditors’ Verification Procedures (FY 2019)** – highlighting the audit steps undertaken to validate disconnections and irrecoverability【2†L147-L155】【7†L17953-L17961】.  
- **Sample Physical Survey Forms for Disconnected Defaulters** – demonstrating on-site evidence collection (meter removal, premises status, etc.)【3†L47-L55】【3†L72-L80】.  
- **Internal Write-off Justification Memos and Recovery Agency Certificates** – evidencing internal assessments and third-party confirmation of uncollectibility【2†L181-L189】.  
- **Extracts from K-Electric Annual Report 2019** – showing the Board’s certification of recovery efforts and the strategies deployed to minimize bad debts【7†L17940-L17948】【13†L4451-L4458】.  

In view of this comprehensive record, we respectfully request that the bad debt expense of FY 2019 be **accepted as an allowable deduction** in K-Electric’s tax assessment. The Company has been fully compliant with the provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (in particular, the conditions for write-off of bad debts that were previously offered to tax as income). We also highlight that allowing these genuine bad debts is consistent with the accrual-based taxation of income; denying the write-off would effectively tax revenue that was never realized despite best efforts. We trust that the information provided addresses the queries raised in the notice.  

K-Electric remains committed to **continued cooperation** with tax authorities. Should your office require any further information or clarification, or wish to review the underlying files and evidence for any specific account, we are ready to provide full access and assistance. We appreciate your attention to this matter and look forward to a favorable resolution of the audit.  

Thank you for your consideration.  

Yours sincerely,

3. Are there any previous communications or assessments relating to this tax credit that need to be referenced?
4. Please confirm if you want the response in the format of a legal reply letter, memo to client, or an internal analysis note.

Once I have this information, I can craft a tailored and comprehensive reply.

**ABC Tax Consultants**  
123 Sunset Boulevard, Phase-II, DHA  
Karachi, Pakistan.  
Ph: +92-21-XXXXXXX | Email: info@abctax.com.pk  

**Date:** June 20, 2025  

**To:**  
Umair Malik  
Assistant Commissioner Inland Revenue (Zone-VI, Range-B, Unit-04)  
Large Taxpayers Office (LTO) Karachi.  

**Subject:** Response to Notice under Section 122(9) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Tax Year 2019 (Tax Credit Claimed under Section 65B)  

**Reference:** Your Notice No. *1543137* dated June 16, 2025 (received under Section 122(9) for TY 2019)  

Dear Sir,  

We write on behalf of our client, **K-Electric Limited** (hereinafter “the Company”), in response to the above-referenced notice questioning the tax credit of Rs. 2,914,224,400 claimed under Section 65B of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”) for Tax Year 2019. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify the facts and legal position. The Company’s response is outlined below in a structured manner for your kind consideration.  

## 1. Tax Credit Claimed under Section 65B – Amount and Basis  
The Company confirms that it claimed a **tax credit of Rs. 2,914,224,400** in its return for Tax Year 2019 under Section 65B of the Ordinance. This amount represents **10% of the Company’s investment in plant and machinery** during the year, as permitted by law【20†L379-L387】. In other words, the Company made qualifying capital investments of approximately Rs. 29.14 billion in new “plant and machinery” in Tax Year 2019, and accordingly availed the 10% tax credit on these investments (0.10 × 29.14 billion ≈ 2.914 billion). The credit was computed and claimed in good faith **in accordance with Section 65B(1)** of the Ordinance, which (prior to amendment by Finance Act 2019) provided a tax credit equal to ten percent of the amount invested by a company in the purchase of plant and machinery for the purposes of extension, expansion, balancing, modernisation, or replacement of industrial undertaking plant and machinery【20†L379-L387】. 

**Statutory Basis:** Section 65B was originally introduced via Finance Act 2010 as an incentive for industrial investments, allowing a 10% tax credit on investment in plant & machinery installed between July 1, 2010 and June 30, 2015【25†L5405-L5413】【25†L5414-L5422】. This incentive was subsequently extended by various Finance Acts (2015, 2016, 2018) to cover investments up to June 30, 2021【13†L213-L218】. Thus, throughout the period up to Tax Year 2018, companies could claim a 10% credit of qualifying capital expenditures, and Tax Year 2019 fell within the intended eligibility period【13†L213-L218】. *(We discuss the Finance Act 2019 amendment and its legal status in Section 3 below.)* 

## 2. Investment in Plant & Machinery during Tax Year 2019 – Factual Details  
**Overview of Capital Additions:** During the financial year ended June 30, 2019 (corresponding to Tax Year 2019), K-Electric Limited undertook substantial capital investment across its generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure. The audited financial statements for FY 2019 evidence capital expenditures of approximately **Rs. 39.98 billion** on system improvements during the year【15†L5037-L5040】. Excluding capitalized borrowing costs, the direct additions to plant and equipment amounted to around **Rs. 35.57 billion** in FY 2019【15†L5103-L5109】. These figures demonstrate the scale of the Company’s commitment to expanding and modernizing its operational capacity. 

In particular, the Company made the following notable additions to fixed assets in the relevant year (as reflected in the audited accounts and supporting documentation): 

- **Generation (“Plant and Machinery”)** – The Company invested in new generation equipment and upgrades. Notably, work commenced on the 900 MW RLNG-fired Bin Qasim Power Station III project (BQPS-III) and other enhancements. The financial statements show additions of approximately **Rs. 15.61 billion** under the “Plant and machinery” category for the year【17†L15799-L15808】. *(This includes major plant equipment purchases and installations completed within the year. BQPS-III’s initial expenditures are reflected, although the project was in progress.)*  

- **Transmission Network** – K-Electric continued its “TP-1000” transmission project (a USD 450 million initiative) to upgrade Karachi’s grid. **Six new grid stations were commissioned** during FY 2019【21†L1-L4】, along with associated transmission lines and equipment. The Company’s books record additions (capitalization) in transmission grid assets (e.g. transformers, switchgear, lines) in Tax Year 2019 (approximately **Rs. 0.158 billion** transferred to fixed assets for fully completed transmission projects in the year【17†L15799-L15808】, with further transmission work in progress as of year-end). 

- **Distribution Network** – A significant portion of the FY 2019 capex was devoted to expanding and modernizing the power distribution network across Karachi. This includes installation of new feeders, pole-mounted transformers (PMTs), low-loss conductors, smart meters, and other system upgrades to reduce losses and improve reliability. The audited financials report about **Rs. 17.34 billion** in additions under “Distribution network & renewals” for the year【17†L15799-L15808】. These assets (being electric plant and equipment) were procured and installed during 2019 to extend service coverage and enhance efficiency. 

- **Other Plant and Equipment** – The Company also invested in ancillary plant, machinery and equipment (e.g. vehicles, tools, IT systems related to operations, etc.) and made improvements to existing facilities. For completeness, we note that total capital work-in-progress transferred to operating fixed assets in FY 2019 was **Rs. 34.84 billion**【28†L25-L33】, which aligns with the scale of completed projects put into use during the year. The **tax credit claim of Rs. 2.914 billion was strictly limited to the qualifying plant & machinery components** of these investments (such as generation, transmission and distribution equipment). Non-qualifying expenditures (e.g. civil works, buildings, land, or intangible assets) were **excluded** from the credit base. 

**Evidence:** The above figures are substantiated by the Company’s audited financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2019 (particularly Notes 4 and 5 to the accounts) and the detailed fixed asset schedules and invoices already furnished to your office. We have attached an annexure summarizing the additions to plant and machinery during the year, with references to relevant ledger accounts and asset commissioning certificates. These documents demonstrate that **new plant and machinery worth ~Rs. 29.14 billion was purchased and installed by the Company within Tax Year 2019**, forming the basis for the Section 65B credit. We respectfully invite attention to the fact that all such assets were **put to use on or before June 30, 2019**, falling squarely within the timeframe stipulated by law for the investment tax credit. 

## 3. Legal Entitlement to 10% Tax Credit – Section 65B and Amendments  
The notice under reply appears to question the allowability of the full 10% tax credit, possibly referencing the amendment introduced through the Finance Act, 2019 (which attempted to reduce the credit to 5% for Tax Year 2019). We address this legal point below: 

- **Section 65B Provisions:** As noted, Section 65B(1) of the Ordinance (pre-amendment) provided a **10% tax credit** to a company that invests in the purchase of plant and machinery for the **balancing, modernisation or replacement** of plant & machinery in an industrial undertaking in Pakistan【25†L5405-L5413】. Over time, the scope was expanded to include **extensions and expansions** of existing undertakings【20†L379-L387】. The credit is allowed against the taxpayer’s normal tax liability for the year of installation, with any unutilized amount carryable forward for up to two subsequent years【27†L5427-L5436】【27†L5437-L5445】. All these conditions were met by K-Electric – the Company is a Pakistani resident **industrial undertaking** (engaged in the generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity, which is explicitly recognized as an industrial undertaking under the Ordinance【32†L23-L31】), and the plant/machinery in question was new, purchased and installed within the legally prescribed period. There is **no statutory bar** on power utility companies availing this credit; on the contrary, K-Electric’s investments fall squarely within the incentivized activities that Section 65B aimed to promote (i.e. upgrading Pakistan’s industrial capacity). 

- **Finance Act 2019 Amendment:** It is acknowledged that the Finance Act, 2019 introduced a proviso to Section 65B(1) which **reduced the tax credit rate from 10% to 5% for the tax year 2019**, and also brought forward the sunset date for investments to June 30, 2019 (from 2021)【13†L213-L218】. In effect, the legislature sought to halve the credit for investments made in Tax Year 2019. However, **critically**, this change was enacted in mid-2019 and was made applicable to an ongoing tax period, thereby retrospectively impairing the incentive for investments that were already under way or completed by June 2019. The Company submits that its claim of Rs. 2.914 billion was correctly based on the original 10% rate, for the following reasons: 

   **(a) The 5% proviso was held **ultra vires** and struck down by the Courts:** The **Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan** has since adjudicated on this very issue and **restored the 10% tax credit entitlement for investments made up to June 30, 2019**【12†L162-L170】. In a landmark judgment issued in 2024 (on appeals against a Sindh High Court decision), the Supreme Court examined the constitutionality of the Finance Act 2019 amendment to Section 65B. The apex court **invalidated the proviso that had reduced the credit to 5% for 2019**, on the grounds that it discriminated between two classes of taxpayers without justification【13†L223-L231】. Taxpayer companies that invested in plant & machinery in years 2010–2018 were allowed a 10% credit, whereas those investing in 2019 (the “first category” of affected taxpayers) were abruptly restricted to 5%, despite no material difference in circumstances【13†L223-L231】. The Court held this differentiation to violate Article 25 of the Constitution (equal treatment) and struck down the proviso as having **no legal force ab initio**【13†L223-L231】. Consequently, the law stands as if the 10% rate was never reduced for Tax Year 2019. The Supreme Court’s judgment categorically **allows taxpayers who had imported/purchased and installed machinery by 30th June 2019 to avail the full 10% credit**【12†L162-L170】. K-Electric squarely falls in this category, having completed its qualifying investments by the stipulated date. We have enclosed copies of the relevant court decision highlights for your ready reference. 

   **(b) Legitimate Expectation and Vested Right:** Even apart from the above judicial verdict, the Company had a legitimate expectation (based on the law prevailing at the time of its investment decisions and installation of assets) that a 10% credit would be available. The abrupt change introduced via Finance Act 2019, after the close of FY 2019, created an unreasonable retrospective effect. This was precisely the injustice that the superior courts have now remedied. In light of the Supreme Court’s ruling, the **legal basis for disallowing or reducing the credit in question no longer exists**. Any adjustment under Section 122(5A) founded on the now-invalidated proviso would not be sustainable. 

In view of the foregoing, the Company’s claim of the tax credit at 10% is firmly supported by both the **law (Section 65B as interpreted by the superior courts)** and the **facts (timely completion of qualifying investments)**. We respectfully submit that the action proposed in the 122(9) notice, to the extent it envisages disallowance or recalculation of the credit, is untenable and should not be carried to an amended assessment. 

## 4. Compliance with Section 65B Conditions and Documentation  
For completeness, we address any other potential concerns raised in the notice regarding the Section 65B credit: 

- **Nature of the Company:** K-Electric Limited is an established industrial undertaking engaged in the generation and distribution of electricity in Pakistan. This status as an “industrial undertaking” is explicitly recognized in tax law【32†L23-L31】, meaning the Company is eligible to avail industrial investment incentives such as Section 65B. The credit in question was not an exemption or income reduction, but a **tax credit** against tax payable, duly accounted for in the return. 

- **Qualifying Assets:** The credit was claimed **only on eligible “plant and machinery”** acquired and installed for the Company’s own business operations (power generation, transmission, distribution). All such assets were new and not previously used, fulfilling the condition that the investment be in new plant and machinery. No part of the credit relates to, for example, office equipment, vehicles for personal use, land or buildings, as those do not qualify. A detailed schedule of the plant and machinery investments, cross-referenced with purchase invoices, has been provided. We would be pleased to furnish any additional evidence you may require to verify that each asset meets the stipulated criteria. 

- **Installation Timeframe:** Each item of machinery on which credit is claimed was **installed and operational within the Tax Year 2019**, i.e. by June 30, 2019. The Company’s records (including fixed asset register entries and commissioning reports) substantiate the commissioning dates. This satisfies the temporal condition of Section 65B(2) (as modified by Finance Acts) that the plant/machinery be purchased and installed between the specified dates. As noted earlier, the investments were completed well within the permissible window (prior to July 2019). 

- **Tax Payment and Carry-forward:** The Company’s tax computation for TY 2019 showed that the 65B credit was applied against its tax liability for the year. Any unutilized portion is being carried forward in accordance with Section 65B(4)【27†L5434-L5442】. We ensure that the aggregate credit does not exceed the 10% of investment cap. All workings have been provided in the tax return and can be reviewed; they are in line with the Ordinance’s mechanism (credit first adjusts the tax payable, and any remaining carries forward up to two years). There is no loss to revenue – in fact, this incentive simply reduced the Company’s effective tax for the year as intended by the legislature to encourage capital expenditure. 

In light of the above, **K-Electric has fully complied with the letter and spirit of Section 65B**. The Company acted within the four corners of the law in claiming the tax credit and has substantiated the claim with proper documentation. We respectfully submit that the issues identified in the 122(9) notice have been adequately addressed by the foregoing explanations, supported by statutory provisions and judicial precedents. 

## 5. Conclusion and Prayer  
In conclusion, we reiterate that the tax credit of Rs. 2,914,224,400 for Tax Year 2019 was rightly claimed under Section 65B, being **10% of eligible plant & machinery investments** made by an industrial undertaking (K-Electric) during the year. The claim is backed by the law as it then stood and as it stands today after the Supreme Court’s clarification【12†L162-L170】【13†L223-L231】. The Company has invested heavily in Pakistan’s power infrastructure, and Section 65B’s incentive was a key policy measure to support such industrial investments. We therefore **request that the proposed amendment/disallowance be vacated**, and the tax credit as claimed be accepted in full. 

We trust that the provided information satisfactorily resolves the queries raised. The Company remains at your disposal for any further clarification or documentation that you may require. Please do not hesitate to contact the undersigned for any additional information.  

Thank you for your consideration. 

Yours faithfully,  

**For ABC Tax Consultants,**  
*(Authorized Representatives for K-Electric Ltd.)*  

Muhammad Ali Khan  
Senior Tax Advisor (Enrollment No. ___)

2. Annexure B – Copies of Invoices, Installation Certificates, and Fixed Asset Register extracts (FY 2019)  
3. Copy of Hon. Supreme Court Judgment dated ______ 2024 (re: Section 65B)【12†L162-L170】【13†L223-L231】
