# Exclusion of Meter Cost Reimbursements from Turnover under Section 113

## Introduction  
This submission explains why receipts from customers relating to electric meters and similar reimbursements – charged on an **actual cost** basis under NEPRA guidelines – **should not be treated as turnover from the sale of goods** for purposes of minimum tax under Section 113 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. In summary, these receipts do not arise from any sale of merchandise or commercially exploitable goods. Rather, they represent cost reimbursements for assets that remain the property of the utility (K-Electric, “KE”) and are provided to customers under regulatory mandate. As such, these amounts fall outside the scope of “turnover” as intended in Section 113. This position is supported by NEPRA’s regulatory framework, relevant accounting principles, and interpretations of Section 113 of the Ordinance, as detailed below.

## Receipts Not Derived from Sale of Goods  
Section 113 imposes a minimum tax based on a taxpayer’s turnover, which is defined as **gross sales or receipts from the business**, excluding sales tax and similar levies【6†L442-L450】. Crucially, the law envisions turnover as income generated **from the sale of goods or provision of services** in the ordinary course of business【6†L442-L450】. Pakistan’s courts have reinforced this interpretation. For instance, the Lahore High Court held that *the tax authority must demonstrate that a taxpayer is “engaged in the business of selling goods” and that the gross receipts in question are **derived from the sale of those goods***【29†L528-L536】. If receipts do not stem from the sale of goods, they do **not form part of turnover** for Section 113 purposes【29†L528-L536】. 

In the case of KE’s meter-related receipts, there is **no sale of goods occurring**. KE is not in the business of trading in electric meters or ancillary equipment; it is a power distribution utility. Amounts recovered from consumers for meters, connection infrastructure, or similar items are **not revenue from selling any product**. Rather, they are payments to cover the cost of equipment that enables the electricity supply service. **No goods are sold or exchanged** – the customer receives no merchandise to own or resell, only the continued provision of electric service. Therefore, such receipts lie outside the ambit of “gross sales or receipts” arising from sale of goods, and should be excluded from turnover in calculating the minimum tax.

## Assets Remain Under KE’s Control (No Transfer of Ownership)  
A defining feature of a **sale of goods** is the transfer of title or ownership of the item to the buyer. In the present case, any meters or equipment provided remain **wholly under the control and ownership of KE**, the distribution company. NEPRA’s Consumer Service Manual makes this clear: distribution companies must provide the appropriate metering installation for a new connection **at the cost of the consumer**, but the meter itself remains part of the company’s system【18†L1155-L1163】. In fact, NEPRA explicitly prohibits utilities from charging ongoing “meter rent” once a consumer has paid for the meter’s cost, confirming that the **consumer’s payment is purely a cost reimbursement, not a purchase price**【18†L1155-L1163】【18†L1164-L1172】. The meter is installed at the consumer’s premises for service delivery, yet it **continues to be the company’s property and responsibility** (the consumer is only tasked with its safe-keeping)【18†L1164-L1172】. 

Because **control of the metering equipment never passes to the customer**, there is no actual sale. The customer does not acquire ownership rights in the meter; they cannot remove it for use elsewhere, nor dispose of it. This is analogous to a lease or service asset rather than a sold product. Under **accounting principles**, revenue is recognized only when control of a good or service transfers to the customer【42†L2120-L2127】. Here, control of the meter does not transfer – KE retains it – indicating that the transaction is **not a revenue-generating sale of a good** in substance. Consequently, the receipts for meter costs should **not be characterized as turnover from goods sold**.

## No Commercial Exploitation by Customers (Not a Typical Sale)  
Another hallmark of a genuine sale of goods is that the buyer can commercially exploit the item (use it, consume it, or even resell it) independent of the seller. In the case of KE’s meter and infrastructure reimbursements, consumers have **no commercial role or benefit** beyond receiving utility service. The items in question (e.g. meters, service cables, transformers for new connections) are **dedicated assets for delivering electricity** to that customer; they are not fungible goods the customer can utilize for other purposes or profit. The customer cannot resell the meter or use it to generate income – it is simply attached to KE’s network, serving as part of the regulated supply system.

This underscores that these transactions **lack the fundamental character of a sale**. The customer’s payment is not in exchange for a tradable good or independent value; it is in exchange for KE installing necessary equipment to provide regulated service. Such an arrangement is effectively a **cost-sharing mechanism** dictated by regulation, not a commercial sale contract. Since the customers do not obtain any asset for business use or resale, the receipts from them **do not constitute turnover from commercial sales** of goods.

## Regulated by NEPRA – Reimbursements at Actual Cost, Not for Profit  
The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA) strictly governs how distribution companies like KE handle meter provision and related charges. Under NEPRA’s guidelines, any charges to consumers for meters or connection infrastructure are structured as **reimbursement of actual costs** incurred, without profit. For example, NEPRA’s Consumer Service Manual specifies that KE (and other DISCOs) must either provide the metering installation at cost or, if the utility’s own meter is unavailable, allow the consumer to procure one meeting the approved specifications【18†L1155-L1163】. In either scenario, the consumer pays no more than the **actual cost of the meter and installation** (plus minimal standard handling or installation fees in some cases)【18†L1143-L1151】【18†L1155-L1163】. The regulator even mandates that if a consumer already bears the meter’s cost, the company **cannot levy any monthly meter rent**【18†L1163-L1166】. This ensures the company does not earn a margin on the meter – the transaction is **cost recovery only**.

Furthermore, broader industry practice confirmed by NEPRA indicates that many network assets are **funded by consumers and then transferred to the DISCOs at no cost**【33†L181-L189】. Consumers finance new connection infrastructure (meters, lines, transformers) and once installed, these assets become part of the company’s network **without any sale consideration**【33†L181-L189】. NEPRA’s concern (echoed by consumer groups) has been that such **consumer-funded assets** should not even be counted in the company’s rate base for profit, since the utility did not invest in them【33†L189-L197】. In other words, the regulatory framework treats these contributions as *pass-through funds* – **not revenue – and precludes utilities from profiting on them**【33†L189-L197】. This reinforces that KE’s meter cost receipts are fundamentally **reimbursements under regulatory compulsion**, not revenue from voluntary market transactions. They lack any profit element by design and therefore should not inflate the “turnover” figure which is intended to reflect gross income from business operations.

## Accounting Treatment (Reimbursements vs. Revenue)  
From an accounting perspective, the nature of these receipts aligns with **liability or contra-asset treatment rather than income**. When a customer pays a utility for equipment that remains the utility’s asset, standard practice is to record it as a **customer contribution** or deferred credit, not as immediate revenue. International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) support this view. Under **IFRS 15 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers)**, revenue is recognized only when a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of a good or service to the customer【42†L2120-L2127】. Here, KE’s performance obligation is the ongoing supply of electricity, and the meter is a facilitating device for that service – its provision does not constitute a separate deliverable of goods transferred to the customer. Since the customer **never takes control of the meter asset**, KE’s receipt of funds for that meter is not treated as revenue from a delivered good. Instead, such contributions would typically be accounted for either as a deferred income, recognized over time as the customer receives service, or as a reduction of the asset’s cost. In either case, the **accounting framework distinguishes these reimbursements from normal sale revenues**. 

This accounting treatment reflects the economic substance: KE is not selling meters to make a profit; it is **recovering a cost**. Therefore, including these receipts in “turnover” (which is essentially gross revenue) would misrepresent the true revenue of the business. It would also conflict with the accrual concept and matching principle, since the receipts are tied to assets providing future service rather than immediate earnings. The appropriate view – for both accounting and tax – is to treat these receipts **not as part of gross sales**, but as cost contributions.

## Interpretations of Section 113 and Turnover  
Pakistan’s tax authorities and courts have recognized that **not all receipts of a business count toward turnover for minimum tax**. As noted, *turnover* under Section 113 means the gross amount earned **from the taxpayer’s trading/business activities**, specifically the sale of goods or rendering of services【6†L442-L450】. Courts have placed the onus on the tax department to prove that a particular stream of receipts was generated by such sales in order to subject it to minimum tax【29†L528-L536】. In a directly relevant precedent, the Lahore High Court examined whether a power sector entity’s receipts fell under “sale of goods” for Section 113. The Court held that a government-owned transmission company (NTDC) was **not subject to turnover tax on amounts it collected**, because the tax department failed to show that NTDC was engaged in any sale of electricity (goods) – NTDC’s licensed role was transmission service, not selling power【29†L528-L536】. By analogy, KE’s meter cost recoveries are ancillary to its service, not sales of goods, and thus should **not be counted in turnover**. 

It is important to emphasize that **Section 113’s minimum tax is not designed as a catch-all on every receipt**, but targets those businesses that, despite high gross revenues from sales, pay little income tax due to deductions or exemptions. Including non-revenue reimbursements in the turnover base would stretch the provision beyond its intent. Leading tax commentators have concurred that **“gross receipts” in the turnover definition refer to revenues from the core business activities**【6†L442-L450】. In KE’s case, the core revenue is from sale of electricity units (which is already subject to turnover tax). In contrast, meter reimbursements are **incidental and recover the company’s outlay** on customer-specific equipment. They are not *income* earned from trading activity. Therefore, subjecting these receipts to minimum tax would not only be inequitable (taxing a recovery of cost as if it were profit), but also inconsistent with the spirit of Section 113 and the jurisprudence requiring a nexus to *sale of goods*.

## Conclusion  
In light of the above, KE’s meter-related and similar reimbursed receipts **should be excluded from the turnover for the purposes of Section 113 minimum tax**. These receipts fail to meet the definition of turnover because they **do not represent proceeds of any sale of goods or services** by the company in the ordinary sense. The meters and equipment funded by these payments remain the **property and under the control of KE**, with customers only benefitting from their use as part of the electrical supply service – not as owners of goods. Customers neither exploit nor resell the items, confirming the non-commercial nature of the transaction. Moreover, NEPRA’s regulatory guidelines constrain these charges to an **actual cost reimbursement model**, with no profit element, reinforcing that they are fundamentally cost recoveries rather than revenue-generating sales【18†L1155-L1163】【33†L189-L197】. 

This treatment is further supported by accounting principles (revenue recognition tied to transfer of control) and by legal interpretation (turnover tax applying only to receipts from sales activity)【42†L2120-L2127】【29†L528-L536】. To include such reimbursements in turnover would be to mischaracterize their nature and effectively tax the company on recouped costs. We respectfully submit that tax authorities acknowledge these facts and **exclude meter cost reimbursements and similar NEPRA-regulated recovery amounts from KE’s turnover** when computing the minimum tax under Section 113 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. This approach is consistent with the law, the regulatory framework, and the principles of fair taxation.

Section 113 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 imposes minimum tax on a taxpayer’s turnover, which is defined as gross receipts from the business excluding sales tax and similar levies. These items remain the property of KE and are fully integrated into its regulated distribution network.

Ownership and control are central to determining whether a transaction constitutes a sale of goods. NEPRA’s Consumer Service Manual expressly stipulates that while consumers may bear the cost of meters, title remains with the utility. Customers merely have physical access to the meter for electricity consumption; they do not own, possess, or control the asset beyond its intended purpose. NEPRA further prohibits utilities from charging ongoing meter rent after cost recovery, underscoring that these payments are purely cost reimbursements, not sales proceeds.

Additionally, the absence of commercial exploitation confirms the non-sale nature of these transactions. Here, consumers have no such rights; meters serve solely as instruments to deliver electricity, fully integrated into KE’s operational network.

NEPRA’s regulatory framework reinforces this characterization. Charges to consumers for meters or related infrastructure are strictly regulated as reimbursements of actual costs incurred, without any profit element. We write on behalf of our client, United Energy Pakistan Limited (“UEP” or “the Company”), in reference to the Penalty Notice dated June 24, 2025 issued under Section 182(10) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”) for Tax Year 2020.

At the outset, we respectfully submit that the very foundation of the penalty proceedings is directly linked to the amended assessment order dated May 8, 2025, passed under Section 122(4) read with Section 122(5A) of the Ordinance. This amended assessment order has already been contested through a duly filed appeal, which is presently pending adjudication before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (“ATIR”). As such, the issues giving rise to the penalty notice are still under judicial consideration, and no final determination on the underlying tax liability has been made. It is thus premature and legally untenable to proceed with penalty proceedings at this stage.

**Factual Background and Nature of Dispute:**

The principal issue under dispute pertains to the disallowance of tax credit amounting to Rs. 661,925,776 claimed by UEP under Section 65B of the Ordinance. The detailed grounds of appeal filed before the ATIR set forth the following key facts and legal arguments which we summarize below for your kind consideration:

1. **Separate and Independent Nature of Tax Credit under Section 65B:**

The Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue (ACIR) erroneously disallowed the tax credit under Section 65B on the ground that the related assets had been allowed 100% depreciation under the Third Schedule to the Ordinance. It is respectfully submitted that the tax credit under Section 65B constitutes a separate and independent incentive, distinct from depreciation allowances. While depreciation provides for a cost recovery mechanism over time (or accelerated in the case of 100% depreciation), the objective of Section 65B is to promote fresh capital investment by allowing an additional credit on qualifying capital expenditures. The disallowance reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the independent nature and purpose of the two provisions.

2. **Nature of Capital Expenditure in E&P Sector:**

The disallowed credit relates to substantial below-ground capital installations necessary for UEP’s exploration and production (E&P) operations, including wellheads, drilling infrastructure, pipelines, and related underground facilities. The ACIR failed to appreciate that, within the specialized context of oil and gas E&P operations, such below-ground infrastructure forms an integral part of the operational extraction plant and qualifies as "plant and machinery" for purposes of Section 65B.

3. **Recognition of Cost under Sections 76(2) and 76(3):**

The ACIR also disregarded the clear statutory language of Sections 76(2) and 76(3) of the Ordinance, which recognize that the acquisition cost of an asset includes all amounts incurred in acquiring, altering, improving, or constructing the asset. The services disallowed — including drilling, rig operations, well services, survey charges, engineering services, and associated support functions — directly contributed to the creation and installation of capital assets essential to UEP’s oil extraction operations. These costs were properly capitalized in the books of account, transferred from Capital Work-in-Progress (CWIP) to operating assets, and fully documented through comprehensive asset schedules, installation records, and sample invoices duly submitted to the department.

4. **Misapplication of Supreme Court Judgment:**

The ACIR improperly invoked the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment dated September 18, 2024 to deny the credit. The said judgment merely upheld the legislative validity of certain amendments to Section 65B but did not categorically preclude the availability of credit where both purchase and installation were completed prior to June 30, 2019 — a condition which UEP fully satisfies. The ACIR’s reliance on the judgment is misplaced and does not justify outright disallowance of the credit.

5. **Procedural Violations and Denial of Due Process:**

It is further submitted that the ACIR finalized the amended assessment without affording a meaningful opportunity of being heard and without adequately examining the extensive documentation provided by the taxpayer, including detailed capitalization schedules, CWIP transfer reports, and supporting contractual records. This procedural lapse constitutes denial of natural justice, as enshrined under Article 10A of the Constitution of Pakistan.

6. **Consistency in Treatment of Below-Ground Assets:**

It is also important to highlight that while the department has allowed 100% depreciation on these very same below-ground assets under the Third Schedule, it has simultaneously refused to recognize them as qualifying assets for purposes of Section 65B. This inconsistent treatment is inherently contradictory and legally untenable. If the nature of the asset is recognized for one purpose, it must logically be recognized for all applicable tax incentives unless expressly excluded by law.

**Premature Invocation of Penalty Proceedings:**

Given the factual and legal complexity of the dispute, as summarized above, it is respectfully submitted that initiating penalty proceedings before final adjudication of the appeal is contrary to well-established principles of fair adjudication and due process. The tax liability itself remains uncertain and under judicial review. Until a final determination of the liability is made by the ATIR, any penalty proceedings would be premature and may prejudge the outcome of the pending appeal.

It is a cardinal principle of tax jurisprudence that penalties are intended to address deliberate or contumacious defaults, not to penalize taxpayers for genuine and bona fide disputes on interpretation of complex statutory provisions. The disputed matter involves intricate legal interpretation of tax incentives applicable to capital expenditures in the E&P sector — an area that inherently warrants specialized consideration and cannot be treated as a simple compliance failure.

**Good Faith Conduct of Taxpayer:**

Without prejudice to its legal stance in appeal, our client has demonstrated good faith by voluntarily initiating the process for settlement of the disputed amount of tax. This voluntary payment initiative, undertaken solely to safeguard revenue interests during pendency of appeal, further demonstrates the bona fide conduct of our client and negates any inference of deliberate default.

**Prayer for Relief:**

In view of the foregoing, we respectfully submit that:

- The issues leading to the penalty notice are presently sub judice before the ATIR;
- The nature of dispute is purely interpretative involving complex legal questions relating to eligibility of tax credits;
- There has been no willful or deliberate default on part of the taxpayer;
- Voluntary payment is already being arranged without prejudice to the taxpayer’s rights in appeal.

Accordingly, we humbly request that the penalty proceedings initiated under Section 182(10) be **withdrawn in entirety**, or in the alternative, be kept in abeyance pending final adjudication of the appeal before the ATIR. This course of action will serve the ends of justice, maintain procedural integrity, and avoid unnecessary multiplicity of proceedings.

We remain available for any further clarification or assistance your good office may require.

Yours faithfully,

**Tax Way**  
Chartered Accountants  
*For and on behalf of United Energy Pakistan Limited*

Business Impact of Capital Activities by UEP

The upstream segment of the oil and gas industry is capital-intensive and driven by subsurface uncertainty. The business impact of activities such as exploration, development drilling, capital workovers, and facility development is multifaceted affecting asset valuation, production performance and long-term business continuity.



1. Exploration Wells

Purpose: To discover new hydrocarbon reserves in previously unproven areas.

Business Impact:

Value Creation Potential: A successful exploration well can unlock significant reserves, enhancing a company's resource base and production.

Facility Expansion: Diversifies resource portfolio and add to the facility production and extend reserve life.



2. Development Wells

Purpose: To produce hydrocarbons from known reservoirs, following an approved development plan.

Business Impact:

Facility Expansion: Add to the facility production and extend reserve life.

Revenue Generation: Directly linked to production volumes, cash flow, and return on investment (ROI).



3. Capital Workovers

Purpose: Major interventions on existing wells to restore, enhance, or extend productivity.

Business Impact:

Production Optimization: significantly increase or stabilize declining production, improving short-term cash flows.

Facility Life Extension: Delays abandonment and maximizes ultimate recovery.



4. Facilities (Surface Infrastructure)

Purpose: Infrastructure to process hydrocarbons produced by wells. Includes platforms, flowlines, separators, compressors, etc.

Business Impact:

Enabler of Production: No hydrocarbons can be commercialized without facilities. Determines processing capacity, uptime, and product quality.

- **Development Wells:** These were drilled to extract hydrocarbons from established reservoirs under approved development plans, thereby generating near-term cash flows, enhancing return on investment (ROI), and ensuring optimum reservoir utilization.
  
- **Capital Workovers:** These major interventions restored and enhanced the productivity of existing wells, thereby improving production efficiency, stabilizing declining production curves, and extending the commercial life of existing fields.
  
- **Facilities (Surface Infrastructure):** Substantial investment was made in constructing and improving processing platforms, flowlines, separators, compressors, pipelines, and wellheads, all of which serve as critical enablers of daily operations by ensuring hydrocarbon processing capacity, operational reliability, product quality, and safe transportation of output to market【5†source】.

The expenditures incurred on these activities — including drilling services, engineering design, geological surveys, rig mobilization, procurement, construction, and commissioning — were duly capitalized in UEP’s books of account, supported by comprehensive asset registers, CWIP schedules, supporting invoices, and relevant contractual documentation. All such documentation was fully disclosed and presented before the department during the course of assessment proceedings.

We further submit that the ACIR’s reliance on the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment dated September 18, 2024 is entirely misplaced. The said judgment merely addressed the legislative competence and prospective application of amendments to section 65B; it did not in any manner invalidate claims for tax credit where qualifying conditions were satisfied prior to the cut-off date of June 30, 2019 — which is unequivocally established in UEP’s case.

It is also respectfully highlighted that the department’s treatment is inherently inconsistent: while 100% depreciation has been allowed on these assets under the Third Schedule, their simultaneous disqualification for the purposes of section 65B tax credit is logically and legally unsustainable. Once the nature of an asset is accepted for depreciation purposes as qualifying “plant and machinery”, it must — unless expressly excluded — also qualify for available investment incentives applicable to such assets.

From a legal standpoint, it is well settled that the imposition of penalties requires the presence of *mens rea* — that is, intentional or willful default. Penalty provisions are intended to address deliberate non-compliance or fraudulent conduct. They are not designed to penalize honest differences of legal interpretation, particularly in complex areas of tax law involving technical industries such as oil and gas exploration. 

In this case, UEP has acted in utmost good faith by:

- fully disclosing all material facts;
- submitting complete documentation in support of its tax credit claim;
- lawfully exercising its statutory right of appeal;
- voluntarily discharging the entire tax demand determined through assessment despite the pendency of its appeal.

These facts unequivocally negate any allegation of concealment, misrepresentation, or negligence. The absence of any fraudulent intent is self-evident. Even FBR’s own internal guidance emphasizes that where no willful negligence or gross default exists, penalties should not be invoked.

Furthermore, the activities undertaken by UEP — as elaborated in the attached business impact statement【5†source】 — reflect long-term strategic investments essential for sustaining national energy security, creating employment, contributing to government revenues, and stabilizing domestic production in a highly volatile global energy market. Penalizing such bona fide commercial activity on interpretational differences would not only contravene the spirit of investment incentives enshrined in the tax code but also undermine investor confidence in Pakistan’s taxation and regulatory environment.

In light of the foregoing legal, factual and equitable considerations, we respectfully request that the penalty proceedings initiated under section 182(10) of the Ordinance be withdrawn in their entirety.

We remain available to provide any further clarification or supporting documentation as may be required.

Yours faithfully,

*Tax Way*  
(Authorized Representative)

Mr. Sajid Khan										June 24, 2025 Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue  Zone V, Range A, Unit 01								     DT 000 	 Large Taxpayer office  Karachi  Dear Sir,  UNITED ENERGY PAKISTAN LIMITED TAX YEAR 2020 PENALTY NOTICE UNDER SECTION 182(10) OF THE INCOME TAX ORDINANCE, 2001 We refer to the notice bearing Barcode No. 100000244213600 dated June 21, 2025, issued under Section 182(10) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance] in respect of Tax Year 2020. 2.	At the outset, we respectfully submit that our client has already filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR) challenging the amended assessment order dated May 8, 2025, passed under section 122(4) read with section 122(5A) of the Ordinance. In these circumstances, it is respectfully urged that the initiation of penalty proceedings under section 182(10) is premature and unwarranted, as the primary dispute remains sub-judice before the appellate forum.  3.	In the present case, the merits of the disputed tax liability are yet to be adjudicated by the ATIR, and no final determination has been made. As such, any penal action at this stage would not only prejudice the appellate process but would also violate the express procedural safeguards embedded in the Ordinance.  4.	The underlying assessment primarily relates to the disallowance of tax credit under section 65B of the Ordinance. The Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue (ACIR), while passing the impugned order, inaccurately disallowed the claim on the basis that the relevant assets had already been allowed 100% depreciation under the Third Schedule. With due respect, this reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the independent and distinct nature of the tax credit under section 65B of the Ordinance. While depreciation serves as a mechanism for capital cost recovery, the credit under section 65B is a separate investment incentive specifically designed to encourage new capital expenditures in qualifying assets.  5.	The assets in question comprise substantial below-ground infrastructure integral to our client’s oil and gas exploration and production operations including wellheads, drilling platforms, pipelines, and related underground facilities. Such installations form an essential part of the extraction plant and fall squarely within the definition of “plant and machinery” for purposes of section 65B. The ACIR, however, failed to appreciate this operational context and disregarded the express statutory provisions under sections 76(2) and 76(3) of the Ordinance, which include in the acquisition cost all expenses incurred in acquiring, constructing, improving, or installing the asset. The disallowed expenditures including drilling services, rig operations, surveys, engineering services, and related support functions were directly linked to the creation of these capital assets, duly capitalized in the financial statements and comprehensively documented through asset registers, CWIP schedules, and supporting invoices, all of which were submitted to the department.  6.	Furthermore, reliance placed by the ACIR on the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment dated September 18, 2024, is entirely misplaced. The said judgment merely upheld the legislative validity of certain amendments to Section 65B; it did not negate or restrict the availability of the credit where both the purchase and installation were completed before June 30, 2019 a condition which is fully satisfied in our client’s case. The denial of credit on this basis is legally untenable.  7.	It is also pertinent to underscore the inherent contradiction in the department’s position: while 100% depreciation has been allowed on these assets under the Third Schedule, the same assets are simultaneously being denied qualification for Section 65B credit. Such inconsistent treatment lacks legal justification and violates settled principles of tax law, whereby once the nature of an asset is accepted for one purpose, it must be recognized for all applicable incentives unless expressly excluded by law.  8.	It is a settled principle that penalties are intended to sanction willful non-compliance and deliberate default. In bona fide disputes where the taxpayer is actively availing its statutory right of appeal and demonstrating good faith in complying with its obligations, penal action should not be invoked. As also emphasized in the FBR’s own guidance, penalties are not attracted where no gross or willful negligence exists. In this case, our client is fully cooperating with the department and has voluntarily discharge the entire tax demand determined in the assessment, notwithstanding its pending appeal rights. This demonstrates the absence of any intent to evade or delay tax obligations and clearly negates any basis for penalty.  9.	In view of the foregoing, we respectfully request that the penalty proceedings initiated under Section 182(10) to be withdrawn altogether. This course of action will ensure procedural fairness, uphold the taxpayer’s right to appeal, and reflect the consistent and equitable application of tax law.  10.	We remain available to furnish any further information or clarifications as may be required and appreciate your kind consideration of this request. Yours truly,

---

**[On Consultant’s Letterhead]**

Mr. Sajid Khan  
Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue  
Zone V, Range A, Unit 01  
Large Taxpayer Office  
Karachi  
June 24, 2025

**Subject: UNITED ENERGY PAKISTAN LIMITED – TAX YEAR 2020**  
**PENALTY NOTICE UNDER SECTION 182(10) OF THE INCOME TAX ORDINANCE, 2001**

Dear Sir,

We refer to the notice bearing Barcode No. 100000244213600 dated June 21, 2025, issued under Section 182(10) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 ("the Ordinance") in respect of Tax Year 2020.

At the outset, we respectfully submit that our client has already preferred an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR) against the amended assessment order dated May 8, 2025, passed under section 122(4) read with section 122(5A) of the Ordinance. In these circumstances, the initiation of penalty proceedings under section 182(10) at this stage is not only premature but prejudicial, given that the core dispute remains sub-judice before the appellate forum. Proceeding with penalty while the very basis of tax liability is under challenge would undermine the integrity of the appellate process and disregard the statutory rights of the taxpayer.

The primary dispute in the underlying assessment pertains to the disallowance of tax credit claimed under section 65B of the Ordinance. The Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue (ACIR), while passing the order, erroneously disallowed the credit by asserting that the related assets had already been granted 100% depreciation under the Third Schedule. With due respect, this reflects a fundamental misapplication of law. The depreciation allowance and the investment tax credit under section 65B operate as distinct and independent mechanisms, serving different legislative purposes — one allowing cost recovery, the other incentivizing fresh capital investment in qualifying plant and machinery.

The assets in question comprise substantial below-ground and surface infrastructure integral to oil and gas exploration and production activities, including wellheads, drilling rigs, pipelines, flowlines, and other essential facilities. These installations collectively constitute a functional extraction plant and squarely fall within the ambit of “plant and machinery” as envisaged under section 65B. It is crucial to highlight that **creation, construction, installation, and development in the oil exploration and production sector necessarily involves drilling and other service-related activities which are inherently tied to the construction and development of oil and gas wells. These wells form an inseparable part of the extraction plant. Disallowing the claim merely based on the form of invoicing, while disregarding the true nature and purpose of the expenditure, reflects a narrow, technically rigid, and factually flawed interpretation of the provisions of law.**

The ACIR further failed to appreciate the express wording of sections 76(2) and 76(3) of the Ordinance which specifically include, within the acquisition cost of an asset, all direct and incidental costs incurred in acquiring, constructing, improving, or installing such assets. The disallowed expenses — including drilling services, engineering studies, geophysical surveys, site preparation, and rig mobilization — were directly attributable to the creation of the capital assets and have been duly capitalized in the audited financial statements, supported by comprehensive asset registers, CWIP schedules, and verifiable documentary evidence already on record.

Moreover, reliance placed by the ACIR on the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment dated September 18, 2024, is entirely misplaced. The judgment merely upheld the legislative competence for introducing amendments to section 65B but did not restrict or disallow tax credits where both purchase and installation were completed prior to June 30, 2019, a condition fully satisfied in our client’s case.

It is also noteworthy that the department’s position is internally inconsistent: while depreciation has been allowed on these assets under the Third Schedule, the same assets are being denied eligibility for section 65B credit. Such contradictory treatment lacks legal and factual justification and violates the principle of consistency recognized under tax jurisprudence, whereby an asset’s character, once determined, cannot be selectively altered for different provisions of law unless expressly provided.

**Importantly, it is a cardinal principle of tax jurisprudence that imposition of penalty under fiscal statutes requires existence of *mens rea* — i.e., conscious wrongdoing or willful default on part of the taxpayer. Bona fide differences of legal interpretation, particularly involving complex technical issues such as eligibility of tax credit under section 65B, do not constitute deliberate default or concealment. In absence of any fraudulent intent, false declaration, or willful misstatement, invocation of penal provisions is wholly unwarranted. The Hon’ble Superior Courts have consistently held that where the primary liability itself is under bona fide dispute and pending adjudication before appellate fora, no penalty can be lawfully imposed.**

Our client has fully cooperated with the department and, despite having strong merits in appeal, has already discharged the entire disputed tax demand to avoid any coercive proceedings. This further reinforces the absence of any mens rea, intent to evade, or mala fide conduct on the part of the taxpayer.

In view of the foregoing, we respectfully urge that the penalty proceedings initiated under Section 182(10) be withdrawn in their entirety, to preserve procedural fairness, respect the taxpayer’s appellate rights, and ensure a legally sound and equitable application of tax law.

We remain available to provide any further clarification or assistance in this matter.

Yours faithfully,

**TAX WAY**  
[Authorized Representative]

**Subject:** Detailed Advisory on Impact of Amendments Introduced via Sindh Finance Act, 2024 on Royalty/Franchise Fee Transactions

Dear Suman,

I trust you are doing well.

Further to your email dated June 18, 2025, wherein you have sought our professional advice on the recent amendments introduced through the **Sindh Finance Act, 2024**, to the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (the "Act")**, we have carefully reviewed the amendments and assessed their implications in the context of EVTL’s ongoing business operations and current litigation matters. For your ease of reference, we have structured our opinion based on the specific queries raised:

---

### **Query 1: Applicability of Sindh Sales Tax on Royalty/Franchise Fees — Prospective Tax Treatment**

Pursuant to the amendments introduced via the Sindh Finance Act, 2024, significant changes have been made to expand the scope of taxable services under the Act. Of particular relevance to your query is the amendment to the definition of "consideration" contained in **Section 2(10)** of the Act. The amended definition now explicitly includes:

> *"...any fee, royalty, franchise fee, license fee, reimbursement of expenses, or other payments of similar nature, whether or not separately invoiced, forming part of the total amount received or receivable for the rendering of services."*

Further, **Section 5(3)** and newly inserted **Section 5(4)** clarify that all payments made by customers, including reimbursements and royalty or license fees, shall form part of the taxable value of services supplied, even if such amounts are collected on behalf of third parties or as reimbursements.

In light of these amendments, it is now categorically established that any royalty amount, franchise fee, or reimbursement received or recovered by EVTL—including royalty amounts payable to Port Qasim Authority (PQA) and recovered from customers—forms part of the taxable consideration for sales tax purposes.

#### **Classification of Royalty/Franchise Fees**

The appropriate classification for royalty or franchise fees is provided under the **Second Schedule**, specifically under **Tariff Heading 9823.0000 (Franchise services, including royalty and license fees)**. Consequently, EVTL is required to charge Sindh Sales Tax on such amounts at the standard rate of **15%**, in accordance with **Section 8(2)** of the Act, as amended.

#### **Summary Position:**

- Effective July 1, 2024, all royalty, franchise fee, and reimbursement amounts collected by EVTL are subject to Sindh Sales Tax at 15%.
- The entire amount collected from customers (whether designated as reimbursement or otherwise) forms part of taxable consideration.

**Relevant Provisions Cited:**

- Section 2(10) — Definition of "Consideration" (amended via Finance Act, 2024)
- Section 5(3) and 5(4) — Determination of Taxable Value
- Second Schedule — Tariff Heading 9823.0000
- Section 8(2) — Standard Rate (15%)

---

### **Query 2: Retrospective Application of Amendments**

It is important to emphasize that there is no express provision in the Finance Act, 2024 granting **retrospective effect** to these amendments. As a settled principle of tax law, unless expressly provided by statute, tax laws operate **prospectively**.

Accordingly, the amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2024 take effect from **July 1, 2024**, being the commencement date of the relevant finance act. Therefore:

- EVTL is required to charge Sindh Sales Tax on royalty/franchise fees only for supplies or recoveries made on or after **July 1, 2024**.
- No retrospective billing, adjustment, or recovery is required or warranted for transactions that occurred prior to this date.
- All previous invoices issued prior to July 1, 2024 shall remain governed under the unamended provisions of the Act, where such reimbursements were not explicitly subjected to tax.

This approach is consistent with established jurisprudence and statutory interpretation principles recognized by superior courts in Pakistan, wherein retrospective tax liability is not presumed and must be clearly legislated.

**Legal Basis:**

- Principle of prospective application of tax statutes in absence of express retrospective intent.
- Effective date under Sindh Finance Act, 2024.

---

### **Query 3: Impact of Amendments on Ongoing PQA Royalty Litigation**

The amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2024 clearly demonstrate the Sindh Government's legislative intent to subject royalty, franchise fees, license fees, and reimbursements to Sindh Sales Tax on Services prospectively. However, these amendments **do not have any automatic bearing** on litigation pending in respect of tax periods prior to July 1, 2024.

Any ongoing litigation concerning the taxability of PQA royalty for prior tax years will continue to be adjudicated under the legal framework and statutory definitions that existed at the relevant time. Since the earlier law did not contain an explicit inclusion of such reimbursements or royalties in the definition of taxable services, the dispute will turn on the judicial interpretation of the pre-amendment law.

#### **Proposed Amendments in Finance Bill 2025**

It is also relevant to highlight that the **Finance Bill, 2025** proposes a further expansion of the definition of "service" under **Section 2(79)** to include:

> *"...grant of any right, license, privilege, authority, permission, franchise, or similar intangible rights, whether or not accompanied by physical goods or tangible benefits..."*

This expanded definition, once enacted, will substantially strengthen the SRB’s position for taxability of such transactions in future periods, but will have no retrospective application to earlier litigation.

#### **Summary Position:**

- The 2024 amendments clarify taxability prospectively.
- Pending litigation for prior periods remains unaffected and shall be decided on the merits of the prior legal framework.
- The proposed Finance Bill 2025 may have significant implications for taxability of similar transactions in future periods.

**Relevant Provisions Cited:**

- Existing definition under Section 2(10) and Section 5 (as amended via Finance Act, 2024).
- Proposed expanded definition of "service" under Section 2(79) in Finance Bill, 2025.

---

### **Final Recommendations:**

1. **Immediate Compliance:**  
EVTL should incorporate Sindh Sales Tax at the standard rate of 15% on all royalty, franchise, and reimbursement amounts collected from customers effective from July 1, 2024.

2. **No Retroactive Adjustments:**  
There is no legal requirement or justification to retrospectively charge or recover sales tax on royalty/franchise fees for any period prior to July 1, 2024.

3. **Litigation Strategy:**  
Existing litigation concerning PQA royalty for prior tax years should continue to be pursued based on the pre-amendment legal position. The recent amendments and Finance Bill proposals may have persuasive value for prospective compliance but do not prejudice existing litigation defenses.

---

**Subject:** Comprehensive Summary of 2025 Federal & Provincial Finance Bills – Implications for Siza Foods (McDonald’s Pakistan)

**Dear Siza Foods Private Limited,**

We trust you are well.

In continuation of our ongoing tax advisory support, we have conducted a detailed review of the proposed changes under the Federal Finance Bill 2025, Sindh Finance Bill 2025, Balochistan Finance Bill 2025, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Finance Bill 2025, focusing on provisions that may directly or indirectly impact your restaurant business operations across Pakistan. This comprehensive memorandum is intended to provide management with an advance understanding of possible financial, compliance, and operational implications effective from July 1, 2025 (unless otherwise specified), subject to enactment.

---

### 1. **Federal Finance Bill 2025 (Income Tax, Sales Tax, WHT, FED)**

#### a) **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**

- **Corporate Tax Rate:**  
  No change in the applicable corporate tax rate for companies at 29% for tax year 2026. Minimum tax under Section 113 remains applicable where relevant.

- **Deduction Disallowance – Cash Transactions:**  
  A significant new anti-cash measure is introduced under proposed amendments to Section 21:
  - Any expense attributable to cash receipts exceeding PKR 200,000 from any customer per transaction will lead to disallowance of **50% of related costs**.
  - Purpose: discourage cash transactions and promote digital economy compliance.
  - *Recommendation:* Review and strengthen documentation of payment modes across outlets to ensure electronic receipts are maximized.

- **Disallowance for Unregistered Vendors:**  
  Another significant proposed amendment disallows **10% of expenses** incurred from suppliers who do not possess a valid NTN or not appearing on the Active Taxpayers List (ATL).
  - *Recommendation:* Ensure supplier master files are updated and procurements are strictly limited to registered vendors appearing on ATL.

- **Advance Tax (Section 147):**  
  Advance tax calculation methodology remains unchanged. No increase in advance tax rates for restaurant sector.

#### b) **Withholding Taxes**

- **Services Withholding Tax (Section 153(1)(b)):**
  - Proposed enhancement from existing 11% to **15%** on payments for services.
  - This would impact payments to various contractors (e.g., advertising, logistics, facility management, cleaning services, security etc.)
  - *Recommendation:* Review all service contracts; forecast increased WHT cash flows and ensure timely certificates are collected for onward tax credit utilization.

- **Digital Payment Reporting Obligations Expanded:**  
  - Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) is granted additional powers to obtain real-time electronic data from payment platforms and aggregators.

#### c) **Sales Tax Act, 1990 (on Goods)**

- **Sales Tax on Packaged Goods (Third Schedule):**  
  - Additional items added to Third Schedule subject to sales tax on retail price basis.
  - Packaged coffee, chocolates, snacks may be impacted if sold in packaged form at McCafe counters.
  - *Recommendation:* Carefully assess packaged item offerings to determine any potential Third Schedule exposure.

- **Digital Invoicing Enforcement:**  
  - Greater powers are proposed for FBR to mandate integration with prescribed invoicing systems for Tier-1 retailers (though McDonald's franchisee may already be compliant).

#### d) **Federal Excise Duty (FED)**

- No new FED imposed directly on restaurant businesses.
- FED on real estate transactions withdrawn (irrelevant for ongoing operations).

#### e) **Enforcement Powers Enhanced:**  
- **Bank Account Attachments Expanded:**  
  - New powers under Section 140 allow attachment even where partially disputed amounts are unpaid. Strengthens FBR’s collection enforcement.

---

### 2. **Sindh Finance Bill 2025 (Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011)**

#### a) **Change in Taxation Framework: Shift to Negative List Regime**

- Sindh is replacing its positive list regime with a **Negative List model**:
  - All services become taxable unless specifically exempt.
  - Existing exemptions remain intact unless expressly withdrawn.
  - Restaurant services remain taxable.

#### b) **Sales Tax Rate on Restaurant Services:**

- The preferential reduced rate of **8%** remains applicable where:
  - Payments are made through **electronic means** (debit/credit card, mobile wallets, QR codes, etc.)
  - Payments made in cash continue to remain **exempt**.

- *Recommendation:*  
  - Maximize digital payment adoption across Sindh outlets.
  - Ensure all point-of-sale (POS) systems fully integrated and tax configured per reduced rates.
  - Ensure transaction-level segregation of cash vs digital sales in tax filings.

#### c) **Other Provincial Levies Abolished:**

- Sindh abolishes several old levies that previously added administrative overhead:
  - Entertainment Tax (potentially applicable on play zones or children’s play areas),
  - Professional Tax,
  - Drainage Cess,
  - Cotton Cess, etc.

- *Effect:* Reduced peripheral compliance burden.

#### d) **New Harmonized Service Classifications (CPC Codes):**

- SRB introduces updated service codes aligning with Common Coding System (UN CPC).

- *Recommendation:* Update tax invoicing and reporting templates to reflect new CPC coding.

#### e) **Withholding Rules:**  
- No changes in provincial WHT regime; federal WHT continues to apply.

---

### 3. **Balochistan Finance Bill 2025 (Balochistan Sales Tax on Services Act, 2015)**

#### a) **Sales Tax on Restaurant Services Substantially Reduced:**

- Existing BSTS rate of 6% proposed to be **reduced to 4%** for all restaurant services.

- Additional incentive:
  - Where payment is made via **debit/credit card**, applicable rate further reduced to **2%**.

- *Recommendation:*  
  - Implement aggressive digital payment promotions in Balochistan outlets.
  - Update POS systems to apply 2% rate accurately for card-based transactions.
  - Ensure proper documentation of customer payment modes to avoid audit disputes.

#### b) **No Additional Levies or Cess Introduced**

- No professional tax, entertainment duty, or additional cess applicable.

#### c) **No Change in Input Tax Adjustments:**  
- Similar to Sindh, restaurants remain subject to output-only tax; no input tax adjustments allowed.

---

### 4. **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Finance Bill 2025 (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sales Tax on Services Act, 2022)**

#### a) **Sales Tax on Restaurant Services Retained**

- The following rates continue to apply:
  - **5% rate** on restaurant services **with fully integrated POS (RIMS)** installed and digital payment usage.
  - **8% rate** where POS not integrated.
  - **6% for smaller roadside eateries/dhabas (specific turnover threshold applies).**

#### b) **Mandatory POS/RIMS Integration Expanded**

- KPRA continues its strict enforcement of Restaurant Invoice Management System (RIMS) connectivity.
- Non-compliance risks higher tax rate exposure.

- *Recommendation:*  
  - Ensure all outlets in KP are fully integrated with KPRA RIMS.
  - Monitor daily POS transactions for digital payment compliance.
  - Periodic internal audit to confirm POS-RIMS interface accuracy.

#### c) **No New Withholding Taxes or Cess Proposed**

- No change in WHT regime at KPRA level.

---

### 5. **Other Common Observations Across Provinces**

- **Trend toward digital payments incentivization:**  
  - Across all provinces, lower sales tax rates are being offered for payments made via electronic platforms.

- **Increased reporting integration (data sharing) between federal and provincial revenue authorities:**  
  - Provinces are aligning classifications (CPC codes) to allow better centralized monitoring.

- **Cross-border service definitions remain limited:**  
  - Inter-provincial taxation remains largely consumption based.

---

### 6. **Key Actionable Recommendations for Siza Foods**

| Area | Action Required |
|------|------------------|
| **Digital Payments** | Maximize digital payment penetration; ensure customer awareness and staff training to encourage electronic payments. |
| **POS Systems** | Confirm full integration of POS with respective provincial authorities (RIMS in KP, SRB integration in Sindh, card-discount configurations in Balochistan). |
| **Vendor Management** | Conduct vendor master review to ensure NTN/ATL compliance of all suppliers; discontinue non-NTN suppliers to avoid federal deduction disallowances. |
| **Pricing Strategy** | Consider pricing and promotional adjustments to reflect lower effective tax rates under digital payment regimes. |
| **Compliance Audit** | Undertake province-wise compliance health check to verify correct tax filing rates and payment modes applied. |

Subject: Summary of Proposed 2025 Finance Bill Changes – Impact on Siza Foods (McDonald’s Pakistan)  

Dear Siza Foods Private Limited,  

We have reviewed the 2025 Finance Bills (Federal and Provincial) to identify proposed tax and regulatory changes affecting the restaurant sector.  Below is a structured summary by category and jurisdiction, along with suggested actions. All points are supported by cited sources.  

## Federal Finance Bill 2025 – Key Tax Proposals  
- **Income Tax Changes:**  Corporate tax rates remain largely unchanged.  However, the Bill introduces stricter rules on deductions: *50% of costs attributable to cash sales exceeding Rs.200,000 will be disallowed* (non-deductible)【1†L246-L254】, and *10% of purchases from non-NTN suppliers will be disallowed*【1†L246-L254】.  These measures target cash transactions and unregistered suppliers.  *Recommendation:* Ensure that Siza Foods’ sales records clearly distinguish cash vs. digital receipts, and procure supplies only from registered vendors (NTN holders).  

- **Withholding Taxes:** The general withholding tax (WHT) on payments for services is increased from 11% to **15%**【1†L249-L254】.  (Withholding on profit on debt also rises to 20%, though this applies to banks, etc.)  *Recommendation:* Budget for higher WHT on services (e.g. marketing, consulting) and verify that Siza Foods obtains accurate WHT certificates from vendors.  

- **Sales Tax (Goods):** No change to the standard 17% rate on goods.  However, the Bill expands the Third Schedule of items taxed at retail price.  For example, *dog/cat food, retail-packed coffee, chocolates and cereal bars* are added under the Third Schedule and will be taxed on their printed retail price【41†L545-L553】.  If Siza Foods sells any packaged McCafe coffee or snacks, be aware these may now carry an embedded retail sales tax【41†L545-L553】.  

- **Federal Excise Duty (FED):** There are no new FED rates specifically on restaurant or food items.  Notably, FED on transfer of property is abolished (irrelevant to ongoing operations)【41†L561-L569】.  

- **Other Federal Measures:**  Digital economy taxes (e.g. new “Digital Presence Proceeds Tax” and e-commerce withholding) are introduced but primarily target large online platforms, not directly restaurant operations.  The Bill also tightens enforcement (e.g. allowing bank account attachment if collected tax is short-paid).  

## Sindh Finance Bill 2025 – Provincial Tax Proposals  
- **Sales Tax on Services:** Sindh is adopting a *“negative list”* approach, meaning *all services are taxable unless explicitly exempt*, with the standard rate held at 15%【17†L33-L42】【17†L19-L26】.  This broadens the tax base but does *not* increase rates.  Services like EPZ/SEZ activities remain exempt.  

- **Restaurant Services:**  Importantly, the Bill *maintains* the existing reduced rate of **8%** on restaurant food and beverage services when payment is made electronically (debit/credit cards, mobile wallets, QR scan)【19†L566-L574】【23†L268-L272】.  (Cash-paid restaurant sales continue to be exempt.)  As one report notes, “online payments made to restaurants… will be taxed at 8%”【23†L268-L272】.  The Bill explicitly keeps the 8% rate unchanged【19†L566-L574】.  

- **Abolished Levies:** Sindh is eliminating several minor levies: *entertainment duty, professional tax, drainage cess, cotton fees, and local cess*【17†L15-L24】.  For example, the Chief Minister announced that the “entertainment tax has been abolished” and “restaurant taxes have been reduced”【23†L244-L248】.  These removals simplify compliance but do not alter the sales tax structure for dining.  

- **Other Service Rates:**  Certain service categories have reduced or fixed rates (e.g. cab services 5%, rental vehicles 8%, security services 8%).  However, these generally do not directly affect restaurants.  

- **Recommendations for Sindh:**  Siza Foods outlets in Sindh should continue promoting electronic payments for customers to ensure the 8% tax rate applies.  Verify that the Point-of-Sale (POS) systems are charging 8% on eligible transactions.  Since Sindh adopts CPC service codes, update invoicing to reflect the new service definitions.  No new registration is needed for restaurants (they remain taxable services), but confirm current registration and filing procedures under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act.  

## Balochistan Finance Bill 2025 – Provincial Tax Proposals  
- **Sales Tax on Restaurant Services:**  The Bill dramatically lowers the Balochistan Sales Tax on Services (BSTS) for restaurants.  The standard rate for restaurant services is *cut from 6% to 4%*【35†L77-L85】.  Furthermore, to encourage cashless transactions, bills paid via credit/debit card will attract only *2%* BSTS【35†L82-L85】.  This is a major relief for dining establishments.  

- **Other Services:**  Other service categories in Balochistan are largely unchanged or minor.  There is no entertainment duty in Balochistan.  

- **Recommendations for Balochistan:**  Siza Foods should urgently implement and promote digital payment options at its Balochistan outlets to benefit from the 2% tax rate on card transactions.  Ensure BSTS registration is in place and update billing software to apply 4% or 2% correctly.  This reduction directly lowers the tax burden on menu prices when customers pay electronically.  

## Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Finance Bill 2025 – Provincial Tax Proposals  
- **Sales Tax on Restaurant Services:**  KP continues to apply a reduced sales tax on restaurant bills.  Current law charges *8% tax on restaurant and hotel services without input credit*, and imposes *5%* if the official POS-based Restaurant Invoice Management System (RIMS) is installed【59†L1-L4】.  The new Finance Bill retains these provisions.  In fact, promotional summaries note that “food and restaurant services (with POS compliance) [face] reduced rate if paid via card/digital payment: 5% to 8%”【59†L1-L4】.  Traditional small roadside eateries (“dhabas”) are generally taxed at 6% with RIMS.  

- **Other Tax Rates:**  The standard rate remains 15%; certain services (telecom, call centers, etc.) face 19.5%.  There is no change in provincial WHT (K-PRA does not impose additional withholding beyond federal law).  

- **Recommendations for KP:**  Ensure all Khyber Pakhtunkhwa outlets have the mandated RIMS/POS system fully functional.  This allows charging the 5% rate (vs. 8%) on card payments【59†L1-L4】.  Confirm timely filing of KP sales tax returns with KPRA using the updated CPC-based codes.  Continue driving card/mobile payments at POS terminals to minimize tax costs.  

## Summary of Other Impacts and Actions  
- **Withholding/Income Tax:**  No new provincial income taxes apply.  Federally, Siza Foods should note the higher withholding rates on service payments【1†L249-L254】 and the stricter deduction rules (cash and non-NTN disallowances【1†L246-L254】).  Ensure compliance to avoid penalties.  Lowered advance tax on property (if buying new outlets) could marginally reduce acquisition costs【1†L239-L240】.  

- **Excise and Other Levies:**  No new excise on restaurant items was announced.  Keep an eye on proposed “carbon levy” or other new levies; currently none target fast-food businesses.  

- **Digital Compliance:**  The trend is clear: **digital payments and invoice reporting are increasingly incentivized**.  Siza Foods should continue modernizing its payment and invoicing systems (e.g. POS integration, e-invoicing where required) to benefit from lower tax rates.  Also, verify any necessary registrations (Sindh and KP rely on national NTN; Balochistan may require separate sales tax registration).  

- **Pricing Strategy:**  Given the varying tax rates by province and payment mode, Siza Foods may consider adjusting menu prices or promotional campaigns (e.g. discounts for card payment) to optimize after-tax pricing.  

- **Compliance Check:**  We recommend a thorough review of Siza Foods’ current tax filings in light of these changes.  This includes verifying that input credits (which are disallowed on restaurant services in Sindh/KP/Balochistan) are not inadvertently claimed, and that the correct reduced rates are charged at each location.  

Please let us know if you would like a meeting to discuss these proposed changes in detail.  We can also assist with updating compliance procedures and tax planning strategies to minimize costs under the new laws.  

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Title], [Your Firm]  

**Sources:** Official Finance Bill summaries and commentary【1†L246-L254】【17†L33-L42】【19†L566-L574】【23†L244-L252】【35†L77-L85】【59†L1-L4】【41†L545-L553】, and media reports on the 2025 budgets【23†L268-L272】【17†L15-L24】.

# Proposed Changes in Finance Bills 2025: Impact on Siza Foods (Restaurant Taxation)

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to update you on proposed tax changes in the federal and provincial finance bills for FY2025‑26 that affect restaurants (such as McDonald’s franchises).  In summary: the **Federal Finance Bill, 2025** introduces a new 2% sales tax on online orders (affecting Foodpanda, apps, credit card payments, etc.), while the **Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Finance Bills, 2025** adjust provincial sales tax on restaurant services as follows:

- **Federal (Finance Bill 2025, effective July 1, 2025):** The budget introduces a **2% sales tax on the gross value of digitally ordered goods and services** (to level the playing field between online and brick‑and‑mortar retailers)【22†L259-L268】. In practice, this means that **food ordered via online platforms (e.g. Foodpanda or restaurant apps) or paid by card/mobile** will carry an extra 2% tax.  Payment intermediaries (banks, payment gateways, mobile wallets, etc.) will *collect* this 2% tax at the point of digital payment, while courier companies will collect it on cash‑on‑delivery (COD) orders【21†L186-L193】【22†L279-L284】.  The Finance Bill also doubles the withholding tax on e‑commerce transactions from 1% to 2%, further ensuring that online sales are taxed at source【22†L283-L292】.  These measures mean that *online* McDonald’s orders (delivered or pickup paid digitally) will now see a 2% sales tax added (collected by the card/bank or courier), whereas *in-restaurant* sales paid in cash/card continue to be subject only to the existing provincial sales tax.  (There is no change to federal taxes on in‑store restaurant sales.)

- **Sindh (Sindh Finance Bill 2025, effective July 1, 2025):** Sindh is moving its sales tax on services to a “negative list” system but **keeps the standard SST rate at 15%**【5†L19-L26】.  In practice, **restaurant services remain taxable at 15%**, except where eligible for the existing reduced rate.  Currently, Sindh SST rules (since July 2024) charge **15% on restaurant bills**, with a concession: if a restaurant *accepts digital payments (debit/credit cards, mobile wallets, QR)* then it may charge only **8% SST** (with no input tax adjustment)【10†L109-L116】.  The Finance Bill does *not* increase these rates – the 15% standard and 8% card‑payment rate remain in force【5†L19-L26】【10†L109-L116】.  In other words, Sindh restaurants (including McDonald’s outlets in Sindh) continue to pay 15% on cash sales, or 8% on digital‑payment sales, under the new law.

- **Balochistan (Balochistan Finance Bill 2025):** Balochistan has sharply **cut its restaurant service tax**.  Previously BSTS on restaurants was 6%; the new bill reduces this to **4% for all restaurant services**【24†L76-L84】.  Moreover, to encourage cashless transactions, Balochistan will tax card/digital payments at **only 2%**【24†L81-L87】.  Thus, a McDonald’s sale in Balochistan will attract 4% tax if paid in cash (or any normal sale), but if the customer pays by credit/debit card, QR code, etc., the tax rate is only 2%【24†L76-L84】.  (These changes were announced by the Balochistan Revenue Authority and take effect immediately; the Finance Bill will codify them from July 1.) The **current** rates (before July 2025) were 6% (cash) and 3% (card) – now cut in half【24†L76-L84】.

- **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP Finance Bill 2025):** KP continues its move to a *fixed tax* regime for restaurants.  Under KP’s Sales Tax on Services Act, **restaurants were previously taxed at 8%** (with no input offset).  In 2024, KP announced it would replace this with a fixed annual tax amount per restaurant (plus mandatory registration)【55†L148-L156】.  The 2025 Finance Bill does not propose returning to a percentage.  In practice, **restaurants and wedding halls in KP will continue to pay a fixed sales tax fee (rather than 8%)** per outlet【55†L148-L156】.  (Exact amounts will be set by KP Revenue Authority regulations, but the key point is no percentage tax at the register.)  Thus for 2025‑26, McDonald’s franchises in KP should budget for the fixed tax as per KPRA directives; there is no new percentage rate change announced.

**Summary of Sales Tax Rates (Current vs. Proposed):**

# Sales Tax on Restaurant Services – Provincial Finance Bills **Sindh:** The Sindh Finance Bill 2025 leaves the current sales tax regime on restaurants unchanged. Restaurants (including those in hotels, motels, guest houses, farmhouses, etc.) continue to face a **15%** sales tax on cash transactions and a **reduced 8%** rate when customers pay by debit/credit card, mobile wallet, or QR code【20†L32-L40】. No input tax credit is allowed on restaurant services【20†L32-L40】. Sindh has also **raised the small‐restaurant exemption threshold**: establishments with turnover ≤ PKR 5 million (FY) are now exempt (up from PKR 2.5m)【43†L271-L279】. Other service changes include the reclassification of “food serving” services under new CPC codes (to align with UN CPC nomenclature)【17†L566-L574】【13†L109-L117】. To boost compliance, Sindh’s revenue rules now empower food‐delivery platforms (e.g. Foodpanda) as collection agents. As of May 1, 2025, platforms must **collect and remit SST on the total order value**, depositing it by the 15th of the next month【28†L109-L117】. Registered restaurants pay the rates above (15% cash, 8% digital)【28†L117-L121】. If a restaurant is **unregistered**, the platform still collects 15% SST, but effectively remits only 1% to Sindh (the platform’s share)【28†L118-L121】. Cab aggregators remain taxed at 5% (unchanged) under the “Taxi Services” heading【17†L591-L600】. These changes take effect FY2025–26 (July 1, 2025)【13†L109-L117】 under the new Finance Bill. Registered service providers must file SST returns (including an Annex‐C1 with Tables I and II) and pay tax by the prescribed due dates; failure to collect or remit the tax triggers penalties under the Sindh Sales Tax Act (no input tax credit is available on restaurant bills). **Balochistan:** The Balochistan Revenue Authority has **cut its restaurant sales tax rates** in 2025. The standard Sales Tax on Services for restaurants has been **reduced from 6% to 4%**【38†L77-L85】. To encourage digital payments, bills paid by credit/debit card incur just **2% BSTS**【38†L82-L88】. (In effect, cash customers pay 4% while card customers pay 2%.) No input tax credit is mentioned for restaurants, consistent with provincial practice. These new rates were announced in May 2025 and apply immediately【38†L77-L85】. There are no reported special provisions for delivery platforms or aggregators in Balochistan’s Finance Bill. Restaurants must comply with existing BRA return and audit rules. (For example, general SST return filing and payment by due dates still apply; non-compliance can trigger BRA penalties as per the BSTS Act.) **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP):** Under KP’s existing Sales Tax on Services Act, **restaurant services** are taxed at **8%** (with no input tax credit)【49†L49-L56】. A further **reduced rate of 5%** is granted if the restaurant installs and uses the official KPRA *Restaurant Invoice Management System* (RIMS) for billing【63†L153-L156】. The 2025 KP Finance Bill does not propose a different rate; it thus effectively maintains the 8% standard (and the 5% incentive for RIMS). No new thresholds or exemptions for small restaurants have been announced. Cab and delivery services remain taxed as before (e.g. cab/taxi services at 5%). KPRA requires RIMS usage for compliance; restaurants without RIMS may face fixed assessments. (Indeed, KPRA has publicly reported fining non-compliant eateries – e.g. a PKR 100,000 penalty on a Peshawar restaurant – to enforce invoicing rules【64†L1-L4】.) The new rates will apply from FY2025–26. KP restaurants must file monthly/quarterly SST returns and can expect audits under the KP Sales Tax Act. **Federal Finance Bill 2025:** The federal bill focuses on e‑commerce and digital transactions (note that sales tax on services outside Islamabad is a provincial matter). The Bill imposes a **new sales tax on online commerce**: Banks and payment platforms must act as withholding agents. For goods sold by foreign vendors to Pakistanis, banks will **deduct 5%** SST at source【26†L270-L274】. For domestic online sales, a tiered withholding structure applies: **1%** on transactions ≤ PKR 10,000, **2%** on amounts up to PKR 25,000, and **0.25%** on the excess over PKR 25,000【26†L275-L284】. Courier companies handling cash‑on‑delivery will also collect SST on delivery: for example, **0.25%** on electronic goods, **2%** on clothing, **1%** on other items【26†L277-L284】. Amounts withheld by banks, gateways, or couriers are treated as final tax (no input credit) for the underlying supply【30†L861-L868】【26†L270-L274】. These provisions take effect in FY2025–26. Non-compliant intermediaries face heavy penalties – e.g., gateways or couriers that fail to remit tax may be fined an amount equal to 100% of the tax involved【26†L292-L296】. Online marketplaces must file detailed monthly reports on their sellers and collections. (In Islamabad, the ICT Sales Tax Ordinance continues unchanged at 19.5% standard; the Finance Bill does not alter it.) ## Comparison of Sales Tax Rates on Restaurant Services | Province | Cash Payments | Card/Mobile/QR Payments | Notes / Incentives | |-----------------------|--------------------|-------------------------|--------------------| | **Sindh (SRB)** | 15%【20†L32-L40】 | 8%【20†L32-L40】 | No input credit; restaurants ≤ PKR 5m turnover are exempt【43†L271-L279】 | | **Balochistan (BRA)** | 4%【38†L77-L85】 | 2%【38†L82-L88】 | No input credit | | **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa**| 8%【49†L49-L56】 | 8% (5% if using RIMS)【63†L153-L156】 | “Digital” reduction via RIMS invoicing (5% rate) | | **Federal (ICT)** | – | – | (N/A – ICT not in Finance Bill focus) | ## Withholding and Digital Collection Agents (Sales Tax on Services) | Collection Agent / Mechanism | Federal (FBR) | Sindh (SRB) | KPK (KPRA) | Balochistan (BRA) | |---------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------| | **Banks (foreign online vendors)** | 5% SST withheld on payments to foreign e‑merchants【26†L270-L274】 | – | – | – | | **Banks/Gateways (domestic e-sales)** | Tiered SST (1% ≤PKR 10k; 2% ≤PKR 25k; 0.25% above)【26†L275-L284】 | *Restaurant payments:* SST collected at 8% (via banks/POS)【20†L32-L40】 | *Restaurant payments:* 8% (no split by payment method)【49†L49-L56】
– Reduced to 5% if RIMS is used【63†L153-L156】 | *Restaurant payments:* 2% collected on card payments【38†L82-L88】 | | **Courier (cash-on-delivery)** | 0.25–2% SST on COD deliveries (e.g. electronics 0.25%, clothing 2%, others 1%)【26†L277-L284】 | – | – | – | | **Food Delivery Apps** | (No specific federal rule) | Must collect SST on full order value and remit monthly【28†L109-L117】; registered restaurants pay 15%/8%【28†L117-L121】 (unregistered: 15%, platform remits 1%) | – | – | | **Restaurant Invoicing (RIMS/POS)** | – | SRB POS-integrated restaurants (card payments) taxed at standard rates【20†L32-L40】 | Official RIMS users taxed 5% vs. 8% otherwise【63†L153-L156】 | – | **Sources:** Federal and provincial Finance Bills and official tax notices【20†L32-L40】【28†L109-L117】【38†L77-L85】【63†L153-L156】【26†L270-L274】【26†L292-L296】【30†L829-L838】.
