United Energy Pakistan Limited (UEP), a non-resident company incorporated in Mauritius and engaged in the exploration and extraction of oil and natural gas in Pakistan, e-filed its return for Tax Year 2015 on December 31, 2015. The return declared total income of Rs. 16.66 billion (including royalty) and claimed a refund of Rs. 5.84 billion. This return was treated as a deemed assessment under section 120(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Subsequently, the return was amended under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance on December 27, 2016, revising the income upward to Rs. 16.89 billion and determining tax payable at Rs. 637.42 million. On the taxpayer’s request, the order was rectified under section 221 on January 25, 2017, resulting in a reduced tax liability and a refund of Rs. 4.12 billion.

UEP challenged the amended assessment by filing an appeal before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals-II), who on November 30, 2017, upheld the major additions made in the amended order. The CIR(A) confirmed the application of section 122(5A), the application of the 55% tax rate, the disallowance of the entire exchange loss in the current year, the levy of super tax under section 4B, and the disallowance of tax credit under section 65B. The only relief allowed was the direction to give consequential relief in respect of Workers’ Welfare Fund (WWF). Subsequently, an appeal effect order under section 124(4) was issued on November 5, 2018, confirming the revised income and computing a tax refundable of Rs. 5.10 billion.
Aggrieved by the CIR(A)’s findings, UEP preferred an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR), Karachi. The Tribunal, vide its order dated June 3, 2023, partly accepted the appeal. It confirmed the application of the 55% tax rate, noted that the issue relating to exchange loss was not pressed, deleted the super tax under section 4B, and directed the allowance of consequential relief on WWF and tax credit under section 65B. In pursuance of the ATIR's directives, another appeal effect order dated November 16, 2023, was issued under section 124, reaffirming the total income at Rs. 16.89 billion and computing a revised refundable amount of Rs. 5.10 billion after giving effect to all allowed reliefs, including credit under section 65B and deletion of super tax.

Following this, the taxpayer filed a refund adjustment application under section 170 of the Ordinance, via letter dated January 2, 2024, requesting adjustment of the determined refund against outstanding tax demands. A refund order dated February 28, 2024, was passed under section 170(4), partially accepting the refund claim. The tax authority acknowledged verified tax deducted at source amounting to Rs. 2.72 billion and payments under section 137(2) and for WWF but rejected a portion of Rs. 1.398 billion on the ground that the corresponding CPRs were marked with "Tax Year 2014." As a result, a net refund of Rs. 3.19 billion was determined and adjusted against outstanding tax demands for Tax Years 2020 (Rs. 197.59 million), 2021 (Rs. 1.25 billion), and 2023 (Rs. 1.74 billion). The balance refund was reduced to NIL.
In response to the partial rejection of refund, particularly the disallowed Rs. 1.398 billion in tax credits and Rs. 515.98 million in refund adjustment from Tax Year 2014, UEP preferred another appeal under section 129 before the CIR(A), Karachi. In the appellate proceedings concluded on May 23, 2024, the CIR(A) highlighted that UEP operates on a special tax year (January–December) and accordingly, the taxes deducted during calendar year 2014 pertain to Tax Year 2015. The CIR(A) referred to section 168(2) of the Ordinance, which allows tax credit in the year in which the tax is deducted and noted that a previous departmental rectification order dated March 31, 2015, had similarly instructed UEP to claim such tax credit in Tax Year 2015. The CIR(A) concluded that the rejection of Rs. 1.914 billion refunds by the DCIR without prior notice or opportunity of hearing were procedurally flawed, violated principles of natural justice, and ignored binding legal provisions. Consequently, the appellate authority annulled the refund rejection and remanded the matter for fresh consideration after verification of tax challans and allowing credit in either Tax Year 2014 or 2015.

**Subject:** Applicability of Sales Tax Rates on Restaurant Services

Hi Iftikhar,

Please note that the standard rate of sales tax under the Act is **15%** on the value of a taxable service. Accordingly, this rate applies to all restaurant sales where payment is made in **cash**.

However, a **reduced rate of 6%** is applicable in cases where restaurant and hotel services are provided to **corporate sector entities**, and the consideration is received through **debit cards, credit cards, prepaid cards, mobile wallets, or QR code scanning**. This reduced rate is subject to the condition that **no input tax adjustment or refund** shall be claimed in respect of such services.

To reiterate, if the payment is received in **cash**, the **standard rate of 15%** continues to apply.

Please feel free to reach out in case further clarification is required.

Best regards,  
Zuhair

# Sindh Finance Bill 2025 – Sales Tax on Services Changes

Dear Team,

We have reviewed the Sindh Finance Bill 2025 and your attached understanding. Below are the clarifications for each query:

- **Reduced-rate Option vs Standard Rate:**  The new law maintains a **15% standard SST rate**. To charge the lower rates (e.g. 8% or 3%), the **service provider** must formally opt in by e-filing an option.  In other words, filing an option is only required to **avail reduced rates**; if no option is filed, the standard 15% applies【46†L228-L232】.

- **Who Files the Option:**  Only the *service provider* may file the option. The Bill explicitly states the “service provider shall e-file an option to charge… sales tax at the reduced rate”【46†L228-L232】.  A service recipient cannot file on the provider’s behalf.  Thus, if the provider (e.g. an overseas franchisor) does not file the option, the reduced rate cannot be applied.

- **Franchise Services on Fuel Sales:**  Franchise or trademark licensing services (CPC 83960) are included in the reduced-rate list.  If you (as the franchise provider) file the option by July 1, 2025, you can charge **8% SST** on these services【36†L899-L906】.  Otherwise, you must charge the standard **15%**.  In summary: *8% with option, 15% without*【46†L228-L232】【36†L899-L906】.

- **Rental of Immovable Property:**  The Bill specifically brings property leasing into the SST base at a **3% rate**.  The law lists “rental or leasing services of immovable property” (for business use) at 3%【33†L882-L889】.  This effectively *continues* the 3% rate you are paying today. There is no increase; the Act simply codifies that renting/leasing for business remains at 3%.

- **International Franchise Payments (e.g. Shell):**  Since only the provider can file an option, and Shell (as a non-resident brand owner) cannot practically file in Sindh, the 8% reduced rate will not be available.  Therefore, such international franchise payments remain taxable at the **15% standard rate** (subject to any withholding rules).  You, as the recipient, cannot file the option – only the service provider can【46†L228-L232】.

Please let me know if you need further details or discussion on these points.

Regards,

Zuhair

**Sources:** Sindh Finance Bill 2025 (Section on reduced-rate services)【46†L228-L232】【36†L899-L906】【33†L882-L889】

**Subject:** Clarification on Proposed Amendments – Sindh Finance Bill, 2025  

Dear Hashim,  

I hope this email finds you well.  

As you are aware, the proposed amendments under the Sindh Finance Bill, 2025 retain the **standard Sindh Sales Tax (SST) rate of 15%**. In order to avail a **reduced rate** (e.g., 8% or 3%), the **service provider** must **formally opt** for the reduced rate by e-filing an option. In the absence of such an option, the standard 15% rate will apply by default.

It is important to note that this option can only be exercised by the **service provider**. The Bill clearly states that *“the service provider shall e-file an option to charge sales tax at the reduced rate.”* A **service recipient** is not authorized to file the option on the provider’s behalf. Therefore, if the provider—such as an **overseas franchisor**—is unable to file this option in Sindh, the benefit of the reduced rate cannot be claimed.

Franchise or trademark licensing services (CPC 83960) are specifically included in the list of services eligible for the 8% reduced rate. Accordingly, if the **franchise provider** files the option by **July 1, 2025**, the reduced rate of 8% may be applied. Otherwise, the standard 15% rate remains applicable. Given that **Wafi**, as a non-resident brand owner, is not practically in a position to e-file the option in Sindh, the reduced rate of 8% will not be available. As a result, franchise payments to such overseas licensors will continue to be subject to the **standard 15% SST**, subject to applicable withholding provisions.

It is also worth mentioning that **sales tax paid at the standard 15% rate is fully adjustable**, whereas no input tax adjustment is available when opting for a reduced rate. Therefore, in this particular case, filing the option would not be beneficial from a credit standpoint.

Additionally, the Bill brings **rental or leasing of immovable property for business use** formally within the SST regime at a rate of **3%**, which is consistent with the current practice. There is no change in rate; the amendment simply codifies the existing treatment.

We trust the above clarifies your queries. Should you require any further explanation or assistance, please do not hesitate to reach out.

Best regards,  
**[Your Name]**

**Subject:** Clarification on Proposed Amendments under Sindh Finance Bill, 2025  

Hi Hashim,  

Hope this email finds you well.  

As you may be aware, the proposed amendment maintains the standard Sindh Sales Tax (SST) rate at 15%. To avail a reduced rate (e.g., 8% or 3%), the **service provider** must formally exercise this option by e-filing through the designated portal. In other words, the filing of such an option is mandatory only when opting for a reduced rate—otherwise, the standard 15% rate shall automatically apply.

Importantly, the option can only be filed by the **service provider**. The Bill clearly states that *"the service provider shall e-file an option to charge sales tax at the reduced rate."* A service recipient cannot file this option on behalf of the provider. Therefore, if the provider (such as an overseas franchisor) does not or cannot file the option, the benefit of the reduced rate cannot be claimed.

Franchise or trademark licensing services (CPC 83960) are expressly included in the reduced-rate category. Accordingly, if you (as the franchise provider) e-file the option on or before **July 1, 2025**, you would be eligible to charge SST at the reduced rate of **8%**. Otherwise, the standard **15%** rate will apply. Since Wafi, being a non-resident brand owner, is not practically in a position to file this option in Sindh, the reduced rate of 8% will not be available. Consequently, franchise fees payable to overseas licensors will remain subject to the standard 15% SST (subject to applicable withholding provisions).  

Please also note that payment of sales tax at the standard 15% rate remains **adjustable** against output tax. Therefore, in this case, filing the option is not only impractical but also unnecessary.

Lastly, the Bill explicitly brings **leasing or rental of immovable property for business use** within the SST regime at a **reduced rate of 3%**. This amendment essentially **formalizes the existing 3% rate** already being charged and does not introduce any increase.

We trust the above clarifications address your queries. Should you require any further assistance, please feel free to reach out.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Designation]

---

**Subject:** Impact of Provincial Finance Bills 2025 on Restaurant Services – Key Tax Updates

Dear [Client's Name],

We trust you are keeping well.

We write to apprise you of significant changes proposed through the **Sindh**, **Punjab**, and **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP)** Finance Bills, 2025, which may have important implications for Siza Foods (Pvt.) Limited, as a provider of restaurant services under the McDonald’s brand across Pakistan.

These proposed legislative amendments aim to restructure the provincial sales tax regimes and introduce greater standardization in the taxation of services. A summary of the key changes relevant to your business is provided below:

---

### 1. **Transition from Positive List to Negative List Regime**

All three provinces—**Sindh**, **Punjab**, and **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa**—have proposed a fundamental shift in their sales tax framework from the existing **“positive list” regime** (where only specifically listed services are taxable) to a **“negative list” regime**, under which **all services are deemed taxable unless expressly exempt**.

This change significantly broadens the tax base and may result in the taxation of ancillary services that were previously outside the purview of provincial sales tax. It also reinforces the need for a careful review of all bundled offerings, promotional campaigns, and non-core services to ensure compliance under the new regime.

---

### 2. **Standard Rate of Sales Tax on Restaurant Services**

The **standard rate of sales tax on restaurant services remains unchanged at 15%** across Sindh, Punjab, and KP. In the absence of any formal election or eligibility for a reduced rate, this default rate will continue to apply on all taxable restaurant services.

---

### 3. **Reduced Rate for Digital Payment Transactions**

#### **a. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa**  
The KP Finance Bill reconfirms that where restaurant services are paid for via **debit or credit cards, mobile wallets, or QR scanning**, a **reduced rate of 6% (without input tax adjustment)** will apply. In all other cases (including cash transactions), the standard rate of 15% will continue to apply.

#### **b. Sindh**  
Sindh has retained the existing reduced rate of **8%** on restaurant services paid via **electronic means**, subject to the condition that **input tax deduction is not admissible**. This applies to restaurants (including those in hotels, motels, and guesthouses) where payment is made through cards, mobile wallets, or QR code scanning.

#### **c. Punjab**  
Punjab’s proposed legislation also retains the reduced rate structure but now reorganizes services under newly introduced schedules. Services attracting reduced or fixed rates remain unaffected in terms of rate, but the condition for **non-admissibility of input tax adjustment continues** to apply where the reduced rate is availed.

**Note:** For each of the above, the reduced rate is conditional upon the **mode of payment**. In the absence of a digital payment, the **standard rate of 15% applies**.

---

### 4. **Mandatory Integration with Restaurant Invoice Management Systems (RIMS)**

All three provinces have proposed stringent enforcement mechanisms concerning the **mandatory use of e-invoicing systems**, such as RIMS. Notable provisions include:

- In **KP**, non-compliance may result in penalties of **Rs. 200,000 or 5% of the tax involved per instance**, whichever is higher.
- In **Punjab**, penalties for failure to comply with electronic invoicing requirements may range from **Rs. 400,000 to Rs. 1 million**, with repeated violations potentially leading to **sealing of business premises**.
- **Sindh** also emphasizes digitization and has aligned its tax system with **CPC-based classifications**, reinforcing the need for integration with compliant invoicing systems.

We recommend that Siza Foods ensures complete and province-wise integration with RIMS or equivalent systems to mitigate compliance risks.

---

### 5. **Expanded Definition of Taxable Services**

The definition of “services” has been significantly broadened across all three statutes to include:

- **Digital and online platforms**
- **Franchise/licensing rights**
- **Associated benefits and facilities**
- **Bundled or auxiliary services**

This expanded scope necessitates a detailed review of **all contractual and operational arrangements**, especially with third-party delivery partners, franchise arrangements, and advertising platforms, to assess whether any new tax obligations arise.

---

### 6. **Clarification on Takeaway and Delivery Services**

All provinces have reiterated that **takeaway and home/delivery services** are squarely covered within the scope of restaurant services and are subject to the same applicable tax rates (standard or reduced, based on mode of payment).

---

### Our Recommendations

In light of the above developments, we recommend the following immediate actions:

1. **Ensure integration of all POS terminals with RIMS** or equivalent invoice management systems in each province.
2. **Encourage digital payment methods** to avail reduced tax rates, subject to forfeiture of input tax credit.
3. **Conduct a tax impact review** of all service streams, including loyalty programs, bundled offerings, online orders, and third-party transactions.
4. **Review franchise/license agreements** to determine any implications under revised CPC-based classification systems.
5. **Stay vigilant for notifications or implementation rules**, especially where formal “options” for reduced rates must be filed by a specified date.

---

Please let us know if you would like us to prepare a province-wise action plan, assist with any RIMS compliance review, or provide further clarification on specific provisions.

We remain at your disposal for any further assistance.

Warm regards,  
**[Your Name]**  
**Tax Way**  
**[Designation]**  
**[Email | Phone]**

Based on a thorough review of both the **Finance Bill, 2025** and the **List of Amendments**, here is a summary of **key changes** made *via the amendments* to the original Finance Bill, 2025:

---

### 🔄 **1. Change in Nomenclature**
- **"Carbon Levy" renamed to "Climate Support Levy"**  
  – Clause 3 of the Bill has been amended throughout to substitute "Carbon Levy" with **"Climate Support Levy"**.

---

### 🛢 **2. Petroleum and Energy Sector**
- **Clause 4(11)**: Wording around early declaration of goods at ports modified for clarity.
- **Clause 4(27)**: Technical correction in reference to Customs Act omitted redundancy.
- **Clause 4(29) & (30)**: 
  - Updated **Customs Tariff Codes**:
    - Split PCT Code **3920.1000** into:
      - 3920.1010: Mineral filled film for food packaging (10%)
      - 3920.1090: Other (15%)
  - **Duty reductions** for:
    - Parts of **Solar Dish Stirling Engines**
    - **Refrigerated outdoor cabinets** (PCT 8418.6940): 0%
    - **PVC Emulsion Grade & Release Paper**: 0% and 3% under specific import conditions.

---

### ✈️ **3. Aviation Sector Exemptions Expanded**
- **MROs and AMOs** (Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul and Aircraft Maintenance Organizations) added to beneficiaries under **Part VI of the Second Schedule**.
- Authority changed from “Aviation Division” to **Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority**.
- Clarified **conditions and approvals** for customs duty exemptions on parts and tools used in aircraft overhaul.

---

### 🛒 **4. E-Commerce & Sales Tax Enforcement**
- **Section 14AC, 14AD & 14AE** changes:
  - Clear procedures for **bar on bank accounts or transfer of immovable property** for unregistered persons.
  - Stronger **committee-based safeguards** and public transparency before coercive action.
  - Substituted word “attached” with “seized” and clarified procedure for **removal of receivership**.

- **Eleventh Schedule Change**:
  - Digital sales by **payment intermediaries and couriers** will now attract **2% final sales tax** on gross value of goods from within Pakistan.

---

### 👮 **5. Arrest & Prosecution for Tax Fraud**
- **Section 37A and 37B**:
  - Strengthened **legal safeguards**:
    - **No arrest** before completion of inquiry.
    - Accused may approach court for **bail under CrPC 497 and 498**.
    - Clearer purpose added: to create deterrence and ensure retribution.
  - Inserted word "duly served" in several subsections to emphasize proper service of notices before action.

---

### 💰 **6. Income Tax Changes**
- **Section 65F**: Restricts tax credit to **coal supplied for power generation projects in Sindh**.
- **Section 114C**:
  - Only “**ineligible persons**” restricted from investment-related benefits.
  - **Cash withdrawal ban** applies only **above specified thresholds** (under Fifteenth Schedule).
  
- **Pension and Annuity Taxation**:
  - Clarified rates for pensions:
    - Up to Rs 10 million: **0%**

- **Exemptions Added**:

  - Institutions added to exemption list:
    - **Beaconhouse National University**
    - **Federal Ziauddin University**
    - **Punjab Police Welfare Organization, Lahore**

- **National Logistics Corporation (NLC)**:
  - Special rate of **3% minimum tax** on income under section 153 and section 236A.

---

### 💳 **7. Fifteenth Schedule – Threshold Changes**
- Heading changed from **"Value Fixation"** to **"Threshold for Economic Transactions"**.
- Entries adjusted, including **removal of S. No. 4**, likely related to real estate thresholds or banking limits (details truncated).

---

### 📝 Final Notes:
The amendments mostly:
- **Clarify ambiguities**, update terminology, and fix internal references.
- Add **new sectors/entities for tax relief/exemptions**.
- Enhance **enforcement mechanisms** but with added procedural safeguards.
- Make **digital and e-commerce taxation more robust and traceable**.

Here is a **detailed breakdown of all key changes made to the Finance Bill, 2025** through the **amendments moved in the National Assembly**, organized clause-by-clause for clarity:

---

### 🔁 CLAUSE 3 — *Terminology Change*

- **"Carbon Levy" renamed to "Climate Support Levy"**:
  - All references in Clause 3 are substituted to reflect this new term, aligning the levy with broader environmental and climate initiatives.

---

### ⚙️ CLAUSE 4 — *Customs, Tariffs & Exemptions*

#### A. **Customs Tariff and Schedule Revisions**:
- **PCT Code 3920.1000** split into:
  - **3920.1010** – Mineral filled film of polyolefins (10%)
  - **3920.1090** – Other (15%)

- **New zero-rated items under Part I of the Second Schedule**:
  - Parts for **Solar Dish Stirling Engines**:
    - Control panel (PCT 8537.1090 / 8537.2000)
    - Stirling Engine Generator (PCT 8501.6100)

#### B. **Restored or Adjusted Exemptions in Part III**:
- **S. No. 102** – Zero-rating on refrigerated outdoor cabinets designed for electronic equipment insertion.
- **S. No. 131** – Conditional exemptions:
  - PVC Emulsion Grade (PCT 3904.1010) – 0% for certain industries.
  - Release Paper (PCT 4811.5990) – 3%, conditional upon import quota & lab tests.

#### C. **Part VI Adjustments (Aviation Sector)**:
- Scope broadened to include:
  - **MROs and AMOs** (Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul Companies, Aircraft Maintenance Organizations).
- Authority changed from **Aviation Division** to **Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority** under the new **Civil Aviation Act, 2023**.
- **New condition**: Import items must be approved by the **Pakistan Airports Authority / Defence Division** per GoP Policy.
- Terminologies such as “tools” expanded to include “kits and parts”, clarifying applicability to broader overhauling activities.

---

### 🏦 CLAUSE 5 — *Anti-Benami, Registration Bar & Enforcement*

#### A. **Sections 14AC & 14AD (Property Transfer Bar)**:
- Clearer processes for **imposing a bar on property transfers** for unregistered persons.
- **Personal hearing mandated** before such a bar is applied.
- Bar may only be imposed **on recommendation by Committee** and with **15-day notice** for registration compliance.
- Applicability of this section will be **notified separately by FBR**.

#### B. **Section 14AE (Property Seizure & Receiver)**:
- Replaces the term **"attached"** with **"seized"**, clarifying enforcement.
- Empowers authorities to **reverse appointment of a receiver** more directly.

#### C. **Section 37A — Arrest for Tax Fraud**:
- Procedural safeguards added:
  - Arrest **only after inquiry is completed**.
  - **"Duly served" notice requirement** inserted at multiple steps.
- **Bail rights clarified**: Courts to apply **CrPC Sections 497 & 498**.
- Purpose: Deterrence and punishment for tax fraud made explicit.

---

### 💻 CLAUSE 5(30) — *Digital Economy Taxation*

- **Eleventh Schedule Revised**:
  - New entry: **2% sales tax on digital supplies**:
    - Payment intermediaries and couriers will withhold tax on **digitally ordered goods supplied from within Pakistan**.

---

### 📜 CLAUSE 7 — *Negative List Concept*

- **Section 3(4)** of Sales Tax Law:
  - FBR may now issue a **Negative List of exempt services** under Table-3 via Gazette notification — offering more centralized power over service exemptions.

---

### 🏢 CLAUSE 8 — *Income Tax Ordinance Amendments*

#### A. **Section 65F**:
- Restricts tax credit to **coal mining projects in Sindh**, where coal is supplied to power generation only — removing broader applicability.

#### B. **Section 114C – Cash Flow Restrictions**:
- **Cash withdrawal restrictions** apply **only above a threshold** as defined in **Fifteenth Schedule**.
- Limits to apply **only to ineligible persons**.

#### C. **Tax Exemptions Expanded**:
- New exempt incomes:
  - **Olympic medal monetary awards** (from public office or government)
  - **Army Officers Benevolent Fund / Bereaved Family Schemes**
  - Additional universities and welfare bodies:
    - Beaconhouse National University
    - Federal Ziauddin University
    - Punjab Police Welfare Organization

#### D. **Section 153 & 236A – NLC Preferential Rate**:
- **3% minimum tax** on:
  - Contracts under Section 153(b) & (c)
  - Toll collection rights under Section 236A
  - Applies to **National Logistics Corporation (NLC)** only.

#### E. **Pension & Annuity Taxation (Division I of First Schedule)**:
- Revised slab:
  - **Up to Rs. 10 million** – 0%
  - **Exceeds Rs. 10 million** – 5% on excess
- **Clarification for annuity income** under “income from other sources.”

---

### 💰 CLAUSE 8(48) — *Donations & Charitable Deductions*

- Additional charitable institutions added to the **list under Clause 61** for tax deduction eligibility.
- Exemptions now also cover **award income for sports medals** under Clause 65B from tax year 2025.

---

### 💸 CLAUSE 8 — *Fifteenth Schedule – Value Threshold Renamed*

- Heading changed from **"Value Fixation"** to **"Threshold for Economic Transactions"**.
- Focus shifts from assessing values to **setting transaction thresholds** for banking compliance.
- **S. No. 4 omitted**, and schedule renumbered — exact deletion redacted in text.

---

### 🧾 Summary: **Major Themes of the Amendments**

| Category                  | Key Changes                                                                 |
|--------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Climate Terminology      | Carbon Levy → Climate Support Levy                                          |
| Energy/Aviation Sector   | Expanded tax exemptions & new authorities (CAA, MROs, AMOs)                 |
| Tax Enforcement          | Procedural safeguards on arrests, bar on transfer, property seizure         |
| Digital Economy          | 2% tax on digitally ordered goods from within Pakistan                      |
| Income Tax               | Olympic awards, pensions, annuities, and NLC taxation refined               |
| Schedules Update         | New exemptions under First, Second, Eleventh & Fifteenth Schedules          |
| FBR Powers               | Can now issue “Negative List” for exempted services via Gazette             |

Based on the reply filed against the rectification notice under Section 221 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, and in light of the legal arguments raised therein, the following **grounds of appeal** are proposed for submission before the **Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR)** on behalf of **K-Electric Limited** for **Tax Year 2007**:

---

### **Before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue**
**Grounds of Appeal**

**Appellant:** K-Electric Limited  
**Tax Year:** 2007  
**Subject:** Rectification order passed under Section 221 read with Section 138(3A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001

The appellant respectfully submits the following grounds of appeal for consideration:

1. **That the learned Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue (DCIR) erred in law and facts in passing the impugned order dated May 26, 2025, under Section 221 of the Ordinance, whereby an attempt was made to retrospectively subject the amount of tariff differential subsidy received by the appellant to minimum tax under Section 113, despite the matter already having been adjudicated and remanded in earlier proceedings.**

2. **That the impugned order is barred by limitation as prescribed under Section 124(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, since the matter was remanded by the Commissioner (Appeals) vide appellate order dated May 19, 2022, and the department failed to pass any consequential order within the mandatory one-year timeframe. Hence, the department became functus officio in the matter and the impugned order is without lawful authority.**

3. **That the action under Section 221 is misconceived and ultra vires the law, as it seeks to create a new tax liability based on a reappraisal of law and facts, rather than correcting a clerical or arithmetic mistake apparent from the record. Section 221 cannot be invoked to re-open concluded assessments or revisit debatable issues of law, as held in various judicial precedents including _National Foods Ltd v. CIR_ (1992 PTD 570) and _CIT v. Abdul Ghani_ (PLD 2007 SC 308).**

4. **That the application of minimum tax under Section 113 to the tariff differential subsidy is a highly contentious and interpretational matter, and cannot be termed as a “mistake apparent from record.” Therefore, the very foundation of invoking Section 221 is erroneous, rendering the entire proceedings without jurisdiction.**

5. **That the issue of minimum tax on tariff differential subsidy was already examined, deliberated, and contested in the original audit proceedings under Section 122(5) of the Ordinance, and formed the subject matter of appeal proceedings culminating in a remand. Any attempt to now re-agitate the same issue under the garb of rectification amounts to double jeopardy and is legally impermissible.**

6. **That the impugned notice and order also refer to Section 138(3A) of the Ordinance, which was inserted through the Tax Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025. The application of this provision to past tax years and pending judicial proceedings is not only unconstitutional and retrospective in nature but also violates the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 10A and 77 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973.**

7. **That the issuance of the rectification notice and passing of the impugned order during the pendency of appeal and judicial proceedings before the Hon’ble Sindh High Court is premature, violative of judicial decorum, and seeks to render the appellate and judicial forums infructuous.**

8. **That the impugned order is arbitrary, passed in disregard of principles of natural justice, and is liable to be vacated on the grounds of excessive exercise of jurisdiction, malafide intent, and violation of the settled principles governing tax administration.**

**Prayer**

In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully prayed that the impugned rectification order dated May 26, 2025, passed under Section 221 of the Ordinance for Tax Year 2007, may kindly be annulled in its entirety, and all consequential actions taken in pursuance thereof may be declared void ab initio. Any tax recovery initiated under Section 138(3A) on the basis of the impugned order may also be stayed, pending final adjudication of the appeal.

# Sindh WWF Act (2014) – Strict Surcharge Liability

Section 5(8) of the Sindh Workers Welfare Fund Act, 2014 (Sindh Act XXXIII of 2015) mandates a default surcharge of 15% per annum on any unpaid WWF contribution【54†L230-L236】.  The language is absolute – an industrial establishment that “fails to pay the amount due…shall…be liable to pay” the surcharge【54†L230-L236】.  There is no carve‐out or “reasonable cause” clause in the statute, nor any discretion to waive the surcharge on grounds of good faith. In law, this has been interpreted as a strict liability provision: once the due date (typically the tax return filing date) is missed, the surcharge automatically accrues.  Courts generally enforce such mandatory penalties unless the statute itself provides relief.

## Case Law: Relief or Waiver of Tax Penalties

While no Sindh WWF case directly waives S.5(8) surcharge, Pakistani courts have emphasized fairness in penal provisions.  For example, the Sindh High Court has held that penalties cannot be imposed without proof of willful default or mens rea, and must be proportionate to the misconduct【92†L100-L108】【92†L111-L114】.  In *Habib Metropolitan Bank Ltd. v. CIR*, the High Court refused an income-tax penalty where no intentional default was shown, underscoring that punitive measures must be justified by evidence of fault (a point now codified by the 2022 WWF amendment specifying “whether willfully or otherwise”【66†L120-L127】).  More recently, the Supreme Court reiterated that any punishment must not be “arbitrary, perverse or based on irrelevant considerations,” and that a finding of no misconduct would ordinarily call for exoneration, not penalty【92†L100-L108】【92†L111-L114】.  By analogy, one can argue that imposing a heavy surcharge on a first-time, inadvertent WWF default (especially where the taxpayer immediately paid the liability upon notice) may be excessive or disproportionate under these principles.  

## SRB Amnesty Schemes and Administrative Relief

The Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) has in the past granted broad waivers of penalties and surcharges to encourage compliance.  For instance, in June 2021 the SRB issued an *“incentive scheme”* under SRO SRB‑3‑4/10/2021 that exempted **all penalties** and most surcharge on WWF arrears outstanding up to 31 May 2021, provided the principal WWF amounts and minimal percentages of the surcharge were paid by specified dates【85†L374-L382】【85†L420-L428】.  Under that scheme, even taxpayers who had already “late paid” WWF contributions could secure full relief by paying just 1% of the outstanding penalty and 1% of the surcharge【85†L420-L428】.  Earlier, the SRB similarly waived entire penalties and surcharges in other tax contexts (e.g. a 2012 notification exempted *all* sales-tax penalties and surcharge if the principal tax was paid by a deadline)【104†L151-L161】.  These examples show that the Board has discretion (often via executive notification) to suspend or moderate surcharge in the public interest or for first-time defaulters.  No current SRB circular covers the 2023 WWF year, but the history of amnesty programs suggests administrative leniency is possible if invoked by authorities.

## 2022 Amendment and “Commercial Establishment” Inclusion

A key development is the Sindh WWF (Amendment) Act, 2021 (Sindh Act XV of 2022), which took effect on enactment (September 26, 2022)【105†L25-L27】.  This amendment greatly broadened the definition of liable “industrial establishment” by explicitly adding **“any establishment to which the Sindh Shops and Commercial Establishment Act, 2015 applies”**【71†L42-L49】.  In practical terms, shops, commercial offices and similar businesses now fall under WWF.  This expansion took effect immediately with no transitional exemption (the Act “shall come into force at once”【105†L25-L27】).  Taxpayers who had not considered themselves covered now faced new liabilities.  While not a waiver per se, this context can support leniency arguments: the obligation and penalties were extended only recently and taxpayers may claim legitimate expectation of notice or relief for first application of the law.

## Arguments for Waiver of Surcharge

In appealing for a full waiver of the Rs.10,130,663 surcharge, the taxpayer can present several legal and equity arguments:

- **Good Faith and Prompt Compliance:** The taxpayer had no deliberate intent to evade WWF; upon receiving a notice they promptly paid the entire 2023 WWF principal.  For tax year 2024 they proactively discharged the WWF due on time. This shows bona fide compliance.  Analogous case law in Pakistan holds that penalties imposed on taxpayers acting in good faith and taking corrective action should be viewed leniently【92†L100-L108】.  The 2021 SRB scheme likewise rewarded quick compliance by drastically reducing surcharges【85†L374-L382】.  

- **First-Time Inadvertent Default:** The surcharge arose from a first-year oversight due to ambiguity and recent law changes, not willful neglect. The Sindh High Court has suggested that when there is no indication of willful default, penalties (and by analogy surcharge) should not be imposed rigidly【92†L100-L108】【92†L111-L114】. Although the amendment now states “whether willfully or otherwise,” courts still balance fairness and proportionality【92†L100-L108】【92†L111-L114】.  Here the alleged “offense” is a one-time delay, and strict penalty may be arguably disproportionate to that minor lapse. The Supreme Court’s proportionality test would ask whether a massive surcharge was a necessary, least-restrictive response, given the taxpayer’s corrective actions.

- **Disproportionate Penalty and Fundamental Fairness:** A 15% per annum surcharge can quickly accumulate to multiples of the tax due.  Civil justice principles in Pakistan (and internationally) require penalties not be excessive.  The Supreme Court has cautioned that an interference with rights (such as property rights by surcharge) must be justified and balanced【92†L100-L108】【92†L111-L114】. Here, the taxpayer may argue that the surcharge is punitive rather than compensatory, exceeding any harm, and thus violates fundamental fairness or Article 4 of the Constitution (lawful action against rights). The recent emphasis on proportionality suggests relief if a penalty “strikes a fair balance”【92†L100-L108】; a blanket surcharge on a first inadvertent default arguably fails that test.

- **Lack of Notice or Due Process:** Although the law is published, the practical awareness of the extended WWF levy on new categories was low. The taxpayer could claim that it lacked reasonable notice of its liability until the SRB notice arrived. Procedural fairness doctrine may require courts/tribunals to consider whether imposing surcharge without warning or hearing is against natural justice.  If the Commissioner issued an order without affording an opportunity to explain the first-time default, an appeal can argue that surcharges should not attach until the taxpayer is heard.

- **Policy and Past Concession:** Given that the government itself has offered sweeping surcharge waivers to spur compliance (e.g. 2021 incentive scheme【85†L374-L382】【104†L151-L161】), it would be consistent and equitable for relief to be granted in similar spirit. A contrary approach might deter industries from voluntary disclosure of liability. Arguably, continuing to penalize after the fact (when the taxpayer is already paying its dues) runs counter to the public policy behind those leniency measures.

In summary, while Section 5(8) provides no express exception, persuasive arguments exist on grounds of equity and proportionality.  The taxpayer should emphasize its immediate payment of WWF, the absence of any willful evasion, and the recent extension of WWF law.  It can urge that, under principles of fairness and past SRB practice, a complete waiver of the surcharge would be reasonable and just.

Sindh WWF Act (2014) – Strict Surcharge Liability
Section 5(8) of the Sindh Workers Welfare Fund Act, 2014 (Sindh Act XXXIII of 2015) mandates a default surcharge of 15% per annum on any unpaid WWF contribution. The language is absolute – an industrial establishment that “fails to pay the amount due…shall…be liable to pay” the surcharge. There is no carve‐out or “reasonable cause” clause in the statute, nor any discretion to waive the surcharge on grounds of good faith. In law, this has been interpreted as a strict liability provision: once the due date (typically the tax return filing date) is missed, the surcharge automatically accrues. Courts generally enforce such mandatory penalties unless the statute itself provides relief.
Case Law: Relief or Waiver of Tax Penalties
While no Sindh WWF case directly waives S.5(8) surcharge, Pakistani courts have emphasized fairness in penal provisions. For example, the Sindh High Court has held that penalties cannot be imposed without proof of willful default or mens rea, and must be proportionate to the misconduct. In Habib Metropolitan Bank Ltd. v. CIR, the High Court refused an income-tax penalty where no intentional default was shown, underscoring that punitive measures must be justified by evidence of fault (a point now codified by the 2022 WWF amendment specifying “whether willfully or otherwise”). More recently, the Supreme Court reiterated that any punishment must not be “arbitrary, perverse or based on irrelevant considerations,” and that a finding of no misconduct would ordinarily call for exoneration, not penalty. By analogy, one can argue that imposing a heavy surcharge on a first-time, inadvertent WWF default (especially where the taxpayer immediately paid the liability upon notice) may be excessive or disproportionate under these principles.
SRB Amnesty Schemes and Administrative Relief
The Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) has in the past granted broad waivers of penalties and surcharges to encourage compliance. For instance, in June 2021 the SRB issued an “incentive scheme” under SRO SRB 3 4/10/2021 that exempted all penalties and most surcharge on WWF arrears outstanding up to 31 May 2021, provided the principal WWF amounts and minimal percentages of the surcharge were paid by specified dates. Under that scheme, even taxpayers who had already “late paid” WWF contributions could secure full relief by paying just 1% of the outstanding penalty and 1% of the surcharge. Earlier, the SRB similarly waived entire penalties and surcharges in other tax contexts (e.g. a 2012 notification exempted all sales-tax penalties and surcharge if the principal tax was paid by a deadline). These examples show that the Board has discretion (often via executive notification) to suspend or moderate surcharge in the public interest or for first-time defaulters. No current SRB circular covers the 2023 WWF year, but the history of amnesty programs suggests administrative leniency is possible if invoked by authorities.
2022 Amendment and “Commercial Establishment” Inclusion
A key development is the Sindh WWF (Amendment) Act, 2021 (Sindh Act XV of 2022), which took effect on enactment (September 26, 2022). This amendment greatly broadened the definition of liable “industrial establishment” by explicitly adding “any establishment to which the Sindh Shops and Commercial Establishment Act, 2015 applies”. In practical terms, shops, commercial offices and similar businesses now fall under WWF. This expansion took effect immediately with no transitional exemption (the Act “shall come into force at once”). Taxpayers who had not considered themselves covered now faced new liabilities. While not a waiver per se, this context can support leniency arguments: the obligation and penalties were extended only recently and taxpayers may claim legitimate expectation of notice or relief for first application of the law.
Arguments for Waiver of Surcharge
In appealing for a full waiver of the Rs.10,130,663 surcharge, the taxpayer can present several legal and equity arguments:
•	Good Faith and Prompt Compliance: The taxpayer had no deliberate intent to evade WWF; upon receiving a notice they promptly paid the entire 2023 WWF principal. For tax year 2024 they proactively discharged the WWF due on time. This shows bona fide compliance. Analogous case law in Pakistan holds that penalties imposed on taxpayers acting in good faith and taking corrective action should be viewed leniently. The 2021 SRB scheme likewise rewarded quick compliance by drastically reducing surcharges.
•	First-Time Inadvertent Default: The surcharge arose from a first-year oversight due to ambiguity and recent law changes, not willful neglect. The Sindh High Court has suggested that when there is no indication of willful default, penalties (and by analogy surcharge) should not be imposed rigidly. Although the amendment now states “whether willfully or otherwise,” courts still balance fairness and proportionality. Here the alleged “offense” is a one-time delay, and strict penalty may be arguably disproportionate to that minor lapse. The Supreme Court’s proportionality test would ask whether a massive surcharge was a necessary, least-restrictive response, given the taxpayer’s corrective actions.
•	Disproportionate Penalty and Fundamental Fairness: A 15% per annum surcharge can quickly accumulate to multiples of the tax due. Civil justice principles in Pakistan (and internationally) require penalties not be excessive. The Supreme Court has cautioned that an interference with rights (such as property rights by surcharge) must be justified and balanced. Here, the taxpayer may argue that the surcharge is punitive rather than compensatory, exceeding any harm, and thus violates fundamental fairness or Article 4 of the Constitution (lawful action against rights). The recent emphasis on proportionality suggests relief if a penalty “strikes a fair balance”; a blanket surcharge on a first inadvertent default arguably fails that test.
•	Lack of Notice or Due Process: Although the law is published, the practical awareness of the extended WWF levy on new categories was low. The taxpayer could claim that it lacked reasonable notice of its liability until the SRB notice arrived. Procedural fairness doctrine may require courts/tribunals to consider whether imposing surcharge without warning or hearing is against natural justice. If the Commissioner issued an order without affording an opportunity to explain the first-time default, an appeal can argue that surcharges should not attach until the taxpayer is heard.
•	Policy and Past Concession: Given that the government itself has offered sweeping surcharge waivers to spur compliance (e.g. 2021 incentive scheme), it would be consistent and equitable for relief to be granted in similar spirit. A contrary approach might deter industries from voluntary disclosure of liability. Arguably, continuing to penalize after the fact (when the taxpayer is already paying its dues) runs counter to the public policy behind those leniency measures.
In summary, while Section 5(8) provides no express exception, persuasive arguments exist on grounds of equity and proportionality. The taxpayer should emphasize its immediate payment of WWF, the absence of any willful evasion, and the recent extension of WWF law. It can urge that, under principles of fairness and past SRB practice, a complete waiver of the surcharge would be reasonable and just.
Sources: Sindh WWF Act, 2014, §5(8); SRB notifications; Sindh WWF Amendment Act, 2021 (Act XV of 2022); Sindh High Court/Supreme Court decisions on tax penalties; Sindh tax-board circulars.

Based on your detailed summary, below are **grounds of appeal** that can be included in your submission before the Appellate Tribunal to contest the imposition of default surcharge under Section 5(8) of the Sindh Workers Welfare Fund Act, 2014:

---

### **Suggested Grounds of Appeal**

1. **That the Learned Officer erred in law and facts in imposing default surcharge under Section 5(8) of the Sindh Workers Welfare Fund Act, 2014, despite the fact that the principal liability for Tax Year 2023 was promptly discharged by the appellant upon issuance of notice, and further compliance for Tax Year 2024 was voluntarily undertaken, demonstrating good faith and bona fide conduct.**

2. **That the default, if any, was inadvertent and occurred in the first year of the appellant’s liability under the expanded scope of the Act introduced via the Sindh WWF (Amendment) Act, 2021, which newly extended the levy to commercial establishments. In the absence of willful default or mens rea, imposition of strict surcharge is excessive and disproportionate to the minor lapse.**

3. **That the mandatory imposition of surcharge without affording the appellant an opportunity of being heard violates the principles of natural justice and due process, especially where the default arose due to genuine unawareness and no mala fide intent was present.**

4. **That the surcharge imposed at 15% per annum is harsh, arbitrary, and not proportionate to the alleged default, particularly when the entire WWF liability was settled in full upon first intimation. The imposition fails the test of fairness and proportionality laid down by superior courts and infringes Article 4 of the Constitution of Pakistan.**

5. **That reliance on Section 5(8) as a strict liability provision without considering mitigating circumstances is contrary to the consistent judicial view that tax penalties and surcharges must not be enforced mechanically and should be assessed in light of taxpayer conduct, intent, and proportionality.**

6. **That the Learned Officer failed to consider the past practice of the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB), which has granted amnesty and waived surcharge and penalties in cases of delayed WWF payments through various notifications (e.g. SRO SRB 3 4/10/2021), thereby establishing a precedent for administrative leniency in good faith compliance cases.**

7. **That the calculation of surcharge itself may be flawed or not in accordance with the methodology prescribed under the Act, and thus requires independent verification and adjudication by the Hon’ble Tribunal.**

“It cannot be invoked or applied independently in isolation and has to be read with Section 8A; and can only be invoked against the petitioners, once an exercise has been carried out and a conclusive finding has been arrived at against them pursuant to section 8A of the Act,” a division bench of SHC comprised of Justice Junaid Ghaffar and Justice Agha Faisal declared in an order.
The bench didn’t declare provision of s.8(1)(ca) of the Act as being ultra vires or unconstitutional while giving the verdict in the pleas were urging the court to declare Section 8(1)(ca) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (“Act”) as ultra vires to the constitution. Petitions were filed in the court by Total Parco Pakistan Limited, Kirthar Pakistan B.V., Proctor & Gamble Pakistan Limited, ENI Pakistan Limited and others.
According to the plea of the petitioners, when they purchase goods from suppliers/active taxpayers, they are required to make payment of the goods as well as the amount of the sales tax involved and once that is paid in terms of relevant provisions of the Act including Section 73 ibid, they are then issued a sales tax invoice on the basis of which they claim input tax adjustment in their monthly sales tax returns. Once it is done, according to them, the suppliers no more remain in their control, and if ultimately a default occurs in depositing the sales tax, input tax claimed by them is then being denied on the basis Section 8(1)(ca) of the Act which according to them is ultra vires, confiscatory, unreasonable and beyond the mandate of the act read with the constitution of the country. On the other hand, the respondents argued that a mere show-cause notice has been issued; hence, petitions are not maintainable; that it is settled that all efforts are to be made to save the law rather than to declare it ultra vires; that input tax is not a fundamental right, but only a statutory right.
The court in its order observed section 8 generally restricts such claim of input tax and for the present purposes it is disallowed in terms of section 8(1)(ca), whereas, 8A9 provides for initiating a joint action against the persons so involved in it. At the same time Section 7310 of the Act requires a purchaser to follow certain guidelines while claiming any such input tax. Therefore, the court didn’t declare the provision of s.8(1)(ca) of the act as being ultra vires or unconstitutional. “We would rather save it and read it down, in the manner, that it cannot be invoked or applied independently in isolation and has to be read with Section 8A; and can only be invoked against the petitioners, once an exercise has been carried out and a conclusive finding has been arrived at against them pursuant to section 8A of the Act,” the order stated.

Below is a summary of the potential **reason for disallowance** under each entry or category:

---

### **Section 8(1)(f) – Goods or services not used in furtherance of taxable supplies**
Under this clause, input tax is disallowed on goods/services that are not directly used in the taxable activity. Below are reasons entry-wise:

- **Promotional items, gift packages, advertising, and event management**: Expenditures on giveaways, advertising goods, and event promotions (e.g. Ad-Change, Retail Media, JBN Jaws) are considered non-core activities and not directly related to taxable supplies.
- **Manpower, maintenance, construction, security, fire safety, and engineering**: While these support business operations (e.g. HRSG, Haseen Habib, Etimaad Engineering), they are often considered ancillary and not directly tied to production or taxable sales.
- **Communications and IT services (e.g. Link Dot Net, M.B. Communication)**: Possibly treated as administrative overheads.
- **Comprehensive site operation services**: These services, while operationally relevant, may be treated as non-direct inputs if not clearly linked to taxable goods sold.

> **Reason for disallowance**: **Input tax not directly attributable to taxable supplies.**

---

### **Section 8(1)(h) – Input tax claimed on fake/fictitious/incomplete/fraudulent invoices or non-registered persons**
This clause allows disallowance where:
- Supplier is not registered;
- Invoice lacks key details;
- Supply is fictitious or unverifiable.

Many of the entries (e.g. Raza ul Hassan, Concept Engineering, Arb) involve repair, piping, structural metal, or electrical materials—potentially from **unregistered suppliers** or invoices not fulfilling documentary requirements.

> **Reason for disallowance**: **Failure to verify genuineness of suppliers/invoices; or goods not properly recorded in stock/supplies.**

---

### **Section 8(1)(i) – Acquisition of goods or services for personal, non-business or non-taxable activities**
This applies to items of **personal, administrative or office use**, such as:

- **Office equipment, furniture, stationery** – Mars Office Products
- **Storage, logistics, and transport services** – Agility Logistics
- **Computer and IT equipment** – GCS (Pvt) Ltd
- **Vehicle parts** – VPL Limited

> **Reason for disallowance**: **Goods/services not used for taxable business activities or not directly linked to supply chain.**

---

### **Section 8(1)(ca) – Non-verification with provincial sales tax returns**
Disallowance under this clause relates to **mismatch** or **non-verification** of input tax claims with provincial sales tax filings of the service providers.

- Some entries (e.g., Shell Pakistan Ltd, Tristar Transport, Sanghi Transport, Rasch Pvt Ltd, etc.) show substantial amounts not verified with provincial returns.
- A few vendors (e.g., “taxpayers without proper NTN”) are also listed, which further weakens documentary compliance.

> **Reason for disallowance**: **Input tax claimed where corresponding supplier sales tax is not reported/verified in provincial returns.**

---

### **Other Disallowances Mentioned:**

1. **Rs. 2,175,150** – Output tax on **disposal of fixed assets** was disallowed due to **failure to produce invoices or Annex C** evidence.

Each disallowance broadly stems from either:

Based on your prior instruction to include a paragraph in the Taxation Officer’s finding (regarding the **ineligibility of section 65B tax credit on consumer-funded assets**), and after reviewing the content you've now provided, here is a refined and legally grounded **additional paragraph** that can be incorporated into the earlier **Taxation Officer’s Finding**:

**Additional Paragraph to be inserted in the Finding:**

It is further noted that a portion of the plant and machinery capitalized during the year, particularly in relation to connection infrastructure such as metering systems and grid components, has been funded through amounts recovered from consumers. These recoveries, although capitalized as part of fixed assets, do not represent capital investments made **by the taxpayer from its own funds**, which is a prerequisite for claiming tax credit under **section 65B(1)** of the Ordinance. The language of section 65B allows credit only in respect of investments “made by a company in the purchase of plant and machinery,” thereby requiring **direct investment by the company itself**. Where the cost of acquisition is borne by third parties (i.e., consumers), the taxpayer cannot be considered to have made the investment within the meaning of section 65B. Accordingly, to the extent the capitalized assets have been funded through consumer recoveries, **no tax credit under section 65B shall be admissible**, and appropriate disallowance is warranted to that extent.

### **Finding by the Taxation Officer**

Upon careful examination of the taxpayer’s explanation and financial disclosures, it is noted that the amount of **Rs. 3,653,196,000** has been recognized as **deferred revenue** in Note 23.1 of the audited financial statements. This amount represents recoveries from consumers in respect of connection infrastructure and metering equipment, which are subsequently capitalized and amortized as income over the useful life of the related assets in accordance with **IFRS 15**.

In the tax year under review, the taxpayer has **amortized Rs. 1,831,470,000** of this deferred revenue as income in the profit and loss account, and a **corresponding amount has been claimed as depreciation**, resulting in a tax-neutral outcome for that portion.

With respect to the **remaining unamortized portion of Rs. 1,821,726,000**, it is acknowledged that the taxpayer has not recognized this as income in its financial accounts. However, under the **accrual basis of accounting** mandated by **section 32(2)** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, and read with **section 34(2)**, the entire recoverable amount may be considered as due and therefore taxable in the current year.

That said, if the **unamortized portion of Rs. 1,821,726,000 is brought to tax**, then, in accordance with the **matching principle** and for the sake of consistency and fairness, the taxpayer must equally be allowed a **corresponding depreciation expense** on the associated assets capitalized using those receipts. Consequently, the transaction would remain **tax-neutral**, with no actual impact on the taxpayer’s taxable income.

**Accordingly, in view of the tax neutrality of the transaction, no adjustment is made on this account.**

### **Finding by the Taxation Officer**

Upon a detailed review of the taxpayer’s explanation and the audited financial statements, it is observed that an amount of **Rs. 3,653,196,000** has been disclosed as deferred revenue, as per Note 23.1. This amount relates to recoveries from consumers against the provision of new service connections, including meters and associated infrastructure. These recoveries are capitalized and recognized as deferred revenue to be amortized over the useful life of the related assets in accordance with **IFRS 15**, particularly paragraph 69.

From a taxation perspective, the taxpayer, being a company, is required to compute income under the **accrual basis of accounting**, as mandated by **section 32(2)** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Accordingly, income becomes chargeable to tax when it becomes due, not merely upon receipt, as further clarified by **sections 34(1) and 34(2)** of the Ordinance.

In the instant case, while the taxpayer has amortized **Rs. 1,831,470,000** as income in the profit and loss account for the year, and claimed an equivalent amount as depreciation, it is important to note that for purposes of taxation, **the entire amount of Rs. 3,653,196,000 has been considered and offered to tax in this tax year** under section 32(2). At the same time, the taxpayer has been allowed corresponding deductions in the form of depreciation on the assets capitalized out of these recoveries.

Thus, the recognition of the full amount as taxable income, together with the allowance of the related depreciation expense, results in a **tax-neutral event**. There is no revenue loss to the exchequer, and the timing of accounting recognition under IFRS has no bearing on the net tax liability.

Accordingly, since the entire recoveries have already been brought to tax in the current year and corresponding deductions have been allowed, **no further adjustment is warranted**. The accounting treatment adopted by the taxpayer does not result in any understatement of income or overstatement of expenses for tax purposes.

**In light of the above, no addition is made on account of deferred revenue in the current tax year.**

The unamortized portion continues to reflect an unfulfilled future obligation of the taxpayer to provide utility over time and, therefore, does **not meet the criteria of “due” or “earned” income** under the accrual basis prescribed by the Ordinance.

It is further emphasized that taxing the remaining balance without simultaneously allowing the corresponding depreciation would result in a **distortion of true income**, contrary to the scheme and spirit of the Ordinance, as well as established accounting standards.

In view of the above, and based on the principle of **fair taxation and matching of income and expenditure**, it is held that although the entire amount of Rs. 3,653,196,000 is ultimately subject to taxation under the accrual regime of section 32(2), the **proportion already taxed (Rs. 1,831,470,000)** has been **appropriately matched** with the corresponding depreciation charge. As to the balance, no income has yet become due or earned, and the matching expense has not been claimed. Therefore, any adjustment would not result in additional tax liability.

**Accordingly, no addition is made in respect of deferred revenue for the year under consideration.**

**Subject:**  Treatment of SIUT Trust and Society under Finance Act, 2025 – Request for Transitional Relief  

Dear Sir,  

We write on behalf of our clients **Sindh Institute of Urology & Transplantation (SIUT) Trust** and **Society for the Welfare of SIUT**.  It has come to our attention that the *Finance Act, 2025* has amended the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 in a manner that materially affects our clients’ tax-exempt status.  Specifically, the amendment has modified Clause 66, Part I of the Second Schedule so that the incomes of SIUT Trust and Society are now exempt **“subject to the provisions of section 100C”**【49†L3543-L3545】【50†L3618-L3622】.  In practical terms, this means that our clients’ income will remain tax-exempt only if they satisfy the conditions of section 100C, including obtaining formal approval as a “non-profit organization” (NPO) under section 2(36) of the Ordinance【56†L115-L122】. 

Previously, by virtue of their inclusion in the Second Schedule (Table I), the SIUT Trust and Society enjoyed unconditional exemption from income tax【38†L165-L169】.  The Finance Act, 2025, however, merges the former unconditional exemption category (Table I) with the conditional one (Table II)【49†L3543-L3545】【50†L3618-L3622】.  As a result, our clients must now apply to the FBR (through the approved process) to secure NPO status under section 2(36) if they are to benefit from the exemption that they previously enjoyed as of right.  This is a new compliance requirement that was not contemplated in prior law. 

Obtaining “approved NPO” status under section 2(36) is a multi-step process【56†L115-L122】, and it may take considerable time to complete the necessary documentation and FBR review.  In the meantime, the Trust and Society would be exposed to taxation on their income (or require retrospective relief) if they fail to meet the new requirement immediately.  Moreover, this change also directly affects donors: under the Ordinance donors receive a tax credit for charitable contributions **only if** the donee institution is an approved NPO【56†L109-L112】.  In short, until our clients achieve NPO approval, donations to SIUT would not carry the usual tax incentives for donors, which could have a chilling effect on future contributions. 

Our clients are renowned, high‑reputation non‑profit medical institutions providing free healthcare to the underprivileged.  They rely heavily on support from the Sindh government and public donors.  For example, in the Sindh budget for 2023–24, the Government allocated Rs.15.316 billion in grants to SIUT【52†L58-L61】.  It is precisely to sustain this vital healthcare service that our clients’ exempt status has long been recognized without condition.  Abruptly imposing a new approval requirement, without any transitional relief, would disrupt SIUT’s operations and its funding. 

In view of the above, we respectfully **request that the FBR grant a reasonable transition period (at least three years)** for compliance.  Concretely, we propose that the Board issue an appropriate notification (via an SRO or an administrative letter) effectively **deeming** the SIUT Trust and Society as NPOs for this grace period, or otherwise exempt from the new condition, so that they continue to enjoy tax exemption on their income as before.  This will allow time for the entities to obtain formal 2(36) approval without penalizing them or their donors for past reliance on an exemption that was lawfully available.  

We trust that the FBR will recognize the unique public welfare role of SIUT and the hardship that an abrupt change would cause.  We would be grateful if this request could be given sympathetic and expedient consideration.  Please feel free to contact us for any further information or clarification.  

Thank you for your attention to this matter.  

Yours faithfully,  

[Name]  
Counsel for SIUT Trust and Society for the Welfare of SIUT  

**Sources:** Finance Act, 2025 (Second Schedule, cl. 66)【49†L3543-L3545】【50†L3618-L3622】; Finance Act, 2020 (Second Schedule, cl. 66)【38†L165-L169】; Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, §§2(36), 100C【56†L115-L122】; Dawn News (Sindh budget grant for SIUT)【52†L58-L61】.

**Subject:** Tax Implications of Paying Directors' Fees in Cash

Dear Mr. Amanullah,

I hope this email finds you well.

Thank you for reaching out with your query regarding the payment of directors’ fees in cash.

Under the current provisions of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, particularly **Section 21(1)**, business expenses exceeding Rs. 250,000 must be paid through a banking channel (such as a bank transfer or crossed cheque) to be eligible for deduction. Payments made in cash for amounts exceeding this threshold are **disallowed as deductions**. Consequently, if directors' fees are paid in cash and exceed Rs. 250,000, they will not be deductible as business expenses, and the company’s taxable income may increase as a result.

Moreover, under **Section 21(1A)**, which was introduced in 2021, any payments above Rs. 250,000 must be made through **digital means** (including bank transfers, debit card payments, or mobile wallet transactions) to qualify for deduction. While the implementation of this section has been deferred, it remains part of the law, and tax authorities may enforce this requirement in the future. 

**Practical Implications:**  
- If directors’ fees of Rs. 300,000 are paid in cash, the entire Rs. 300,000 will be disallowed as a business expense, and the company will face an increase in taxable income, which could lead to higher corporate taxes and potentially super tax.
- Withholding tax on directors’ fees, under **Section 153**, would also need to be properly documented. Cash payments may raise concerns regarding withholding compliance.

Given these considerations, it is strongly recommended that the company make payments to directors via **bank transfers** or **digital payment methods** to ensure proper documentation and compliance with tax regulations. This will help preserve the deductibility of the fees and avoid potential tax penalties or disallowances.

If you require further clarification or need assistance with adjusting the company’s payment processes, please feel free to reach out.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Best regards,  
Zuhair Minhas

# Tax Treatment of Directors’ Fees Paid in Cash

Under Pakistan’s tax laws, business expenses paid in cash above a specified threshold are **disallowed as deductions**.  In particular, **Section 21(1)** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 provides that any business expenditure “under a single head” exceeding Rs 250,000 must be paid through a banking channel (crossed cheque, bank transfer, etc.) to be deductible【3†L161-L164】.  In other words, **any payment over Rs 250,000 made in cash is not allowed as a deduction** for income-from-business.  For example, Section 21(1) states that expenditures exceeding Rs 250,000 paid otherwise than through normal banking channels are inadmissible【3†L161-L164】.  Notably, directors’ fees do not fall into the narrow exceptions (such as small bills or utility payments) – they are a regular business expense – so paying them in cash violates this rule. 

Furthermore, **Section 21(1A)** (added in 2021) imposes an even stricter requirement on companies.  Under this rule, payments by a company exceeding Rs 250,000 must be made through **“digital means”** (from its registered business bank account) to qualify for deduction【29†L81-L89】.  In effect, for a corporate taxpayer, even a bank cheque may not suffice once Section 21(1A) is enforced; payments should be made via electronic channels (online transfer, debit card, Raast/mobile payments, etc.) as defined in the Ordinance.  (The term “digital means” is broadly defined under tax law to include online payment portals, mobile wallets, ATM/debit card transfers, Raast, and other electronic methods.)  The Finance (Supplementary) Act, 2022 deferred the effective date of Section 21(1A) indefinitely【16†L459-L464】, but the provision remains on the books.  Tax authorities may enforce it in future, so companies should already treat **bank transfers or other electronic payment records** as essential for any high-value expenses.

- **Practical implication:**  If the company pays directors’ fees above Rs 250,000 in cash, the entire fee amount cannot be deducted as a business expense.  The tax officer will likely add back the disallowed amount to taxable income. 

- **Example:**  If a director’s fee of Rs 300,000 is paid in cash, the full Rs 300,000 would be disallowed under Sec. 21.  The company’s taxable income would increase by Rs 300,000, resulting in additional corporate tax (at 29%) and potentially higher super-tax (4% on incomes above Rs 150 million). 

- **Withholding tax:**  Separately, directors’ fees are subject to withholding under Sec. 153 (generally final tax at a specified rate).  Paying fees in cash might also raise issues if withholding is not properly documented.  However, the principal risk here is the **expense disallowance** under Sec. 21 for non-banking payment.

Given these rules, the company should **document directors’ fee payments via banking channels**.  Failure to do so not only violates Section 21 but may also trigger penalties for inadequate record-keeping.  Tax authorities have been focusing on cash transactions (as part of broader digitalization efforts), so cash payments for large expenses are likely to be scrutinized【3†L161-L164】【29†L81-L89】.

In summary, under the Income Tax Ordinance (as amended up to Finance Act, 2025), cash payments of directors’ fees exceeding Rs 250,000 are non-deductible.  To avoid disallowance, such fees should be paid through crossed cheques or digital banking transfers from the company’s business account【3†L161-L164】【29†L81-L89】.  Ensuring proper documentation will help preserve the deduction and prevent unexpected tax liabilities.  

**Sources:** Key provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (as amended) and authoritative tax commentaries【3†L161-L164】【29†L81-L89】. These confirm that Section 21(1) disallows large cash expenditures and Section 21(1A) requires digital payments for companies.

**Federal Finance Act, 2025 – Digital Ordering & E-Commerce**

The Finance Act 2025 introduces a final tax regime on all “digitally ordered” goods and services delivered in Pakistan. When a customer pays through digital channels—such as online banking platforms, mobile wallets, or payment gateways—a withholding of **1%** on the gross transaction value is applied. In the case of cash-on-delivery (COD), the withholding rate is **2%**. These deductions constitute final discharge of income tax liability on such sales. The responsibility to withhold lies with the payment intermediaries or courier companies facilitating the transaction.

In addition, the sales tax rate on **online retail sales** of goods delivered locally has been reduced to **2%**, down from the standard 18%. However, this concessional rate is **not applicable** to **Tier-1 retailers** or cottage industry. Accordingly, **Siza Foods**, being a **Tier-1 retailer**, is not eligible for this reduced sales tax rate.

To summarise, online sales by Siza Foods—whether through their own digital platforms or third-party aggregators like Foodpanda—will attract:
- **1% final income tax** (digital payments) or **2%** (COD),
- **Standard sales tax**, as the reduced 2% rate is not applicable to Tier-1 entities.

---

**Punjab Finance Act, 2025 – Punjab Sales Tax on Services**

The Act amends the Punjab Sales Tax on Services regime by adopting a **negative list** approach, whereby all services are deemed taxable unless specifically exempt. Notably, restaurants are now subject to a **dual-rate structure**:
- **5% sales tax** (without input tax adjustment) on payments made via **debit/credit cards, mobile wallets, or QR codes**;
- **16% standard rate** on all other payment modes, particularly **cash**.

This incentivises digital payments by offering a lower tax rate. However, **Siza Foods has formally exercised its option to apply the standard 16% rate across all transactions**, thereby disregarding the reduced rate otherwise applicable on digital payments—an option permitted under the law and duly approved by the Punjab Revenue Authority.

To enforce compliance, the Act imposes **significant penalties** on businesses that **refuse to accept digital payments**:
- First offence: minimum penalty of **Rs 400,000**;
- Subsequent offences: **Rs 300,000** each;
- After three violations, **the business premises may be sealed for up to one month**.

The law also strengthens digital invoicing obligations and input tax controls for multi-rate service providers, although such provisions are of general application and not specific to the restaurant sector.

---

**Sindh Finance Act, 2025 – Sindh Sales Tax on Services**

The Act updates the nomenclature of taxable restaurant services to **“Food serving services”** and **“Beverage serving services”**. This change is nominal, and the underlying tax treatment remains the same.

The standard **Sindh Sales Tax (SST)** rate continues at **15%**. However, consistent with existing practice, **payments made via debit/credit cards, mobile apps, or other online platforms are taxed at a reduced rate of 8%**. This preferential rate has been formally codified under the Finance Act 2025 and is intended to align with the incentive-based approach adopted by Punjab.

That said, **Siza Foods has exercised its option to apply the full 15% rate**, irrespective of the reduced rate available on digital payments. This option was duly granted and continues to govern their operations in Sindh.

In summary:
- **8% SST** applies on digital transactions (unless opted out);
- **15% SST** applies on cash payments or where standard rate election is made.

Sindh has also adopted a negative-list taxation approach, expanding the scope of taxable services in general, though the specific treatment of restaurant services remains unchanged apart from the formal codification of digital payment incentives.
