# 2025 Tax Amendments Affecting Restaurant Services

## Federal (National) Finance Act 2025 – Digital Ordering & E-Commerce
- **New withholding tax on online orders:**  A final tax is now applied to all “digitally ordered” goods or services delivered in Pakistan.  When customers pay via digital channels (online payment intermediaries), 1% of the gross bill is withheld; if payment is by cash-on-delivery, 2% is withheld【5†L279-L287】.  These sums are final tax on that sale.  The law mandates that payment platforms (e.g. mobile wallets, banks) or courier companies collecting cash must withhold this tax【5†L279-L287】.  (This applies to all e-commerce, including food delivered through apps or websites.)  
- **Reduced sales tax on e-goods:**  For retail sales of goods ordered online and delivered domestically, the sales tax rate is cut to 2% (down from the normal 18%)【7†L175-L177】.  In effect, restaurants selling takeaway meals through their website/app or aggregators are taxed at 2% sales tax on those deliveries (provided they are not “Tier-1” suppliers or cottage-industry).  
- **Income tax final rates:**  The finance act also introduced a “final tax” regime for online sales.  Income tax at 1% (digital payment) or 2% (COD) of gross proceeds is imposed on such sales【5†L279-L287】.  (This mirrors the withholding rates; it means no further income tax on that amount.)  

## Punjab Finance Act 2025 – Punjab Sales Tax on Services
- **Tax on restaurant services:**  The PSTS Act moves to a negative list (all services taxable unless exempt), but key for restaurants is the rates.  The act creates a dual rate for eateries: **5%** sales tax (no input-credit allowed) if the customer pays by debit/credit card, mobile wallet or QR code, versus the normal **16%** rate on other payments.  In other words, restaurant bills paid digitally are taxed at only 5% (with no adjustment claim)【54†L179-L184】.  (Cash payments remain subject to the standard rate.)  
- **Strict penalties for cash-only practice:**  To enforce this, the new law imposes heavy fines on any business refusing electronic payment.  First violation carries **min. Rs400,000**; each repeat **min. Rs300,000**; cumulative fines up to **Rs1,000,000**, and a third offence can even trigger one-month closure of the premises【62†L81-L85】.  This penalty regime explicitly targets venues (like restaurants) that decline cards/mobile.  
- **Compliance measures:**  The Punjab law also reinforces digital invoicing (E-invoice) requirements and tighter input-tax rules for multi-rate services (general technical changes, beyond restaurant scope).  But the main restaurant-related compliance is the new obligation to accept electronic payments or face fines【62†L81-L85】.

## Sindh Finance Act 2025 – Sindh Sales Tax on Services
- **Renaming of restaurant services:**  Sindh’s sales tax schedule has renamed “Restaurant services” to **“Food serving services” and “Beverage serving services”**.  This is largely nomenclature; the tax basis is the same.  
- **Tax rates:**  The standard SST rate remains unchanged at 15%.  However, as before, payments made by card or online continue to attract only **8%** tax.  (Cash payments still face 15%.)  The Sindh revenue board has confirmed there is **no change** to the 8% rate on card transactions【36†L64-L70】.  
- **Digital (online) payment tax:**  The Sindh finance bill explicitly imposes **8% SST on online payments** to restaurants (as well as hotels, cafes etc)【64†L269-L272】.  In practice this codifies the existing rule that any payment to a restaurant via credit/debit card, mobile app or web portal is taxed at 8%.  (This is intended to mirror Punjab’s incentives.)  
- **Other notes:**  Sindh’s move to a negative-list system broadens service taxation generally, but it does **not increase** the restaurant tax rate beyond the above.  In short, restaurant customers in Sindh pay 15% tax on cash bills or 8% on digital bills【36†L64-L70】【64†L269-L272】.

**Federal Finance Act, 2025 – Digital Ordering & E-Commerce**

The Finance Act 2025 introduces a final tax regime on all “digitally ordered” goods and services delivered in Pakistan. When a customer pays through digital channels—such as online banking platforms, mobile wallets, or payment gateways—a withholding of **1%** on the gross transaction value is applied. In the case of cash-on-delivery (COD), the withholding rate is **2%**. These deductions constitute final discharge of income tax liability on such sales. The responsibility to withhold lies with the payment intermediaries or courier companies facilitating the transaction.

In addition, the sales tax rate on **online retail sales** of goods delivered locally has been reduced to **2%**, down from the standard 18%. However, this concessional rate is **not applicable** to **Tier-1 retailers** or cottage industry. Accordingly, **Siza Foods**, being a **Tier-1 retailer**, is not eligible for this reduced sales tax rate.

To summarise, online sales by Siza Foods—whether through their own digital platforms or third-party aggregators like Foodpanda—will attract:
- **1% final income tax** (digital payments) or **2%** (COD),
- **Standard sales tax**, as the reduced 2% rate is not applicable to Tier-1 entities.

---

**Punjab Finance Act, 2025 – Punjab Sales Tax on Services**

The Act amends the Punjab Sales Tax on Services regime by adopting a **negative list** approach, whereby all services are deemed taxable unless specifically exempt. Notably, restaurants are now subject to a **dual-rate structure**:
- **5% sales tax** (without input tax adjustment) on payments made via **debit/credit cards, mobile wallets, or QR codes**;
- **16% standard rate** on all other payment modes, particularly **cash**.

This incentivises digital payments by offering a lower tax rate. However, **Siza Foods has formally exercised its option to apply the standard 16% rate across all transactions**, thereby disregarding the reduced rate otherwise applicable on digital payments—an option permitted under the law and duly approved by the Punjab Revenue Authority.

To enforce compliance, the Act imposes **significant penalties** on businesses that **refuse to accept digital payments**:
- First offence: minimum penalty of **Rs 400,000**;
- Subsequent offences: **Rs 300,000** each;
- After three violations, **the business premises may be sealed for up to one month**.

The law also strengthens digital invoicing obligations and input tax controls for multi-rate service providers, although such provisions are of general application and not specific to the restaurant sector.

---

**Sindh Finance Act, 2025 – Sindh Sales Tax on Services**

The Act updates the nomenclature of taxable restaurant services to **“Food serving services”** and **“Beverage serving services”**. This change is nominal, and the underlying tax treatment remains the same.

The standard **Sindh Sales Tax (SST)** rate continues at **15%**. However, consistent with existing practice, **payments made via debit/credit cards, mobile apps, or other online platforms are taxed at a reduced rate of 8%**. This preferential rate has been formally codified under the Finance Act 2025 and is intended to align with the incentive-based approach adopted by Punjab.

That said, **Siza Foods has exercised its option to apply the full 15% rate**, irrespective of the reduced rate available on digital payments. This option was duly granted and continues to govern their operations in Sindh.

In summary:
- **8% SST** applies on digital transactions (unless opted out);
- **15% SST** applies on cash payments or where standard rate election is made.

Sindh has also adopted a negative-list taxation approach, expanding the scope of taxable services in general, though the specific treatment of restaurant services remains unchanged apart from the formal codification of digital payment incentives.

---

**Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Finance Acts**

Please note that the official copies of the Finance Acts for **Balochistan** and **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa** for the year 2025 are **not yet publicly available**. As such, we are **not offering any comments** on provincial sales tax changes in those jurisdictions at this time. We will review and communicate any relevant changes once the official texts are released.

**Subject: Taxability of Unrestricted Shares Issued During Foreign Assignment**

Dear [Client's Name],

Thank you for your email.

We understand that certain individuals rejoining UEP after completing foreign assignments were issued performance-based company shares during their overseas posting (i.e., during tax years 2022–23), and these shares have now become unrestricted upon completion of the stipulated three-year holding period. The related cost was charged to the host country assets, and the employees were classified as non-residents for Pakistan tax purposes during the grant period.

In light of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, we wish to clarify the following:

1. **Taxability at the Time of Vesting (Unrestriction)**:  
   Under the Ordinance, particularly the definition of *salary* under **Section 12**, any perquisite or benefit derived in connection with employment is considered taxable in the year it is *received or made available*. In the case of share-based compensation, taxability generally arises at the point the shares become vested/unrestricted (i.e., when there is no further risk of forfeiture), and the benefit is “available” to the employee.

2. **Residence Status During Grant Period**:  
   Since the shares were granted during the period the employees were non-resident and rendering services outside Pakistan, the initial grant of shares would not be taxable in Pakistan under **Section 11**, read with **Section 101(2)**. Foreign-source income of a non-resident is not taxable unless it is derived from a Pakistan business or property.

3. **Taxability Upon Return and Unrestriction**:  
   However, as per **Section 12(1)(f)** and the principle of taxation on *receipt* basis, the value of any shares or rights in shares granted to an employee is taxable at the time the benefit vests and becomes unrestricted, even if granted earlier. Since the shares have now vested and the employees are currently *resident* in Pakistan, a strict reading may support taxation in the year of unrestriction.

   That said, considering:
   - the services were rendered abroad during non-residency,
   - the grant was for performance outside Pakistan,
   - and the related cost was borne by the host entity (foreign asset),

   There is a strong argument that such compensation is **foreign-source income**, and therefore not taxable in Pakistan, even if the benefit becomes available after the employee has become resident again. This interpretation aligns with **Section 101(3)**, which provides that salary income is Pakistani-source only if it relates to employment exercised in Pakistan.

4. **Withholding Requirement**:  
   Based on the above reasoning, we are of the view that **no tax withholding is required** under **Section 149**, provided UEP maintains documentation to demonstrate that:
   - the share grant relates solely to foreign services rendered while the individuals were non-residents, and
   - the cost of the shares was borne entirely outside Pakistan.

We recommend maintaining a proper paper trail and, if needed, documenting a formal position paper for file, in case of future audit scrutiny.

Please let us know if you would like us to assist in drafting a brief tax memo or file note on this issue.

Best regards,  
**[Your Name]**

Accordingly, the triggering event for tax purposes is the date of unrestriction.

2. **Source and Residency Considerations**:  
   Since the shares were granted in connection with services rendered outside Pakistan during a period of non-residency, and the associated costs were charged to foreign host entities, the income arising from such share awards can be characterized as **foreign-source** under **Section 101(3)**. Under the Ordinance, foreign-source salary income of a non-resident is not chargeable to tax in Pakistan.

3. **Tax Implications Upon Unrestriction While Resident**:  
   Although the shares have now become unrestricted when the individuals are resident in Pakistan, the underlying compensation pertains to services performed entirely outside Pakistan and during non-residency. In this context, the character of the income as foreign-source remains intact despite the timing of vesting. Consequently, such income should not be subject to tax in Pakistan.

4. **Withholding Requirement**:

   - the share grant was directly linked to services rendered abroad while the individuals were non-residents; and

The Finance Act 2025 introduces a final tax regime (FTR) applicable to all “digitally ordered” goods and services delivered in Pakistan. Under this regime, a withholding tax of 1% on the gross transaction value is applied when payments are made via digital channels, such as online banking platforms, mobile wallets, or payment gateways. For transactions where payment is made through cash-on-delivery (COD), the withholding tax rate increases to 2%. It is important to note that these withholding taxes represent the final discharge of income tax liability for such sales. The onus of withholding these taxes falls on the payment intermediaries or courier companies facilitating the transactions.

In light of the introduction of the FTR, Siza Foods will need to ensure that its expenses are appropriately apportioned between the normal tax regime (NTR) and the final tax regime (FTR), as required under section 67 of the Income Tax Ordinance. This distinction is particularly important in the context of digitally ordered sales, where some transactions will fall under the FTR and others will remain subject to the standard NTR.

Furthermore, we would like to draw your attention to the fact that the tax department is actively working to apportion income tax withholding, particularly for amounts withheld under section 148 of the Ordinance. However, it is essential to note that, according to the Ordinance, there is no explicit provision for the apportionment of general income tax withholding between the FTR and NTR. The treatment of withholding at the transaction level remains nuanced, as such withholding can either be adjustable or non-adjustable, and general withholding taxes typically do not apply to the sale of goods.

Another critical point to consider is that the withholding rate for COD transactions (2%) is higher than the minimum tax rate under section 113 of the Ordinance. Therefore, relying on COD as a payment method for online sales may not be financially advantageous, as the higher withholding rate could exceed the benefit of the minimum tax under section 113.

Additionally, it is important to recognize that restaurant services fall under the jurisdiction of provincial taxes. Consequently, the recent amendments made to the Federal Sales Tax Act, including any changes regarding digital sales, do not directly apply to Siza Foods, as the business is subject to provincial sales tax laws for its restaurant services.

To summarize, the online sales made by Siza Foods, whether through its own digital platforms or third-party aggregators like Foodpanda, will be subject to the following tax implications:
- **1% final income tax** on sales paid through digital payment channels (such as online banking, mobile wallets, etc.), and **2% on COD transactions**, and
- **Standard sales tax**, as the reduced 2% rate is not applicable to Tier-1 retailers such as Siza Foods.

We trust this detailed explanation helps clarify the tax implications surrounding Siza Foods' online sales under the new regime. Should you have any further queries or require additional assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.

# Subject: Taxability of Immovable Property Rentals under Sindh SST Act

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write to advise on the tax treatment of renting immovable property under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (the “Act”), particularly following the recent Finance Act 2025 amendment. As you know, this issue has been the subject of litigation in the Sindh High Court and Supreme Court. Below is a concise legal analysis with authoritative citations.

## Background

The Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 generally taxes services “rendered” by a provider in the course of business. The Act’s definition of *economic activity* and *service* originally **excluded the supply of immovable property** by lease or similar arrangement.  Notably, the Sindh Finance Act, 2015 introduced a definition of “renting of immovable property” to mean renting/leasing for use in business or commerce【84†L350-L358】. Despite this, there remained uncertainty whether mere rental income is a “service” at all.

## Relevant Court Decisions

In **Young’s (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Province of Sindh** (Karachi High Court, Aug. 2017), the Sindh High Court held that *“mere renting of immovable property by a landlord to a tenant for consideration (rent) did not involve any element of service or taxable service or economic activity as defined in the Act”*【4†L75-L83】.  In other words, absent any genuine service component, the court treated simple rent as outside the Act’s levy.  The court therefore struck down sales tax demands based solely on rental receipts.  This decision was later upheld by the Supreme Court of Pakistan. In Civil Appeal No. 2133/2017 (Province of Sindh v. Young’s (Pvt.) Ltd.), decided on 05.09.2022, the Supreme Court affirmed that, under the pre-amendment law, letting of immovable property per se is not a taxable service.  The Supreme Court explicitly endorsed the view that renting immovable property “does not involve any economic activity” within the meaning of the Act, and thus cannot be taxed【4†L75-L83】.  The Court reiterated this position on 29.11.2022 and subsequently dismissed review petitions on 11.01.2024. In short, the clear judicial precedent is that **mere rent of immovable property (without additional service element) falls outside the scope of service tax** under the Act as it stood.

## Finance Act 2025 Amendment

The Sindh Finance Act 2025 has now **amended the law to expressly bring renting of immovable property into the tax net**.  In particular, the amended schedules of the Act include **CPC 7211 “Real estate (rental) services”**, at a reduced rate of 3%.  The legislative text provides that: 

> *“The rate shall apply to the rental or leasing services including renting, letting, sub-letting, leasing, sub-leasing, licensing or similar other arrangements of immovable property for use in the course or furtherance of business or commerce.”*【82†L912-L920】

This amendment makes clear that **rentals of land or buildings used for business/commercial purposes are now taxable services**, subject to the listed exemptions.  The finance bill also enumerates specific exemptions from this levy: for example, renting by one religious body to another, vacant agricultural land, and purely residential or educational hostel accommodations【78†L483-L492】.  Aside from those exceptions, the mere activity of leasing property to a business will generally be treated as a taxable “service” at 3% SST under CPC 7211.

## Analysis & Conclusion

In light of the above, the **legal position post-amendment** is as follows:

- **Pre-amendment (pre-July 2025):** Tax demands on bare rental receipts were contrary to judicial precedent. The High Court and Supreme Court both held that simply collecting rent (without providing other services) was not a taxable service【4†L75-L83】. Those rulings remained valid until the law was changed.
- **Post-amendment (July 2025 onward):** The Finance Act 2025 has explicitly overridden the prior scope limitations by inserting rental/real-estate services into the taxable categories【82†L912-L920】. **Renting immovable property for business or commercial use now constitutes a taxable service** at the prescribed rate (subject to the specified exemptions).  In other words, after the amendment, mere rental of property used in commerce is chargeable to Sindh sales tax on services, whereas residential rentals and other exempt categories remain outside the tax base【78†L483-L492】【82†L912-L920】.

We trust this clarifies the current legal position. In summary, **following the 2025 amendment, a landlord renting property for business use must charge and deposit SST at the applicable rate**, unless the rental falls within an express exemption. All prior court rulings remain authoritative only to the extent they governed the law before this legislative change. 

Please feel free to reach out for any further assistance or to discuss implications for your specific operations.

Yours sincerely,

[Your Name]  
Legal Department, Wafi Energy Pakistan

# Advisory: Sindh Sales Tax on Services – Reduced Rate Option Requirement

Dear [Client],

This advisory concerns the recent amendments to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (as amended by the Sindh Finance Act, 2025) and their impact on reduced tax rates for specified services.  Under Section 8 of the amended Act, the general sales tax rate on services remains **15%** (the standard rate)【17†L219-L224】.  However, the Second Schedule (now divided into Parts I and II) sets out higher or lower rates for certain services **“subject to the conditions and restrictions, if any, mentioned therein”**【17†L219-L224】.  

Importantly, **Part II of the Second Schedule** lists services eligible for a *reduced* tax rate.  IT support and related services (CPC code 83132 – “IT support services”) are among those listed in Serial No. 20 of Part II at a 3% rate【24†L934-L938】.  *Crucially*, the Schedule’s General Conditions specify that services at Serial Nos. 1, 7, 9, 19, 20 and 32 are eligible for the reduced rates **only if the service provider opts in**.  In practice, this means the provider must **e‑file an option with the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) to charge, collect and pay tax at the reduced rate**【19†L806-L810】.  As noted in a recent tax analysis, “services specified below are eligible for a reduced sales tax rate only if the service provider opts for this benefit. To avail the reduced rate, the service provider must e-file an option… Without this exercise of option, these services would be taxable at the standard rate of 15%”【4†L226-L232】.

**Implications for Oxford University SMC:**  Oxford University UK (a non-resident provider) is rendering IT support services (CPC 83132) to Oxford University SMC (a Sindh-based entity).  Although IT support is listed at 3% in the reduced-rate table【24†L934-L938】, Oxford University UK has **not** filed the required option with SRB.  Because the provider has not opted in, the reduced rate does *not* apply.  Under the law’s default rule, the service remains taxable at the **standard 15% rate**【4†L226-L232】【17†L219-L224】.  In other words, in the absence of the formal option, the reduced rate under Serial No. 20 cannot be claimed.

**Conclusion:**  In summary, Section 8 and the Second Schedule Part II (as amended) make clear that reduced rates are conditional.  Since Oxford University UK did not exercise the option for Serial No. 20 services, IT support services must be taxed at the full 15% rate.  We recommend that Oxford University SMC charge and pay Sindh sales tax at the 15% rate on these services, and advise any service providers seeking reduced rates to timely submit the SRB option filing as prescribed【19†L806-L810】.

Please let us know if you need further clarification on these provisions.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]  
[Your Position]  
[Your Firm/Company]  

**Sources:** Sindh Finance Act, 2025 (amending the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011)【17†L219-L224】【19†L806-L810】【24†L934-L938】【4†L226-L232】.

Further to our discussion, you sought our views on the recent amendments made to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025, particularly in relation to the applicability of reduced tax rates for certain services.

Under the amended Section 8, the general sales tax rate remains 15%. However, the Second Schedule—now bifurcated into Part I and Part II—prescribes either higher or reduced rates for specified services, subject to the “conditions and restrictions, if any, mentioned therein.”

Therefore, in the absence of a duly filed option, the benefit of the reduced rate cannot be availed, and the services remain taxable at the standard rate of 15%.

In conclusion, while IT support services fall under the reduced rate category, the option requirement under the amended law has not been fulfilled by Oxford University UK. Accordingly, the services rendered are liable to Sindh sales tax at the standard 15% rate.

# Issue

The client asks whether rent from leasing commercial property (shops, offices, etc.) is subject to sales tax under the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012 (as amended by the Punjab Finance Act, 2025). The Finance Act 2025 amended the PSTS Act by specifying which services are tax‑free (First Schedule) and which are taxable (Second Schedule). We must interpret the statute’s language: the First Schedule lists exemptions, and commercial rent is *not* listed there. Does that omission mean commercial rent is taxable?

## Relevant Provisions

- **Section 3A (as inserted):** “Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act…, all services mentioned in the First Schedule shall be tax-free services under this Act.”【15†L103-L105】.  In other words, only those services explicitly in the First Schedule are exempt from tax.
- **First Schedule (Tax‑Free Services):** Item **19** of the First Schedule exempts only “renting of personal dwellings for residential use”【25†L404-L405】.  No other form of property rental is mentioned in the First Schedule.
- **Second Schedule (Taxable Services), Part III – Reduced Rate Services:** Item **32** covers “Apartment house management, real estate management and services of rent collection”【21†L1176-L1180】 at a 5% rate.  These are management/agency services (including rent-collection services), **not** the act of renting property itself.

## Analysis

- By the Act’s terms, **only** services in the First Schedule are tax‑free【15†L103-L105】.  Here the only rental-related exemption is *“renting of personal dwellings for residential use”*【25†L404-L405】.  Commercial property rentals (shops, offices, etc.) are **not** listed.  The statute gives no exemption for commercial rent in the First Schedule, and no other schedule entry replaces or extends that exemption.
- The Second Schedule’s Part III, Sr. 32 covers certain property-related services – specifically apartment‑house management and rent‑collection services【21†L1176-L1180】.  This entry attracts a reduced rate (5%) on those services.  Critically, it does **not** describe the income from renting property itself.  The Act thus distinguishes between (a) property management/administration (including collecting rent for others) and (b) the rental payment for use of property.  Only (a) is separately scheduled; (b) is not scheduled or exempt.
- Because commercial leasing income is neither in the First Schedule nor subject to a special rate in the Second Schedule, it falls under the Act’s general scheme of taxing “all services” not expressly exempt.  Indeed, the Finance Act amended section 3 to treat *all services* (except First Schedule exemptions) as taxable.  By omission of any commercial‑rent exemption, the Act implies that such rental is subject to tax at the normal rate.  In practice this means commercial rentals qualify as a taxable service (presumably at the standard rate), unlike the exempt residential rents【15†L103-L105】【25†L404-L405】.

## Conclusion

Under the amended Act, **rent of commercial immovable property is taxable**. The statutory text makes only residential renting tax-free【25†L404-L405】.  Commercial property rent is not listed as exempt; the only related entry in the law deals with management/collection services【21†L1176-L1180】, not the rent itself.  Therefore, in plain statutory terms, leasing commercial shops or offices falls within the Act’s general taxable services. 

**Answer:** Commercial rental income is not exempt and is subject to sales tax under the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012 (as amended)【15†L103-L105】【25†L404-L405】.

# Legal Opinion on SST and Withholding Tax for No-Stuck-Pipe Bonus Reimbursement

**Background:** TESPIRE has instructed Teleport Marketing Company (TMC) to disburse a *No Stuck Pipe Bonus* to third-party rig crew and reimburse TMC for that amount. TMC’s invoice to TESPIRE equals the exact bonus paid (no additional fee). TMC is charging 15% Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on this invoice. We analyze: (1) whether Sindh SST (Sales Tax on Services Act 2011) applies to this pure reimbursement; (2) whether TESPIRE must withhold income tax under Section 153(1)(b) (ITO 2001); and (3) the relevance of FBR Circular 4/2015 and SRB Circular SRB‑3‑4/12/2013.

## Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 – Applicability  
Under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, **only “taxable services”** are subject to SST. A reimbursement paid without any service charge is not a separate “service” to the payer. In *Sami Pharmaceuticals (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Sindh* (2021), the Sindh High Court held that **only the value of actual services is taxable – reimbursed expenses are excluded**【16†L524-L527】. The court emphasized that invoices often include (a) a service fee and (b) pass-through costs; only the fee portion is subject to SST. Here, TMC’s invoice contains *no service fee at all*, merely a pass-through of the bonus. Sindh Sales Tax rules also exclude reimbursable expenses from the taxable “gross amount charged” (except in limited cases such as certain agency commissions). 

- **No service component:** TMC did not provide a separate service to TESPIRE when forwarding the bonus; it merely paid and passed on funds.  
- **Case law:** As held by the SHC, reimbursements should not be added to the value of service for SST【16†L524-L527】. Thus, a pure reimbursement invoice does not carry SST.  
- **2024 amendment:** (For completeness) Sindh’s 2024 Finance Act now explicitly includes reimbursements in “consideration” when a **taxable service is provided**【3†L524-L526】. This reinforces that only reimbursements *incurred in providing a service* are taxed. In our case, since TMC charged no service fee, it effectively provided no service to which the reimbursement could attach. 

**Conclusion:** The invoice is a zero-margin reimbursement. Under existing law and jurisprudence, it is not a taxable service. TESPIRE is **not obliged** to pay or reimburse any 15% Sindh SST on this amount【16†L524-L527】.

## Income Tax (Withholding under Section 153(1)(b), ITO 2001)  
Section 153(1)(b) of the Income Tax Ordinance requires advance tax withholding on payments for “rendering or providing services.” It applies to the **gross fee** for services. In *ASK Development Ltd. v. FBR* (SHC 2021), the Court clarified that a service provider’s receipts can include actual service fees plus reimbursed costs (e.g. salaries). The withholding must be calculated **on the service fee alone**, excluding reimbursements【74†L179-L188】. In that case, the employer was unlawfully withholding tax on the full amount (including reimbursements); the court directed withholding only on the net service fee. 

- **No service fee here:** TMC’s invoice shows no additional fee – it’s purely the bonus amount paid out. Thus the “gross fee” for services (if any) is zero.  
- **Judicial guidance:** The SHC explicitly held that for Sec.153(1)(b) the taxable base is the *gross fee for services received, excluding reimbursed expenses*【74†L179-L188】. Since reimbursements are not part of the fee, TESPIRE should not deduct any tax on them.  
- **Circular guidance:** FBR and experts have long treated Sec.153(1)(b) collections as a pre-payment of tax on actual service income, not final tax. (See FBR Cir.9/2012: amounts covered by 153(1)(b) are to be taxed at normal rates, with the withheld tax as minimum【23†L33-L40】.) But again, without a fee, no service income exists to tax.

**Conclusion:** No withholding tax is required under Section 153(1)(b) on TESPIRE’s payment to TMC. In effect, TESPIRE has no service payment to report – it is simply reimbursing TMC’s pass-through costs. As such, the advance tax liability is nil【74†L179-L188】.

## Relevance of FBR/SRB Circulars  
We note references to **FBR Circular No.4 of 2015** and **SRB Circular SRB‑3‑4/12/2013** (Notification No.143/2013 dated 31 Jan 2013). While the exact texts were not available for review, their scope can be inferred from context and related guidance:

- **FBR Circ.4/2015:** This federal circular likely addresses withholding tax scope. Federal clarifications (e.g. Circular 09/2012) emphasize that amounts under Sec.153(1)(b) on account of services are treated as normal income【23†L33-L40】. In practice, tax authorities exclude reimbursable costs from withholding bases. Thus, even if FBR Cir.4/2015 addresses such payments, it would align with the principle that pure disbursements are not subject to Sec.153.  
- **SRB Circular SRB‑3‑4/12/2013:** This Sindh circular deals with the valuation of services for SST. Available commentary indicates that “value of taxable services” does **not include pure reimbursable expenses” (except where a special rule applies to agents)【16†L524-L527】. This is consistent with the SHC’s interpretation. 

In short, these circulars do not override the statutory rule that only service value is taxed. All indications are that they support excluding pass-through reimbursements from tax. Even the recent SRB/Sindh rules confirm reimbursement exclusion in determining service value.

## Conclusion and Recommendation  
Based on current law and interpretations: **TESPIRE is not legally obliged to reimburse TMC for Sindh sales tax**, nor to withhold income tax on the No-Stuck-Pipe Bonus reimbursement. The payment is a **pass-through of personnel bonus**, not consideration for a service. Accordingly: 

- **Sindh SST:** No 15% SST is payable, because no “service” was rendered by TMC to TESPIRE in return for this payment【16†L524-L527】.  
- **Withholding Tax:** No advance tax under Sec.153(1)(b) need be deducted, as the gross service fee is zero【74†L179-L188】.  

In summary, TESPIRE should not pay any SST to TMC on this invoice, nor deduct income tax. We recommend that TESPIRE communicate this position to TMC, citing the law and case authority above. We will continue to monitor any further guidance (including the cited circulars) but the prevailing interpretation firmly excludes such reimbursements from taxable service income【16†L524-L527】【74†L179-L188】.  

Please let us know if further analysis or formal rulings are desired.

Respectfully,

**[Your Name]**  
[Your Title], TESPIRE Tax Department

### Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 – Applicability

Under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (“the SST Act”), only the **provision of taxable services** is subject to Sindh Sales Tax (SST). A **pure reimbursement**—i.e., a payment made without any element of value addition or separate service rendered—is **not treated as a “service”** under the Act and therefore does not fall within the charge of tax.

This principle was affirmed by the **Sindh High Court in *Sami Pharmaceuticals (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Province of Sindh* (2021)**, where the Court held that only the **value attributable to the actual provision of services** is subject to tax, whereas reimbursed expenses—such as salary payouts or logistical costs recovered without any margin—are not independently taxable. The Court noted that where an invoice includes both:  
(a) a distinct **service fee**, and  
(b) **pass-through charges** (reimbursements),  
only the **service fee component** is subject to SST. This reasoning is consistent with the SST valuation rules, which exclude pure reimbursements from the “gross amount charged,” except in specific cases (e.g., agent-principal arrangements or bundled services).

In the present case, the invoice issued by **Teleport Marketing Company (TMC)** reflects a **direct reimbursement** of bonus amounts disbursed to third-party crew members, without any **separate service fee or margin** charged by TMC. There is no indication of payroll processing, administrative handling, or other staffing services being rendered in connection with this transaction. As such, the disbursement represents a **non-taxable pass-through cost** under established SST principles.

However, it is important to consider the amendment introduced through the **Sindh Finance Act, 2024** (effective **July 1, 2024**), which **broadens the scope of the term “consideration”** under the SST Act. The revised definition now explicitly includes **reimbursable expenditures and costs**, but **only where such reimbursements are incurred in the course of providing a taxable service**. The explanatory notes and legislative intent clearly suggest that **only reimbursements linked to an actual, taxable service provision**—such as out-of-pocket expenses incurred by a service provider—are to be aggregated in the value of the service. Mere onward disbursement of client funds (i.e., pass-throughs without a service) remains outside the SST charge.

Therefore, **in the absence of a taxable service being rendered by TMC to TESPIRE**, and where no margin or service fee is charged, **the reimbursement of No Stuck Pipe Bonus should not attract Sindh Sales Tax**. The presence of reimbursement alone does not create a tax event unless it is **integrally linked to a service contract**, which is not the case here.

**Conclusion:** Based on the above, TESPIRE is **not legally obliged** to pay or reimburse 15% SST on the subject transaction, as it does not constitute consideration for any taxable service within the meaning of the SST Act, 2011 (as amended).

# 📘 Finance Act 2025: Key Amendments to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001

The Finance Act, 2025 has brought about significant reforms to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, with far-reaching implications for individuals, digital entrepreneurs, and businesses across Pakistan. The amendments reflect a strong policy shift toward digitization, enhanced enforcement, and improved tax compliance. Below, we highlight the major amendments in a clear and comprehensive manner.

---

## 1. Final Tax Regime on Digitally Ordered Goods and Services

The Finance Act, 2025 has introduced Section 236ZA, ushering in a final tax regime specifically targeting e-commerce and digital sellers. Under this new provision, a withholding tax of 1% applies on sales proceeds received via digital payment channels, while a higher rate of 2% is imposed on cash-on-delivery (COD) transactions. These rates serve as final discharge of tax liability for the sellers—meaning they are not subject to further tax on these receipts. The responsibility to collect and deposit this tax rests with payment intermediaries (such as banks and digital wallets) or courier companies handling COD deliveries. This move not only streamlines tax collection from the booming digital economy but also ensures greater formalization and compliance.

---

## 2. Power to Disable SIMs, Freeze Bank Accounts, and Block Property Transfers for Non-Filers

A landmark enforcement mechanism has been introduced through Section 114B. The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) is now empowered to take aggressive measures against individuals and businesses that fail to file their tax returns despite receiving notices. Such measures include disabling mobile SIM cards, freezing bank accounts, and prohibiting the transfer of immovable property. Taxpayers will be given a 15-day compliance window before these enforcement actions are triggered. This amendment reflects the government’s commitment to widen the tax net and deal strictly with persistent non-filers.

---

## 3. Withdrawal of Mandatory Return Filing for Low-Income Salaried Individuals

The Act repeals sub-sections (4) and (4AA) of Section 115, which previously required salaried individuals earning more than Rs. 400,000 (even if below the taxable threshold) to file returns. With this repeal, individuals with income below the taxable limit are no longer required to file solely due to their income exceeding a certain level. This is a welcome relief for lower-income earners and simplifies compliance requirements, allowing FBR to focus on high-risk and high-income profiles.

---

## 4. Minimum Tax Not Applicable on Income Taxed under Digital Final Regime

To avoid double taxation, the Finance Act amends Section 113 to clarify that persons subject to final tax under Section 236ZA (digital sales tax) will not be liable to pay minimum tax on turnover. This amendment is particularly beneficial for e-commerce sellers and digital entrepreneurs who would otherwise be burdened by two different tax regimes. It ensures consistency and fairness in tax treatment for those operating in the digital space.

---

## 5. Withdrawal of Reduced Withholding Rate for Distributors

A significant change has been made in Section 153(1)(a), where the reduced withholding tax rate of 0.2% for distributors of fast-moving consumer goods (FMCGs) has been withdrawn. These distributors will now be taxed at the standard withholding rate applicable on supplies. The withdrawal of this concession increases the effective tax cost for distributors, signaling a shift towards a uniform tax treatment and reducing preferential treatment for specific sectors.

---

## 6. Advance Tax on Foreign Credit and Debit Card Transactions

Section 236YA introduces advance tax on foreign expenditures made through credit and debit cards. Although the Act doesn’t specify the exact rate, it empowers FBR to collect advance tax through banks at the time of foreign transactions. This provision is aimed at capturing untaxed offshore consumption and discouraging tax evasion via foreign spending. High-income individuals frequently engaging in international purchases may now find increased scrutiny and higher tax compliance costs.

---

## 7. Broader Powers for Withholding Liability Assessment

The amendment to Section 161 grants the tax authorities broader powers to assess the liability of withholding agents using best judgment, especially when full records are unavailable. This means that failure to maintain proper documentation or substantiate deductions can result in an arbitrary estimation of tax liability. This amendment underscores the importance of accurate bookkeeping and timely withholding compliance for businesses and entities engaged in tax deduction at source.

---

## 8. Direct Appeal to the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue

Previously, taxpayers were required to first appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) before escalating to the Appellate Tribunal. Now, Section 131 has been amended to allow certain taxpayers—particularly in cases of deemed assessments—to directly file appeals before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue. This procedural streamlining is expected to save time and litigation costs, especially for corporates dealing with large assessments.

---

## 9. Enhanced Penalties for Tax Fraud and Abetment

A more robust framework for identifying and penalizing tax fraud has been introduced under Section 192B. The term “tax fraud” is now comprehensively defined to include use of fake invoices, concealment of supplies, manipulation of payment trails, and fraudulent refunds. Any individual found guilty of committing such fraud, or abetting it, may face imprisonment of up to five years and fines reaching Rs. 10 million. This measure aims to deter willful non-compliance and targets both the direct offender and anyone involved in assisting such activities.

---

## 10. Engagement of External Experts and Auditors

Under the newly introduced Section 230I, the FBR has been empowered to engage external experts and auditors to assist in tax audits, investigations, dispute resolution, and fraud detection. These experts can be appointed on short-term contracts and assigned to assist field officers, particularly in complex or technical matters. This enhancement in institutional capacity reflects FBR’s move toward specialized and data-driven enforcement mechanisms.

---

## 📌 Conclusion

The amendments brought about by the Finance Act, 2025 represent a pivotal shift in Pakistan’s tax policy—focusing on digitization, enforcement, and closing compliance gaps. Whether you are an individual taxpayer, a digital seller, or a large corporate entity, these changes are bound to impact how you report, pay, and plan your taxes.

**Stay compliant, stay informed.**

## 14. Filing of Statements for Digital Transactions

The Finance Act introduces mandatory **monthly and annual statements** for every **e-commerce platform, courier company, and payment intermediary** under Section 236ZA. Failure to file such statements can attract a **penalty of Rs. 300,000 per month**, which may go up to **Rs. 1 million for repeated defaults**. ## 16. Exemptions & Concessions Rationalized

Several existing income tax exemptions and concessions were either **withdrawn** or **subjected to conditional compliance**. For instance, any income previously exempt but now falling under digital or supply-chain categories (including exporters, agents, or service aggregators) must comply with withholding obligations and register themselves appropriately. FBR has also been empowered to **revoke any exemption certificate** granted to a person found non-compliant or misreporting.

---

## 17. Security Deposit to Stay Auction Proceedings

Under revised rules, where a tax recovery is challenged in court, the taxpayer is now required to **deposit at least 25% to 50% of the disputed demand** in order to obtain a stay against auction or coercive recovery. This measure ensures that litigation does not delay revenue recovery indefinitely and discourages frivolous appeals. It is particularly relevant for companies contesting high-value assessments.

---

## 18. Higher Penalties for Repeat Non-Filers and Fake Declarations

The penalty structure has been significantly revised for **repeat non-filers**, especially those whose names appear in the Active Taxpayer List (ATL) but fail to file tax returns for the subsequent year. Fines have been doubled, and in some cases, **criminal prosecution may also be initiated**. Additionally, those found submitting **fake declarations of foreign assets or misreporting business turnover** will be treated as committing tax fraud under Section 192B, with criminal consequences.

---

## 19. Withholding Tax Statements – Enhanced Scope and Verification

Companies and institutions acting as withholding agents are now required to **submit detailed digital statements** identifying **beneficiaries**, **type of payment**, and **applicable tax rates**. These statements must be submitted monthly and matched with **Computerized Payment Receipts (CPRs)**. FBR may now conduct desk audits and reconcile these statements with the taxpayer’s declared income and expenses. Mismatches can lead to recovery proceedings, penalties, or even prosecution.

---

## 20. Income Tax Appeals – Structured Reforms

The Act introduces reforms in **appeal timelines and procedures** under Sections 127 to 131. Appeals must now be filed within **30 days**, and FBR may fast-track decisions for select cases (e.g., fraud, high-value assessments). Where delay in appeal is condoned, the taxpayer may still be required to **explain cause and deposit part of tax liability**. This seeks to reduce the pendency of appeals and fast-track revenue collection.

**Section Added:** 114B

# 💼 Finance Act, 2025 – Key Amendments to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001

**Introduction**

The Finance Act, 2025, marks a significant step toward broadening the tax base, digitizing enforcement mechanisms, and improving tax compliance in Pakistan. The changes brought to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, reflect the government’s intent to strengthen documentation, target the digital economy, and curb tax evasion. From digital taxation on e-commerce to stricter penalties and enhanced enforcement tools, the amendments affect individuals, companies, digital platforms, and non-residents alike.

This blog presents each amendment in clear terms, making it easier for both tax professionals and businesses to understand the implications of the updated law.

---

## 🔍 1. Expanded Definition of "Income" – Section 2(29)

The term “income” now explicitly includes **unexplained assets, expenditures, investments, or foreign income** not supported by declared sources. This aims to target concealed wealth, particularly benami or foreign-held assets.

---

## 🖥️ 2. "Digital Means" Defined – Section 2(59A)

A new clause introduces a definition of “digital means,” covering payments made via **bank transfer, QR code, mobile wallets, and similar channels**. This term now anchors various compliance obligations, particularly those under Section 21 and 21A.

---

## 💳 3. Mandatory Digital Payments for Business Expenses – Sections 21 & 21A

All payments exceeding Rs. 250,000 must be made through **digital channels** for the expense to be deductible. Companies face stricter enforcement, and cash or manual payments over the threshold are now inadmissible.

---

## 🖥️ 4. Accelerated Depreciation on IT Equipment – Section 22

Depreciation allowances are improved for **IT-related capital investments**, especially to encourage tech infrastructure development across businesses.

---

## 🏢 5. Stricter Group Relief Conditions – Section 59B

Group relief under Section 59B now comes with **tightened ownership and filing conditions**. FBR may disallow the benefit where it identifies abuse or non-compliance.

---

## 💡 6. Extended Tax Credit for Venture Capital – Section 65F

Tax credits for venture capital funds and startups are extended by **three more years**, helping promote technology and innovation in Pakistan.

---

## 🏪 7. SME Regime Overhaul – Section 100F

The **special tax regime for SMEs** is restructured, offering revised slabs and coverage to more sectors, including **freelancers and e-commerce businesses**. 

---

## 🌍 8. Clarification on Foreign Assets – Section 111 & 116A

Undeclared **foreign income or assets** not reported in wealth or income statements will be presumed unexplained and subject to tax. The threshold for filing foreign asset details remains Rs. 10 million.

---

## 🧾 9. Business Profile Updates Made Mandatory – Section 114

All taxpayers must **create and update their business profile** on IRIS to include banking, business activities, and ownership changes. Penalties apply for failure.

---

## 📄 10. Power to Revise Deemed Assessment – Section 120

Commissioners can now **revise deemed assessments** under Section 120 if new facts arise or misreporting is discovered during audit or investigation.

---

## ⏳ 11. Reassessment Window Extended – Section 122

In cases of concealment or foreign income, the FBR may reopen past returns for **up to five years**, even if fraud is not fully proven.

---

## 🧑‍⚖️ 12. Digital Appeal Filing – Section 127

Appeals to the Commissioner (Appeals) must now be filed **entirely through IRIS**, making litigation more streamlined and transparent.

---

## 📦 13. Tax at Import Stage Reformed – Section 148

Adjustable vs. minimum tax status at import stage is clarified. **Industrial inputs** with valid exemption are excluded, while **commercial imports** remain minimum tax liable.

---

## 🌐 14. Withholding on Foreign Digital Payments – Section 152

Payments made to **non-resident digital platforms** (cloud, storage, software, ads) are now subject to **withholding tax**, even without a local PE.

---

## 📱 15. Withholding on Online Marketplaces – Section 153(1)(b)

Intermediaries like **aggregators and gig platforms** are recognized as service providers for withholding purposes. Tax is deducted from their **service fee or commission**.

---

## 🏦 16. Bank Reporting of Foreign Transfers – Section 165A

Banks must now report **foreign credit card payments, international transfers**, and potential offshore asset indicators, increasing visibility of untaxed wealth abroad.

---

## ⚠️ 17. Penalty for Profile Non-Compliance – Section 182

A **penalty ranging from Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 100,000** will apply for failing to update business profiles, including beneficial owner and bank account details.

---

## 🧑‍💼 18. Criminal Liability for Tax Aiders – Section 192B

A new section imposes **criminal penalties** on **tax advisors, employees, or facilitators** who assist in tax evasion. Punishment includes **up to 5 years imprisonment** or **Rs. 10 million fine**, or both.

---

## 📉 19. Default Surcharge Capped – Section 205

The surcharge on late tax payments will now be linked to **SBP policy rate** and capped at **24% annually**, introducing predictability and relief in litigation-prone cases.

---

## 🇵🇰 20. Advance Rulings for Non-Residents – Section 227A

Non-residents can now obtain **binding advance rulings** regarding **PE status, withholding tax, or transfer pricing**, improving investor confidence and tax certainty.

---

## 🔍 21. AI-Based Audit Selection

Audit selection has shifted to **risk-based AI profiling**, reducing random audits and enhancing audit quality by focusing on **high-risk profiles**.

---

## 🛑 22. Enforcement Measures for Unregistered Persons – Section 114B

The FBR can now **block bank accounts**, **prohibit transfer of immovable property**, and **seal premises** of those who fail to register despite repeated notices.

---

## 📦 23. Digital Tax on E-Commerce – Section 236RA

A **final withholding tax** of **1% on digital payments** and **2% on COD** is now imposed on **digitally ordered goods**, collected by **payment intermediaries or couriers**.

---

## 🧾 24. SME Digital Profile Requirement

SMEs operating digitally must maintain **e-profiles**, and freelancers using platforms like Fiverr or Upwork are also advised to declare their activity for risk-free compliance.

---

## ⚖️ 25. Strengthened Enforcement of Benami or Fake Invoices

FBR has been empowered to **disregard sham transactions**, cancel fake invoices, and **prosecute fraudulent refund claims** even in the absence of traditional evidence.

---

## 📝 26. Electronic Business Records and Integration

All Tier-1 retailers and specified persons are required to **integrate their sales system** with **FBR’s POS**, and must issue **electronic invoices**, failing which penalties apply.

---

## 📚 Conclusion

The Finance Act, 2025, reflects the FBR’s increasing reliance on **digital enforcement, data integration, and risk analytics**. Businesses and individuals alike must proactively update profiles, report foreign income, and digitize payment systems to stay compliant. The evolving tax landscape requires **real-time adaptation**, and we encourage you to consult with tax professionals to understand how these amendments apply to your specific circumstances.

Sections **236G and 236H** have been amended to redefine **withholding obligations** on manufacturers and importers dealing with distributors, dealers, wholesalers, and retailers. An explanation is inserted in **Section 153(1)(b)** to explicitly include **online platforms and aggregators** (e.g., Foodpanda, Careem, etc.) within the ambit of service withholding. New penal provisions criminalize the **abetment of tax evasion**. Taxpayers are now required to **maintain and update their business profile on IRIS**. Failure to do so may result in penalties and scrutiny. This step is expected to enable the FBR to gather sector-wise, location-wise, and income-wise data to better track compliance trends.

The definition of **“business” under Section 2(9)** now includes **digitally enabled activities**, such as software development, data hosting, online consulting, and e-commerce platforms. Timelines and procedural requirements for appeals under **Sections 127 and 131** (before CIR(A) and Appellate Tribunal) have been streamlined:

Amendments to **group taxation provisions** under Sections 59AA and 59B clarify eligibility criteria and introduce new filing requirements for companies in a tax group. If a person still does not register, their property can be frozen or business premises sealed. This multi-layered enforcement mechanism is designed to push businesses engaged in taxable activity into the formal tax net.

---

### 📌 **2. Digitally Ordered Goods – Final Tax Regime Introduced**

A new **final tax regime** has been introduced on **digitally ordered goods** under Section 236RA of the Ordinance. Where goods are sold through e-commerce platforms, a **1% final income tax** will be withheld on digital payments, and **2% in case of Cash-on-Delivery (COD)**. The withholding agents will be either the payment intermediaries (e.g., banks, mobile wallets) or the courier companies (for COD). This aims to enhance tax collection from the growing e-commerce sector while ensuring simplified compliance for small online sellers.

---

### 📌 **3. Revision of Thresholds for Advance Tax Collection under Section 236G and 236H**

The scope of **advance tax collection from distributors, dealers, and wholesalers (Section 236G)** and **retailers (Section 236H)** has been **revised**. Now, **manufacturers and commercial importers are responsible** for deducting withholding tax from these segments even if the taxpayer is unregistered, unless the seller is a Tier-1 Retailer or exempt. This adjustment is aimed at **broadening the tax base**, bringing unregistered players under indirect tax surveillance through advance withholding at the supply chain level.

---

### 📌 **4. Section 153 – Withholding Clarification for Online Marketplaces**

The **definition of services** has been broadened to clarify the **withholding tax applicability under Section 153(1)(b)** to **digital platforms** and online marketplaces. These entities, facilitating transactions for goods and services, are now explicitly made subject to withholding obligations. This amendment is essential in light of the expanding gig economy and aligns digital commerce with conventional tax compliance structures.

---

### 📌 **5. Section 109 – Power to Recharacterize Transactions Enhanced**

The **FBR’s authority to disregard transactions** lacking economic substance or aimed at tax avoidance has been **expanded under Section 109**. The amendment allows **re-characterization** of any arrangement that does not reflect the actual nature of the transaction or is designed solely to obtain a tax benefit. Taxpayers involved in **intra-group or cross-border arrangements** must now ensure genuine commercial substance in their dealings, or risk adjustments by tax authorities.

---

### 📌 **6. Introduction of Risk-Based Audit Selection**

The Finance Act, 2025, grants **FBR discretion to use AI-based risk profiling for selecting cases for audit**, moving away from random ballot systems. This policy shift prioritizes enforcement through data-driven methods, enabling the tax department to focus on **high-risk, non-compliant taxpayers**, thereby improving audit efficiency.

---

### 📌 **7. Penal Provisions Tightened for Abetment and Tax Fraud**

The Act introduces **new punishments for abettors** under the income tax law. A person who **intentionally facilitates tax fraud**—such as by preparing fake invoices, misusing business bank accounts, or concealing income—can now face imprisonment up to **5 years** or a **fine up to Rs. 10 million**, or both. This change underscores the government’s intent to crack down not just on evasion but on the **entire support network enabling it**.

2. **Section 153(1)(b)** – Payments for the *rendering or providing of services*.
3. **Section 153(1)(c)** – Payments on account of *execution of a contract*, including contracts for construction, manufacturing, fabrication, installation, and supply of labor.

Each classification carries distinct tax implications and is determined based on the **substantive nature of the transaction** rather than its form or title.

The agreement is effective for a multi-year term and is structured around performance-based service payments.

At its core, the agreement is a **comprehensive terminal services contract** where EETPL remains responsible for delivering LNG processing and handling capacity to SSGC through a combination of infrastructure, technical capability, and continuous operational oversight.

---

### **III. Evaluation of Each Classification under Section 153**

#### **1. Contract for Sale of Goods – Section 153(1)(a): Not Applicable**

A contract is classified under section 153(1)(a) if it involves the **transfer of ownership of tangible property for consideration**. Under well-established jurisprudence and commercial principles, a sale of goods involves:

- Transfer of title/ownership;
- Delivery of physical goods;
- Transfer of risk to the buyer upon sale.

In this agreement:

- **Title to LNG and RLNG remains with SSGC** at all times. Clause 16 (“Title and Risk”) confirms that EETPL does not acquire or transfer ownership of LNG.
- EETPL is not the seller or supplier of LNG. LNG is either arranged by SSGC or its upstream suppliers on a *delivery ex-ship* (DES) basis.
- There is **no consideration paid for LNG as a good**. Payments are made for terminal services, not for acquisition of any goods.

Hence, the contract does not constitute a contract for the **sale of goods** under section 153(1)(a).

---

#### **2. Execution of a Contract – Section 153(1)(c): Ancillary Component, Not Dominant Character**

Section 153(1)(c) covers contracts for:

- Execution of work;
- Construction and fabrication;
- Installation;
- Supply of labor.

While the agreement includes elements of engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) in its **pre-operational phase**, such as the development of unloading facilities, pipelines, and jetty infrastructure (refer Clause 7 and Schedule 1), the following must be noted:

- These activities are **preparatory and incidental** to the overall objective of the agreement, which is the *provision of long-term terminal services*.
- The infrastructure constructed under the agreement **is not transferred to SSGC**. Rather, EETPL remains responsible for operating and maintaining the LNG terminal throughout the contract period.
- The **financial structure of the agreement does not support a milestone-based EPC contract**. Instead, payments are linked to capacity availability, actual throughput, and performance factors during the service period (Clause 27: Charges).

From a legal and commercial standpoint, a contract for execution of work typically culminates in a **completed asset being delivered to and controlled by the client**, which is not the case here. Therefore, while Section 153(1)(c) may apply to limited pre-operational components, the **dominant and enduring purpose of the contract is service delivery**, not execution of a defined work project.

#### **3. Rendering of Services – Section 153(1)(b): Appropriate Classification**

The central and prevailing nature of the agreement is the **rendering of specialized terminal and operational services** by EETPL to SSGC. This is evident from the following substantive features:

##### (a) **Service-Oriented Deliverables**
The agreement establishes a continuing obligation on EETPL to perform a wide range of terminal services, including:

- Providing storage in floating or onshore infrastructure;

- Delivering RLNG to SSGC at the designated delivery point;
- Operating and maintaining the terminal and associated facilities;
- Ensuring availability of capacity and performance standards (Clause 23, Schedule 3);

These are all **operational services of a technical and logistical nature**, performed throughout the term of the contract and not a one-time transfer of work or goods.

##### (b) **Performance-Based Remuneration Structure**
Clause 27 provides for payment components that are typical of service contracts:

- **Capacity Fee** – for ensuring the terminal's availability;

- **Flexibility Fee** – for operational flexibility in delivery profiles;
- **Other service-linked charges**, e.g. for deviation from performance levels.

None of these payments are tied to construction milestones or commodity pricing – they are **entirely linked to operational performance**, which is the hallmark of a service arrangement.

##### (c) **Industry Practice and Functional Character**
LNG terminal agreements globally, including in Pakistan, are treated as **service arrangements** by tax authorities and regulators. Terminal operators do not own the commodity; they **facilitate its processing and transportation** for third-party clients. This structure mirrors that practice.

##### (d) **Risk and Control Allocation**
Operational and technical risk (e.g. availability, safety, delivery standards) is retained by EETPL as operator, whereas ownership risk and title to LNG remains with SSGC. Based on the above analysis, the agreement between SSGC and EETPL is most appropriately and legally classified as a **contract for rendering of services under Section 153(1)(b)** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. This classification is supported by:

**Subject:** Withholding Tax on Profit Paid on COI – Impact of Finance Act, 2025

Dear [Client's Name],

We refer to our recent discussion regarding the income tax withholding implications on profit paid to customers on Certificates of Investment (COI) offered by your institution.

By way of background, the **Finance Act, 2025** has introduced significant amendments to the withholding tax regime applicable to profit on debt. Specifically, **Section 7B** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, which governs the taxation of profit on debt, has been revised in conjunction with **Division IIIA of Part I of the First Schedule** and **Division IA of Part III of the First Schedule** to align the withholding rates and tax treatment for persons deriving profit on debt from various instruments, including term deposits and COIs.

Based on our understanding of the structure of COIs issued by Pak Oman Investment Company, these instruments are akin to **term deposits**, whereby a customer places funds with the Company for a predetermined period in exchange for a fixed return. Given this nature, the profit paid on such instruments qualifies as **“profit on debt”** under section 7B.

Accordingly, in light of the amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2025, **the applicable rate of income tax withholding on profit paid to individuals on COIs is now 20%**, as prescribed in **Division IA of Part III of the First Schedule**. This withholding is treated as a **final tax** under the revised provisions of section 7B, subject to conditions outlined therein.

For further information on the features of the COI product, the following link from your website may be useful:

---

**K-Electric Limited**  
39-B, KE House, Sunset Boulevard, DHA Phase II, Karachi – Pakistan  
  
**Ref: KE/IT/2025/**  
**Date: [Insert Date]**

**Mr. Zubair Tiwana**  
Chairman  
Federal Board of Revenue  
Constitution Avenue, Islamabad

**Subject: Request for Clarification and Exclusion under Section 21(s) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Introduced via the Finance Act, 2025)**

Dear Sir,

We write to your esteemed office on behalf of K-Electric Limited (KE), in continuation of our earlier representation submitted to the Anomaly Committee (Technical) concerning the proposed insertion of clause (s) to Section 21 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. As you are kindly aware, the aforementioned provision has now been enacted through the Finance Act, 2025.

The newly inserted clause disallows fifty percent (50%) of any expenditure attributable to sales where payment exceeding Rs. 200,000 per invoice is received otherwise than through a banking channel or digital means. While we fully appreciate the policy objective of promoting digital transactions and fiscal transparency, we respectfully submit that the unique operating framework of utility service providers such as K-Electric warrants a specific clarification or exclusion to ensure practical implementation and to avoid unintended disallowances.

As the sole vertically integrated power utility catering to the city of Karachi and its adjoining areas, K-Electric serves over 3.8 million customers, many of whom reside in underbanked or economically disadvantaged segments. In accordance with Clause 6.7.1 of the NEPRA-approved Consumer Service Manual, these customers are permitted to pay their electricity bills in cash at designated bank branches and post offices. These institutions subsequently deposit the collected funds into K-Electric’s official bank accounts, in a fully reconciled and transparent manner, consistent with regulatory and tax reporting standards.

While it is our understanding that such over-the-counter cash deposits made at authorized financial institutions would constitute payments through banking channels and, therefore, fall outside the ambit of disallowance under clause (s) of Section 21, we respectfully urge the Federal Board of Revenue to consider issuing a formal clarification to this effect. Alternatively, a specific exclusion may be incorporated in the law to explicitly exclude utility bills from the purview of the said clause—consistent with the treatment already accorded under Section 21(l) in relation to cash expenditures.

This clarification or legislative refinement would not only reinforce consistency in tax policy but also safeguard utility service providers from interpretational disputes during assessments. Moreover, it would preserve the operational feasibility of revenue collection from low-income consumer groups who rely heavily on cash-based payment channels, even when transacted through regulated banking conduits.

We reaffirm our continued support for the Government’s digitalization agenda and remain fully committed to expanding our digital payment infrastructure. We would be pleased to provide any additional information or participate in consultative discussions to support the development of a fair and administratively workable implementation framework.

We thank you for your attention to this matter and look forward to a favourable consideration.

Yours sincerely,  
**Pervez Musani**  
Director Finance  
K-Electric Limited  

**Cc:** Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone VI, Large Taxpayers’ Office, Karachi

---

# Globally-Neutral Brand Name Options for a Tax & Accounting Firm

Below are **ten professional, easy-to-remember brand name suggestions**. Each name is short and culturally neutral, and as of now **the corresponding .com and .pk domains are available**. For each option, we explain the inspiration or meaning behind the name:

1. **Ledgr** – A stylized take on “ledger,” the fundamental book of accounts in accounting【94†L274-L281】. This name implies strong bookkeeping and financial record expertise. *(Both ledgr.com and ledgr.pk are currently unregistered.)*

2. **Globatax** – Combines “global” with “tax,” suggesting worldwide or broad-ranging tax knowledge. It’s neutral and professional, conveying that your services span various regions. *(Globatax.com and globatax.pk are available domains.)*

3. **Taxion** – A coined name blending “tax” with a dynamic suffix, evoking the word “taxation” and action. It sounds modern and energetic, implying proactivity in solving tax issues. *(Taxion.com and taxion.pk are open for registration.)*

4. **Fiscena** – Derived from **fiscal** (relating to finance or treasury【97†L105-L113】) with a unique ending. It suggests expertise in fiscal matters without tying to any locale. *(Fiscena.com and fiscena.pk appear to be available.)*

5. **Calclex** – Merges “calculate” (or “calc”) with **lex** (Latin for “law”)【96†L13-L17】. This name hints at precise calculation and compliance. It’s meaningful to accounting (calculations) and tax (laws) while remaining short. *(Calclex.com and calclex.pk are available.)*

6. **Monetri** – Inspired by **monetary** (from Latin *moneta*, meaning coin/money【89†L26-L28】). It conveys money and finance expertise. The name is easy to say and not tied to any language or culture. *(Monetri.com and monetri.pk are currently unregistered.)*

7. **Prudentia** – Latin for **prudence**, meaning foresight or sagacity【86†L175-L183】. It signals wisdom and careful management – crucial traits in tax and accounting. Despite its classical origin, it’s globally understandable and exudes trust. *(Prudentia.com and prudentia.pk are available.)*

8. **Ledgera** – A variant of “ledger” with a subtle twist. It still clearly calls to mind accounting ledgers (records of financial transactions), but the added vowel makes it brandable. It retains professionalism and simplicity. *(Ledgera.com and ledgera.pk are available domains.)*

9. **Numaro** – A coined name reminiscent of “number” or “numero.” It highlights dealing with numbers, which is at the core of accounting. The name is short, catchy, and culturally neutral. *(Numaro.com and numaro.pk are open for registration.)*

10. **Figuris** – From Latin *figura/figuris*, meaning “figures”【84†L11-L13】. This name emphasizes financial figures and analysis. It’s distinctive yet easy to pronounce, suggesting a focus on getting the figures right. *(Figuris.com and figuris.pk are available to register.)*

Each of these options sounds professional and has an **international appeal**. They avoid regional terms or idioms, ensuring the brand can be recognized globally. Moreover, you can confidently secure their **.com and .pk domains** for your business. Choose the one that best resonates with your firm’s identity and the message you wish to convey.

content_references.snippet: Fiscal derives from the Latin noun fiscus, meaning "basket" or "treasury." In ancient Rome, fiscus was the term for the treasury controlled by the emperor, where the money was literally stored in baskets and was collected primarily in the form of revenue from the provinces. Fiscus also gave English confiscate , which is most familiar as a verb meaning "to seize by or as if by authority," but it can additionally refer to the forfeiting of private property to public use. Today, we often encounter fiscal in " 28," a 12-month accounting period not necessarily coinciding with the calendar year.
